questions.stem: A student asks why viruses are excluded from the traditional definition of living organisms, given that they carry genetic material and evolve over time. Which of the following best explains why viruses are not considered truly alive?

choices.label: A
choices.text: They are destroyed by ordinary environmental exposure

choices.label: B
choices.text: They are made only of lipid, with no protein at all

choices.label: C
choices.text: They are too small to be seen by any microscope

choices.label: D
choices.text: They cannot reproduce without taking over a host cell

choices.label: E
choices.text: They contain no genetic code of their own

explanation.summary: Viruses straddle the line between living and nonliving because they cannot replicate outside a host cell.
explanation.whyCorrect: Viruses are small particles of genetic code, lipids, and proteins that must commandeer a living cell's machinery to reproduce. Because they cannot reproduce on their own, they are not considered truly alive. Being nonliving does not keep them from being one of the greatest problems in modern medicine.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Non-enveloped viruses are in fact quite stable in the environment, so fragility is not the criterion.
whyWrongByChoice.B: All viruses have a protein coat called a capsid; the lipid envelope is the optional component.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Viruses are too small for light microscopes, but small size is not what excludes them from being alive.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Every virus carries a genome of either DNA or RNA; having no genetic code is not the issue.

questions.stem: A virus recovered from a contaminated countertop several days after it was deposited is found to have no lipid bilayer surrounding its capsid. Which of the following is most likely true of this virus?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It is readily inactivated by ethanol-based hand sanitizer

choices.label: B
choices.text: It must carry reverse transcriptase inside the virion

choices.label: C
choices.text: Its capsid is helical rather than icosahedral in shape

choices.label: D
choices.text: Its capsid is icosahedral and it is environmentally stable

choices.label: E
choices.text: Its genome must consist of double-stranded DNA

explanation.summary: All non-enveloped viruses are icosahedral and are stable in the environment.
explanation.whyCorrect: Capsids are either icosahedral or helical, and viruses lacking an envelope are always icosahedral. Without a lipid envelope to dry out or dissolve, these virions persist on surfaces, which is exactly why one was still recoverable days later.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Ethanol works by dissolving a lipid envelope, so naked viruses resist it rather than succumb to it.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Reverse transcriptase is the hallmark of retroviruses, not of non-enveloped viruses.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Helical capsids are found in enveloped viruses; a naked virus is icosahedral.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Envelope status says nothing about the genome; naked viruses may carry DNA or RNA.

questions.stem: Electron microscopy of a newly released virion shows a lipid bilayer studded with surface proteins surrounding the capsid. This lipid bilayer is most directly derived from which of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Lipid synthesized de novo by virally encoded enzymes

choices.label: B
choices.text: Membrane of the host cell from which it budded

choices.label: C
choices.text: Serum lipoproteins that adsorb onto the capsid surface

choices.label: D
choices.text: The peptidoglycan wall of a co-infecting bacterium

choices.label: E
choices.text: The protein capsid itself, which flattens into a sheet

explanation.summary: A viral envelope is a lipid bilayer taken from the host cell membrane.
explanation.whyCorrect: Some viruses are covered by an envelope, which is usually a remnant of cell membrane from the host cell. Newly assembled virions move to the cell membrane and form an envelope from it as they bud outward, which is how influenza and RSV acquire their envelopes.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Viruses take a membrane from the host rather than synthesizing bilayer lipid themselves.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The envelope is an organized bilayer acquired during budding, not adsorbed serum lipid.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Peptidoglycan is a bacterial cell wall polymer and is not part of any viral particle.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The capsid is a protein coat that sits inside the envelope; it is not a lipid structure.

questions.stem: A virology text groups the clinically important viruses into DNA viruses, RNA viruses, and retroviruses. Which of the following best describes the genome of the DNA virus group?

choices.label: A
choices.text: All DNA viruses carry their own RNA replicase enzyme

choices.label: B
choices.text: All DNA viruses package a segmented RNA genome

choices.label: C
choices.text: All DNA viruses use a single-stranded DNA genome

choices.label: D
choices.text: All use double-stranded DNA except parvovirus

choices.label: E
choices.text: Half use double-stranded and half single-stranded DNA

explanation.summary: DNA viruses use double-stranded DNA, with parvovirus the single-stranded exception.
explanation.whyCorrect: All DNA viruses use dsDNA except parvovirus, which is single stranded. Whatever the strandedness, the genome must first be transcribed into messenger RNA before viral replication can proceed.

whyWrongByChoice.A: RNA replicase is introduced by (−)ssRNA viruses, not by DNA viruses.
whyWrongByChoice.B: By definition DNA viruses use DNA, not RNA, as their genome.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Single-stranded DNA is the exception, seen with parvovirus, not the rule.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The split is far from even; dsDNA is the near-universal pattern among DNA viruses.

questions.stem: Almost all RNA viruses package a single-stranded RNA genome. Which of the following groups is the exception that uses double-stranded RNA?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Herpesviruses

choices.label: B
choices.text: Parvoviruses

choices.label: C
choices.text: Poxviruses

choices.label: D
choices.text: Reoviruses

choices.label: E
choices.text: Retroviruses

explanation.summary: Reoviruses are the double-stranded RNA exception among RNA viruses.
explanation.whyCorrect: Almost all RNA viruses use ssRNA, but reoviruses use dsRNA. These viruses introduce multiple RNA molecules that code for multiple proteins once inside the host cell.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Herpesviruses are dsDNA viruses known for establishing latent infections.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Parvovirus is the single-stranded DNA virus, not an RNA virus at all.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Poxviruses are dsDNA viruses, notable instead for replicating in the cytoplasm.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Retroviruses are (+)ssRNA viruses that carry reverse transcriptase, not dsRNA viruses.

questions.stem: The purified genome of a (+)ssRNA virus is added to a cell-free system containing ribosomes, transfer RNAs, and amino acids. Viral protein is produced with no intervening nucleic acid step. Which property of (+)ssRNA best explains this?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It carries a polymerase covalently attached to each end

choices.label: B
choices.text: It is a template that must first be copied into (−)ssRNA

choices.label: C
choices.text: It is double stranded and unwinds inside the ribosome

choices.label: D
choices.text: It is equivalent to mRNA and can be translated directly

choices.label: E
choices.text: It must be reverse transcribed into DNA before any use

explanation.summary: Sense, or (+)ssRNA, is equivalent to mRNA and is translated straight to protein.
explanation.whyCorrect: Single-stranded sense RNA has the same polarity as messenger RNA, so host ribosomes read it directly without forming an intermediate molecule. This is why only ribosomes and building blocks are needed for protein to appear in the system.

whyWrongByChoice.A: No attached polymerase is needed, since the host ribosome does the translating.
whyWrongByChoice.B: It is antisense (−)ssRNA that must first be copied into (+)ssRNA, not the reverse.
whyWrongByChoice.C: (+)ssRNA is single stranded by definition; dsRNA is the reovirus pattern.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Reverse transcription into DNA is the retroviral strategy and is not required here.

questions.stem: A (−)ssRNA virus uncoats inside a host cell. Before any viral protein can be produced, which of the following must occur?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Host DNA polymerase must copy the genome into cDNA

choices.label: B
choices.text: RNA replicase must copy the genome into (+)ssRNA

choices.label: C
choices.text: The genome must be carried into the nucleolus by importins

choices.label: D
choices.text: The genome must be cleaved into several smaller ssRNA segments

choices.label: E
choices.text: The genome must be integrated into host chromosomal DNA

explanation.summary: Antisense (−)ssRNA must be transcribed to (+)ssRNA by RNA replicase before translation.
explanation.whyCorrect: Most (−)ssRNA viruses introduce RNA replicase, also called RNA-dependent RNA polymerase, which forms (+)ssRNA from the antisense genome. That (+)ssRNA then behaves like mRNA and is translated into protein by host ribosomes.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Copying RNA into cDNA requires reverse transcriptase, which these viruses do not carry.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Most RNA viruses replicate in the cytoplasm; nuclear import is not the prerequisite.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Segmenting the genome is not a required step for protein production here.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Integration into the host genome is a retroviral step carried out by integrase.

questions.stem: A 57-year-old woman with metastatic pulmonary adenocarcinoma is enrolled in a trial of an antiviral agent that inhibits viral RNA replicase within infected cells. This drug would be expected to work best against which of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A double-stranded DNA virus

choices.label: B
choices.text: A double-stranded DNA-RT virus

choices.label: C
choices.text: A retrovirus that carries reverse transcriptase

choices.label: D
choices.text: A single-stranded DNA virus

choices.label: E
choices.text: An antisense single-stranded RNA virus

explanation.summary: RNA replicase is the enzyme (−)ssRNA viruses must introduce to make (+)ssRNA.
explanation.whyCorrect: A drug aimed at RNA replicase blocks the step in which antisense RNA is copied into (+)ssRNA. Without that copy the virus cannot produce the mRNA-equivalent it needs to code for viral components, so replication of a (−)ssRNA virus halts.

whyWrongByChoice.A: dsDNA viruses use host transcription machinery to make mRNA and need no RNA replicase.
whyWrongByChoice.B: dsDNA-RT viruses carry their own polymerase for RNA intermediates rather than RNA replicase.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Retroviruses depend on reverse transcriptase to make DNA from RNA, a different enzyme target.
whyWrongByChoice.D: ssDNA viruses replicate much as dsDNA viruses do, again without RNA replicase.

questions.stem: A 31-year-old man is newly diagnosed with HIV infection. Which enzyme carried within the HIV virion converts the viral RNA genome into a DNA copy?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Host RNA polymerase

choices.label: B
choices.text: Integrase

choices.label: C
choices.text: Neuraminidase

choices.label: D
choices.text: Reverse transcriptase

choices.label: E
choices.text: RNA replicase

explanation.summary: Retroviruses carry reverse transcriptase, which produces DNA from their RNA genome.
explanation.whyCorrect: HIV is a (+)ssRNA retrovirus. Reverse transcriptase transcribes its RNA into DNA, the reverse of the usual flow of genetic information, and the resulting DNA transcript is then read by the infected cell as if it were host DNA.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Host RNA polymerase transcribes DNA into RNA, the opposite of what is needed here.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Integrase inserts the DNA copy into the host genome after reverse transcription has occurred.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Neuraminidase is not the enzyme responsible for copying a retroviral genome.
whyWrongByChoice.E: RNA replicase makes (+)ssRNA from antisense RNA and is used by (−)ssRNA viruses.

questions.stem: After reverse transcriptase produces a DNA copy of the HIV genome, that DNA is inserted into the chromosome of the infected cell. Which viral enzyme performs this insertion?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Integrase

choices.label: B
choices.text: Neuraminidase

choices.label: C
choices.text: Peptidyl transferase

choices.label: D
choices.text: Reverse transcriptase

choices.label: E
choices.text: RNA replicase

explanation.summary: Integrase splices the reverse-transcribed viral DNA into the host genome.
explanation.whyCorrect: Retroviruses use reverse transcriptase to make DNA and then integrate that DNA into the host genome using integrase. Host machinery subsequently replicates the virus from the integrated DNA, which is why HIV becomes a permanent part of the infected cell.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Neuraminidase is not involved in inserting viral DNA into host chromosomes.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Peptidyl transferase is a ribosomal activity of protein synthesis, not of integration.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Reverse transcriptase performs the preceding step, producing the DNA copy from RNA.
whyWrongByChoice.E: RNA replicase forms (+)ssRNA from (−)ssRNA and plays no role in integration.

questions.stem: A virion has attached to a respiratory epithelial cell, has been taken into the cell, and has just shed its protein coat, releasing its nucleic acid and enzymes. Which step of the viral life cycle occurs next?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Assembly

choices.label: B
choices.text: Attachment

choices.label: C
choices.text: Penetration

choices.label: D
choices.text: Release

choices.label: E
choices.text: Replication

explanation.summary: The six steps proceed attachment, penetration, uncoating, replication, assembly, release.
explanation.whyCorrect: Shedding the protein coat is uncoating, the third step. Replication follows, in which viral nucleic acids, enzymes, and proteins are copied using host machinery, before the new components are assembled into virions.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Assembly of new virions comes after the components have been replicated.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Attachment to a surface receptor is the first step and has already occurred.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Penetration, entry into the cell, has already happened before uncoating.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Release of mature virions is the final step of the cycle.

questions.stem: An influenza virion bound to receptors on an airway epithelial cell is drawn inside the cell. In the general scheme of viral infection, penetration occurs by which of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Endocytosis or fusion of the viral envelope with the membrane

choices.label: B
choices.text: Injection of the genome through a rigid tail structure

choices.label: C
choices.text: Passive diffusion of the intact virion across the membrane

choices.label: D
choices.text: Phagocytosis carried out only by tissue macrophages

choices.label: E
choices.text: Transport through nuclear pores set in the plasma membrane

explanation.summary: Viruses penetrate cells either by endocytosis or by fusing their envelope with the cell membrane.
explanation.whyCorrect: Viral attachment to the cell surface allows entry through two general mechanisms: receptor-mediated endocytosis, in which the virus signals the cell to engulf it, and fusion of the viral envelope with the cell membrane, which releases the capsid into the cytoplasm.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Genome injection through a tail is a bacteriophage device, not the general mechanism described.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Virions are far too large and polar-coated to diffuse passively across a bilayer.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Entry is not restricted to macrophages; any cell bearing the right receptor can be penetrated.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Nuclear pores sit in the nuclear envelope, not in the plasma membrane.

questions.stem: Mature virions have been assembled inside an infected cell. By which of the following does the cell release them?

choices.label: A
choices.text: By exocytosis and budding, or by lysis of the host cell

choices.label: B
choices.text: By packaging into mitochondria that are then extruded

choices.label: C
choices.text: By reverse endocytosis driven by surface integrins

choices.label: D
choices.text: Only by active transport through membrane ion pumps

choices.label: E
choices.text: Only by passive leakage across intact tight junctions

explanation.summary: Virions exit either by budding and exocytosis or by lysing the host cell.
explanation.whyCorrect: Release is the final step of the viral life cycle and occurs by two primary methods. Unchecked replication can produce enough virions to burst the cell, a lytic infection, while viruses that use host membranes as envelopes are released by budding outward from the cell surface.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Mitochondria are not used as carriers to export newly made virus particles.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Endocytosis brings material into the cell; integrins here serve as attachment receptors.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Ion pumps move small charged solutes and cannot transport an assembled virion.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Tight junctions seal the space between cells and are not a route of virion escape.

questions.stem: Influenza virus primarily affects the respiratory system while HIV primarily affects the immune system. Which of the following best explains this difference in the tissues each virus targets?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Basement membrane thickness differs between the two tissues

choices.label: B
choices.text: Capsid protein is present only in respiratory pathogens

choices.label: C
choices.text: Complement selectively destroys virions at off-target sites

choices.label: D
choices.text: Each organ system is kept at a different ambient temperature

choices.label: E
choices.text: Each virus has affinity for specific receptors on host cells

explanation.summary: Viral tropism is determined largely by the receptors a virus can bind on host cells.
explanation.whyCorrect: The answer to why some viruses affect certain organs and spare others is receptors and the affinity of a virus for them. These target receptors are a major part of viral tropism, the selection of tissues a virus can infect. Some receptors are highly restricted to one cell type, while others, such as the integrins CMV uses, are widespread.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Basement membrane thickness does not determine which cells a virus can enter.
whyWrongByChoice.B: All viruses have a capsid, so its presence cannot distinguish target tissues.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Complement is a host defense, not the reason a virus selects a tissue in the first place.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Temperature differences are not the explanation the brick gives for tissue targeting.

questions.stem: HIV enters its target cells by binding a primary receptor together with a co-receptor. Which of the following combinations does HIV use?

choices.label: A
choices.text: ACE2 with nicotinic receptors

choices.label: B
choices.text: CD21 with heparan sulfate

choices.label: C
choices.text: CD4 with CCR5 or CXCR4

choices.label: D
choices.text: ICAM-1 with sialic acid

choices.label: E
choices.text: P antigen with integrins

explanation.summary: HIV uses CD4 plus the co-receptors CCR5 and CXCR4.
explanation.whyCorrect: HIV targets CD4 T lymphocytes, monocytes and macrophages, and dendritic cells, using CD4 along with the co-receptors CCR5 and CXCR4 to enter the host cell. This receptor requirement explains its tropism for the immune system.

whyWrongByChoice.A: ACE2 is used by SARS-CoV-2 and nicotinic receptors by rabies virus.
whyWrongByChoice.B: CD21 on B cells is used by EBV; heparan sulfate relates to the integrins CMV binds.
whyWrongByChoice.D: ICAM-1 is the rhinovirus receptor and sialic acid the influenza receptor.
whyWrongByChoice.E: P antigen on red blood cells is the parvovirus B19 receptor.

questions.stem: Epstein-Barr virus shows marked tropism for B lymphocytes. Which receptor does it bind to enter these cells?

choices.label: A
choices.text: ACE2

choices.label: B
choices.text: CD21

choices.label: C
choices.text: CD4

choices.label: D
choices.text: ICAM-1

choices.label: E
choices.text: P antigen

explanation.summary: EBV enters B cells through CD21.
explanation.whyCorrect: CD21 is found on B cells, and EBV binds it to gain entry. Because that receptor is restricted to B lymphocytes, the virus shows a correspondingly narrow tropism for those cells.

whyWrongByChoice.A: ACE2 is the receptor SARS-CoV-2 uses to enter respiratory epithelium.
whyWrongByChoice.C: CD4 is the primary receptor used by HIV, together with CCR5 or CXCR4.
whyWrongByChoice.D: ICAM-1 is bound by rhinovirus, not by EBV.
whyWrongByChoice.E: P antigen sits on red blood cells and is used by parvovirus B19.

questions.stem: A 6-year-old boy with sickle cell disease develops a sudden fall in hemoglobin with absent reticulocytes after a parvovirus B19 infection. The virus enters erythroid cells by binding which of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Angiotensin-converting enzyme 2

choices.label: B
choices.text: CD21 expressed on the cell surface

choices.label: C
choices.text: Nicotinic acetylcholine receptors

choices.label: D
choices.text: P antigen on red blood cells

choices.label: E
choices.text: Sialic acid residues on surface glycoproteins

explanation.summary: Parvovirus B19 uses P antigen on red blood cells as its receptor.
explanation.whyCorrect: P antigen on red blood cells is the receptor for parvovirus B19. Restricting entry to cells of the erythroid line explains why this infection strikes the red cell precursors and produces a drop in hemoglobin with no reticulocyte response.

whyWrongByChoice.A: ACE2 is the receptor bound by SARS-CoV-2.
whyWrongByChoice.B: CD21 is found on B cells and is used by EBV.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Nicotinic acetylcholine receptors are the entry point for rabies virus.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Sialic acid receptors are used by influenza virus on airway epithelium.

questions.stem: A 40-year-old man is bitten on the hand by a bat and weeks later develops agitation, hydrophobia, and encephalitis. The responsible virus reaches neurons by binding which receptor?

choices.label: A
choices.text: CD4 with its co-receptor complexes

choices.label: B
choices.text: Heparan sulfate-linked integrins

choices.label: C
choices.text: Intercellular adhesion molecule-1

choices.label: D
choices.text: Nicotinic acetylcholine receptors

choices.label: E
choices.text: Sialic acid on surface glycoproteins

explanation.summary: Rabies virus binds nicotinic acetylcholine receptors.
explanation.whyCorrect: Rabies uses nicotinic acetylcholine receptors, which are concentrated at the neuromuscular junction and on neurons. That receptor choice is what gives the virus its neurologic tropism after inoculation into peripheral tissue.

whyWrongByChoice.A: CD4 with CCR5 or CXCR4 is the receptor combination used by HIV.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Integrins with heparan sulfate are the receptors CMV uses across many cell types.
whyWrongByChoice.C: ICAM-1 is the receptor for rhinovirus in the upper airway.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Sialic acid receptors are used by influenza virus, not rabies.

questions.stem: Rhinovirus, a frequent cause of the common cold, attaches to nasal epithelium using which of the following cell surface receptors?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Angiotensin-converting enzyme 2

choices.label: B
choices.text: CD21 expressed on B cells

choices.label: C
choices.text: Intercellular adhesion molecule-1

choices.label: D
choices.text: Nicotinic acetylcholine receptors

choices.label: E
choices.text: P antigen on erythroid cells

explanation.summary: Rhinovirus attaches using ICAM-1.
explanation.whyCorrect: ICAM-1 is the receptor listed for rhinovirus. Attachment to a surface marker is the first step of infection, and the distribution of that marker on respiratory epithelium sets where the virus can establish itself.

whyWrongByChoice.A: ACE2 is the receptor used by SARS-CoV-2.
whyWrongByChoice.B: CD21 on B cells is used by EBV.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Nicotinic acetylcholine receptors are used by rabies virus.
whyWrongByChoice.E: P antigen on red blood cells is the parvovirus B19 receptor.

questions.stem: SARS-CoV-2 attaches to respiratory epithelium through a specific host cell surface protein. Which of the following is that receptor?

choices.label: A
choices.text: ACE2

choices.label: B
choices.text: CD21

choices.label: C
choices.text: CD4

choices.label: D
choices.text: ICAM-1

choices.label: E
choices.text: P antigen

explanation.summary: SARS-CoV-2 uses ACE2 as its entry receptor.
explanation.whyCorrect: ACE2 is the receptor listed for SARS-CoV2. Because ACE2 is expressed on respiratory epithelial cells, the virus establishes itself in the airway, which is why a nasal swab is an appropriate specimen for testing.

whyWrongByChoice.B: CD21 is restricted largely to B cells and is used by EBV.
whyWrongByChoice.C: CD4 is the primary HIV receptor on T lymphocytes and macrophages.
whyWrongByChoice.D: ICAM-1 is the rhinovirus receptor.
whyWrongByChoice.E: P antigen on red blood cells is used by parvovirus B19.

questions.stem: Influenza virus becomes attached to target epithelial cells of the airway at the start of infection. Which of the following does it bind?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Angiotensin-converting enzyme 2

choices.label: B
choices.text: CD21 on the epithelial cell surface

choices.label: C
choices.text: Nicotinic acetylcholine receptors

choices.label: D
choices.text: P antigen on red blood cells

choices.label: E
choices.text: Sialic acid receptors

explanation.summary: Influenza virus attaches to sialic acid receptors.
explanation.whyCorrect: Influenza binds sialic acid receptors on target epithelial cells, the attachment step that precedes penetration by endocytosis. Its receptor distribution in the airway explains its respiratory tropism.

whyWrongByChoice.A: ACE2 is used by SARS-CoV-2 rather than by influenza.
whyWrongByChoice.B: CD21 is a B cell marker used by EBV.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Nicotinic acetylcholine receptors are the rabies virus receptor.
whyWrongByChoice.D: P antigen on red blood cells is bound by parvovirus B19.

questions.stem: Maraviroc is given to a patient with HIV infection and occupies the host CCR5 co-receptor. Which step of the viral life cycle does this agent block?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Assembly

choices.label: B
choices.text: Attachment

choices.label: C
choices.text: Release

choices.label: D
choices.text: Replication

choices.label: E
choices.text: Uncoating

explanation.summary: Blocking a host receptor that a virus recognizes prevents attachment.
explanation.whyCorrect: Maraviroc blocks CCR5 and inhibits viral entry. Because CCR5 is the host receptor HIV must recognize at the cell surface, occupying it prevents the virus from attaching, the first step of the life cycle. Individuals with a naturally mutated CCR5 are highly resistant to HIV for the same reason.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Assembly of new virions takes place well after entry has succeeded.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Release is the final step and would only matter if the cell had been infected.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Replication is inhibited by other agents, such as reverse transcriptase inhibitors.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Uncoating occurs after the virus is already inside the cell and is not affected.

questions.stem: During a cruise ship outbreak of vomiting and diarrhea, ethanol-based hand sanitizer fails to interrupt transmission, though the same product helped control an influenza outbreak the previous season. Which property of the responsible virus best explains this failure?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It carries reverse transcriptase within the virion

choices.label: B
choices.text: It establishes latency within enteric ganglia

choices.label: C
choices.text: It has a helical rather than an icosahedral capsid

choices.label: D
choices.text: It has no lipid envelope for ethanol to dissolve

choices.label: E
choices.text: It replicates within the enterocyte nucleus, where ethanol cannot reach it

explanation.summary: Ethanol works by dissolving lipid envelopes, so non-enveloped viruses such as norovirus survive it.
explanation.whyCorrect: Ethanol-based sanitizers inactivate enveloped viruses, including SARS-CoV-2, herpesviruses, influenza, RSV, and parainfluenza, by dissolving their lipid envelope. Non-enveloped viruses such as noroviruses remain infectious after exposure, and washing with soap and water is the most effective way to remove them from the hands.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Reverse transcriptase is carried by retroviruses and confers no resistance to ethanol.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Latency describes a dormant intracellular state and does not protect virions on the hands.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Non-enveloped viruses are icosahedral; helical capsids belong to enveloped viruses.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Replication site has no bearing on whether a disinfectant can inactivate a virion on the skin.

questions.stem: Most DNA viruses replicate within the nucleus of the host cell. Which of the following is the noted exception that replicates in the cytoplasm?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Cytomegalovirus

choices.label: B
choices.text: Epstein-Barr virus

choices.label: C
choices.text: Herpes simplex virus

choices.label: D
choices.text: Parvovirus B19

choices.label: E
choices.text: Poxviruses

explanation.summary: Poxviruses are dsDNA viruses that break the rule by replicating in the cytoplasm.
explanation.whyCorrect: DNA is normally kept in the nucleus, and DNA viruses generally replicate there to reach the nucleic acid synthesis machinery. Poxviruses are the exception called out: although they are dsDNA viruses, they replicate in the cytoplasm.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Cytomegalovirus is noteworthy for its broad receptor use, not for cytoplasmic replication.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Epstein-Barr virus is a DNA virus notable for its B cell tropism through CD21.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Herpes simplex virus is a DNA virus that follows the usual nuclear pattern.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Parvovirus B19 is the ssDNA exception by genome, not by replication site.

questions.stem: Most RNA viruses replicate in the cytoplasm. Which of the following is the exception noted for replicating in the nucleus?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Influenza and retroviruses

choices.label: B
choices.text: Poxvirus and parvovirus

choices.label: C
choices.text: Rabies virus and norovirus

choices.label: D
choices.text: Reovirus and rhinovirus

choices.label: E
choices.text: Rhinovirus and norovirus

explanation.summary: Influenza and the retroviruses are the RNA viruses that replicate in the nucleus.
explanation.whyCorrect: Most RNA viruses replicate in the cytoplasm using their own machinery together with host ribosomes, but influenza and retroviruses are exceptions that replicate in the nucleus. Influenza viral RNA enters the nucleus, where it is copied by viral RNA polymerase, while retroviral DNA is integrated into the host genome there.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Poxvirus and parvovirus are DNA viruses, and poxvirus is in fact a cytoplasmic exception.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Rabies and norovirus are not the viruses named as nuclear exceptions.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Reovirus and rhinovirus are not the pair singled out as nuclear replicators.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Rhinovirus and norovirus follow the usual cytoplasmic pattern for RNA viruses.

questions.stem: After a double-stranded DNA virus injects its genome into a host cell, the genome travels into the nucleus. What does the virus gain by going there?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A lipid bilayer from which to construct a new envelope

choices.label: B
choices.text: Lysosomal enzymes that strip away the remaining capsid

choices.label: C
choices.text: Nucleic acid synthesis machinery to make mRNA and proteins

choices.label: D
choices.text: Reverse transcriptase supplied by the host nucleolus

choices.label: E
choices.text: Ribosomes that translate the viral genome directly into protein

explanation.summary: DNA viruses enter the nucleus to use the cell's nucleic acid synthesis machinery.
explanation.whyCorrect: Once a DNA virus has injected its DNA into a host cell, that DNA enters the nucleus and accesses the nucleic acid synthesis machinery it needs to produce mRNA and proteins for new virions. This mirrors the normal cell, in which DNA stays in the nucleus and mRNA is exported for translation.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Envelope lipid is acquired from the plasma membrane during budding, not in the nucleus.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Uncoating strips the capsid before replication; that is not the reason for nuclear entry.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Reverse transcriptase is a viral enzyme carried by retroviruses, not a host nuclear product.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Ribosomes sit in the cytoplasm, and DNA cannot be translated directly in any case.

questions.stem: A (+)ssRNA virus that is not a retrovirus infects a hepatocyte. How is its genome used to produce viral proteins?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Host ribosomes translate it into one large protein that is processed

choices.label: B
choices.text: Host RNA polymerase transcribes it into several separate small mRNAs

choices.label: C
choices.text: It is first copied into double-stranded DNA inside the nucleolus

choices.label: D
choices.text: Reverse transcriptase copies it into DNA that is later transcribed

choices.label: E
choices.text: Viral integrase inserts it into host DNA before any transcription

explanation.summary: A (+)ssRNA genome is translated by host ribosomes into a single large protein that is then cleaved.
explanation.whyCorrect: For (+)ssRNA viruses the genome is directly translated by host ribosomes into a single large protein, which is then processed into smaller functional proteins. No intermediate nucleic acid is required, since the genome already has the polarity of mRNA.

whyWrongByChoice.B: The genome is read by ribosomes as mRNA; it is not transcribed into separate messages first.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Making a DNA copy in the nucleus is not how non-retroviral (+)ssRNA viruses work.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Reverse transcription is the retroviral route, which the stem excludes.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Integration into host DNA is a retroviral step performed after reverse transcription.

questions.stem: In a laboratory, RNA purified from virions, containing no viral protein at all, is introduced into susceptible cells and infectious virus is produced. The genome of this virus is most likely which of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Antisense single-stranded RNA

choices.label: B
choices.text: Double-stranded DNA

choices.label: C
choices.text: Double-stranded RNA

choices.label: D
choices.text: Sense single-stranded RNA

choices.label: E
choices.text: Single-stranded DNA

explanation.summary: Purified (+)ssRNA is infectious on its own because it functions as mRNA.
explanation.whyCorrect: Because (+)ssRNA is effectively equivalent to mRNA, purified (+)ssRNA viral RNA is contagious by itself. If it reaches the cytoplasm of a cell, it is translated immediately, replication begins, and new virus is produced without any accompanying viral protein.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Antisense RNA needs RNA replicase carried in the virion, which was absent here.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A dsDNA genome is likewise excluded, since only RNA was introduced.
whyWrongByChoice.C: dsRNA cannot be read directly by ribosomes and would not be infectious on its own.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The material introduced was RNA, so a DNA genome is excluded by the stem.

questions.stem: An infected cell accumulates so many new virions that it bursts, spilling them into the surrounding tissue, where each goes on to infect and eventually destroy another cell. This pattern is best described as which of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Cytopathic effect

choices.label: B
choices.text: Latent infection

choices.label: C
choices.text: Lytic infection

choices.label: D
choices.text: Persistent infection

choices.label: E
choices.text: Viral reactivation

explanation.summary: Release by bursting the host cell defines a lytic infection.
explanation.whyCorrect: Each cell can hold only so much volume, and unchecked replication produces so many virions that the cell lyses. This releases a large quantity of virus locally or systemically, and each released virion can infect and lyse a cell of its own, which is what makes the infection lytic.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Cytopathic effect refers to histologic changes used diagnostically, not to this release mechanism.
whyWrongByChoice.B: In a latent infection the virus lies dormant and no virus is produced at all.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Persistent infection involves continued replication over months to years without this burst pattern.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Reactivation is the triggering of a latent virus back into replication.

questions.stem: Influenza virus and respiratory syncytial virus acquire an envelope as newly assembled virions move to the plasma membrane and push outward. Apart from allowing exit, what advantage does this coat of host membrane give the virus?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It allows replication to proceed without any host ribosomes

choices.label: B
choices.text: It helps the virion evade recognition by host defenses

choices.label: C
choices.text: It lets the virion survive drying on hard surfaces for weeks

choices.label: D
choices.text: It stores the enzymes needed to lyse the next host cell

choices.label: E
choices.text: It supplies the receptor the next host cell will use for entry

explanation.summary: Budding wraps the virion in host membrane, which helps it evade host defenses.
explanation.whyCorrect: Viruses released by budding form an envelope from host cell membrane as they leave. The coating of host membrane gives these viruses a way to evade host defenses, and influenza and RSV are the examples given of viruses that use host membranes in this way.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Viral protein synthesis still depends on host ribosomes regardless of the envelope.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Environmental stability is a property of non-enveloped viruses; envelopes are fragile.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Budding is an alternative to lysis, and the envelope carries no lytic enzyme store.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Receptors are host cell molecules; the envelope carries viral surface proteins instead.

questions.stem: A 38-year-old man has had detectable virus in his blood for eight years. The viral genome has become a permanent part of the infected cells and virus continues to be produced. Which of the following best describes this type of infection?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Cytopathic effect

choices.label: B
choices.text: Latent infection

choices.label: C
choices.text: Lytic infection

choices.label: D
choices.text: Persistent infection

choices.label: E
choices.text: Viral tropism

explanation.summary: Persistent infection means continued viral replication over months to years, as with HIV.
explanation.whyCorrect: Some viruses stay within the host cell and continue to replicate over many months or years, through integration into the host genome, evasion of host defenses, or viral mutation. HIV causes exactly this sort of persistent, chronic infection, incorporating into the host genome and becoming a permanent part of the cell.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Cytopathic effect is a histologic change used for diagnosis, not a category of infection.
whyWrongByChoice.B: In latency the virus lies dormant and no virus is produced, unlike this case.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A lytic infection destroys cells as virions burst out; it does not smolder for years.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Tropism describes which tissues a virus can infect, not the duration of infection.

questions.stem: A 44-year-old man begins immunosuppressive therapy after a kidney transplant and develops painful cold sores around the mouth. No virus had been produced at that site for years beforehand. Which of the following best describes the state of the virus before therapy began?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Latent infection, with no virions being produced

choices.label: B
choices.text: Lytic infection confined to basal epithelial cells

choices.label: C
choices.text: Persistent infection, with ongoing virion production

choices.label: D
choices.text: Primary infection acquired at the time of transplant

choices.label: E
choices.text: Re-exposure from the donor organ during surgery

explanation.summary: Latent virus lies dormant with no virus produced until a trigger causes reactivation.
explanation.whyCorrect: Latent infection occurs when an infection lacks a trigger for replication and the virus lies dormant inside the cell, producing no virus during that time. Immunosuppressive therapy for an organ transplant is a classic trigger for reactivation, and herpes simplex virus-1 reactivation typically presents as cold sores.

whyWrongByChoice.B: A lytic infection is actively destroying cells and would not have been silent for years.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Persistent infection involves continuous replication, which was not occurring before therapy.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A newly acquired primary infection would not explain a virus dormant at that site for years.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Reactivation of the patient's own latent virus, not a new exposure, is the described mechanism.

questions.stem: A 27-year-old man has had cough, mild fever, fatigue, and anosmia for 4 days. Several coworkers have been absent with similar symptoms. Which of the following tests is most likely to confirm the diagnosis at this stage of his illness?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Antigen-capture assay on a nasal swab

choices.label: B
choices.text: Gram stain and light microscopy of sputum

choices.label: C
choices.text: Serum IgG titer against the suspected virus

choices.label: D
choices.text: Serum IgM titer against the suspected virus

choices.label: E
choices.text: Viral culture of a nasopharyngeal specimen

explanation.summary: Early in infection, antigen-capture assays and NAAT outperform serology.
explanation.whyCorrect: Symptoms have been present only 4 days, so viral load is high while antibody titers have not yet risen. Antigen-capture assays and nucleic acid tests such as RT-PCR are more sensitive than serology early in infection, and a nasal swab run on an antigen-capture assay is the appropriate confirmatory test here.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Viruses are far too small to see and stain poorly, so microscopy is not an option.
whyWrongByChoice.C: IgG becomes predominant only weeks later and would be undetectable this early.
whyWrongByChoice.D: IgM rises first but still takes roughly 1-2 weeks, so it is not useful at day 4.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Viral culture is time consuming and difficult and is not standard practice.

questions.stem: A patient with 3 days of symptoms has a negative serologic test for a suspected viral infection, yet RT-PCR on a respiratory swab is positive. Which of the following best explains this discordance?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Antibody titers have not yet risen above the detection limit

choices.label: B
choices.text: Circulating virus consumes the antibody before sampling

choices.label: C
choices.text: RT-PCR measures host antibody rather than viral nucleic acid

choices.label: D
choices.text: Serologic assays detect only IgG and never detect IgM

choices.label: E
choices.text: Serology becomes valid only after the patient has recovered

explanation.summary: Serology fails early because antibody titers need weeks to become detectable.
explanation.whyCorrect: Early in an infection antibody titers may not have risen enough for detection, so a symptomatic patient can be antibody-negative yet truly infected. IgM is the first class to rise and IgG predominates a few weeks later, which is why serology is better suited to prolonged, persistent, or latent infections than to an illness of a few days.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Antibody consumption by virus is not the explanation offered for early negative serology.
whyWrongByChoice.C: RT-PCR makes cDNA from pathogen RNA and amplifies it; it does not measure antibody.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Serology detects both IgM and IgG, and their pattern helps separate current from past infection.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Serology is informative during prolonged infection as well, not only after recovery.

questions.stem: A respiratory panel uses reverse transcriptase polymerase chain reaction to detect an RNA virus. Which step distinguishes RT-PCR from conventional PCR?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It compares antibody titers in paired acute and later samples

choices.label: B
choices.text: It first makes complementary DNA from pathogen RNA to amplify

choices.label: C
choices.text: It grows the pathogen in cell culture prior to any amplification

choices.label: D
choices.text: It stains the specimen to reveal characteristic cellular changes

choices.label: E
choices.text: It uses tagged antibodies to bind pathogen antigen in the sample

explanation.summary: RT-PCR converts pathogen RNA to cDNA with reverse transcriptase, then amplifies that cDNA.
explanation.whyCorrect: Both are nucleic acid amplification tests. PCR amplifies pathogen DNA directly, while RT-PCR first uses reverse transcriptase to make complementary DNA copies from pathogen RNA and then amplifies the cDNA. That extra step is what allows an RNA virus to be detected.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Comparing antibody titers is serology, which measures the host response rather than the pathogen.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Culture is a separate and impractical approach for viruses; amplification needs no growth step.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Staining to show cellular changes is histology, used to detect cytopathic effects.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Using tagged antibodies to detect antigen describes an antigen-capture assay.

questions.stem: A tissue biopsy from an infected organ shows distinctive changes within the infected cells that are characteristic of one particular virus. This diagnostic approach depends on which of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Amplification of viral nucleic acid present in the specimen

choices.label: B
choices.text: Detection of host antibody bound to circulating viral antigen

choices.label: C
choices.text: Direct visualization of intact virions by light microscopy

choices.label: D
choices.text: Histology showing characteristic cytopathic effects

choices.label: E
choices.text: Measurement of paired acute and convalescent antibody titers

explanation.summary: Some viruses produce characteristic cytopathic effects that histology can recognize.
explanation.whyCorrect: Histology is one of the general approaches to confirming a viral diagnosis. Some infections produce unique characteristics in cells or tissues, called cytopathic effects, and these distinctive changes can narrow down the responsible pathogen when other assays are unavailable or unhelpful.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Amplifying nucleic acid describes NAAT such as PCR or RT-PCR, not tissue examination.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Detecting host antibody is serology, which is performed on serum rather than on a biopsy.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Viruses are too small to be resolved by light microscopy and stain poorly.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Paired titers are again a serologic method and do not involve examining tissue.

questions.stem: A 4-year-old boy is brought to the clinic with 3 days of fever, irritability, and refusal to eat. Examination shows swollen, erythematous gums and multiple painful vesicles and shallow ulcers on the lips, tongue, and buccal mucosa. After this illness resolves, the responsible virus will persist for life at which of the following sites?

choices.label: A
choices.text: B lymphocytes and some epithelial cells

choices.label: B
choices.text: CD4 T lymphocytes of the peripheral blood

choices.label: C
choices.text: Monocytes, macrophages, and marrow progenitors

choices.label: D
choices.text: Neurons of the sacral dorsal root ganglia

choices.label: E
choices.text: Neurons of the trigeminal sensory ganglia

explanation.summary: Herpetic gingivostomatitis is a primary HSV-1 infection, and HSV-1 becomes latent in sensory ganglia, most commonly the trigeminal ganglia.
explanation.whyCorrect: Painful swollen gums with vesicular and ulcerative lesions in and around the mouth of a child is the classic picture of herpetic gingivostomatitis, which the brick attributes to initial infection with HSV-1. HSV-1 travels from the mucocutaneous site of inoculation up peripheral sensory nerves and establishes latency in sensory ganglia, most commonly the trigeminal ganglia. The illness itself resolves in 2-3 weeks, but the latent virus remains and can reactivate as herpes labialis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: B lymphocytes (and some epithelial cells) are where Epstein-Barr virus, HHV-4, establishes latency.
whyWrongByChoice.B: CD4 T lymphocytes are the latency site of HHV-6 and HHV-7, the agents of roseola infantum.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Monocytes, macrophages, and bone marrow progenitor cells harbor latent cytomegalovirus, HHV-5.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The sacral ganglia are the usual latency site of HSV-2, which causes genital rather than oral disease.

questions.stem: A 26-year-old woman has had three episodes in 2 years of painful genital ulcers, each preceded by a day of tingling. PCR of a lesion swab is positive for herpes simplex virus type 2. Between these episodes, where does the virus reside?

choices.label: A
choices.text: B lymphocytes of the regional lymph nodes

choices.label: B
choices.text: Bone marrow hematopoietic progenitor cells

choices.label: C
choices.text: Neurons of the cranial nerve ganglia

choices.label: D
choices.text: Neurons of the sacral dorsal root ganglia

choices.label: E
choices.text: Neurons of the trigeminal sensory ganglia

explanation.summary: HSV-2 establishes latency in sensory ganglia, most commonly the sacral ganglia.
explanation.whyCorrect: HSV-2 is inoculated at genital mucosa and is carried by retrograde transport up the peripheral sensory nerves that serve that territory, which drain to the sacral dorsal root ganglia. The virus remains latent there and, on reactivation, travels back down the same nerves to produce recurrent genital lesions. This is the mirror image of HSV-1, which uses the trigeminal ganglia.

whyWrongByChoice.A: B lymphocytes are the latency reservoir for Epstein-Barr virus.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Bone marrow progenitor cells harbor cytomegalovirus, not herpes simplex virus.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Cranial nerve ganglia, along with dorsal root ganglia, are latency sites for varicella zoster virus.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The trigeminal ganglia serve the face and are the usual latency site for HSV-1, not genital HSV-2.

questions.stem: Epstein-Barr virus (HHV-4) persists for the life of the host after primary infection. Which of the following is its primary site of latency?

choices.label: A
choices.text: B lymphocytes and some epithelial cells

choices.label: B
choices.text: CD4 T lymphocytes of the peripheral blood

choices.label: C
choices.text: Circulating monocytes and tissue macrophages

choices.label: D
choices.text: Neurons of the sacral dorsal root ganglia

choices.label: E
choices.text: Neurons of the trigeminal sensory ganglia

explanation.summary: EBV (HHV-4) is the herpesvirus that establishes latency primarily in B lymphocytes.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick groups the human herpesviruses by where each establishes latency. EBV is unusual among them in choosing a lymphoid reservoir: it primarily becomes latent in B lymphocytes, although it can also be found in epithelial cells and other cell types. This lymphotropism is why EBV disease is dominated by lymphoid rather than neurologic findings.

whyWrongByChoice.B: CD4 T lymphocytes are the latency site of HHV-6 and HHV-7.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Monocytes and macrophages, together with bone marrow progenitors, harbor latent cytomegalovirus.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Sacral dorsal root ganglia are the usual latency site of HSV-2.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Trigeminal sensory ganglia harbor latent HSV-1.

questions.stem: Cytomegalovirus reactivates in a kidney transplant recipient who is receiving immunosuppressive therapy. Before reactivation, the latent viral genomes in this patient were most likely carried in which of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: B lymphocytes and mucosal epithelial cells

choices.label: B
choices.text: CD4 T lymphocytes of the peripheral blood

choices.label: C
choices.text: Monocytes, macrophages, and marrow progenitors

choices.label: D
choices.text: Neurons of the sacral dorsal root ganglia

choices.label: E
choices.text: Neurons of the trigeminal sensory ganglia

explanation.summary: Cytomegalovirus (HHV-5) establishes latency in monocytes, macrophages, and bone marrow progenitor cells.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick lists CMV as establishing latency in various cells including monocytes, macrophages, and bone marrow progenitor cells. Because the reservoir is myeloid rather than neuronal, reactivating CMV can seed many organs through the circulation rather than reappearing in one dermatome or at one mucocutaneous site. Immunosuppression, as in transplantation, is the classic trigger for reactivation of any herpesvirus.

whyWrongByChoice.A: B lymphocytes and epithelial cells are the reservoir for Epstein-Barr virus.
whyWrongByChoice.B: CD4 T lymphocytes harbor latent HHV-6 and HHV-7.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Sacral dorsal root ganglia harbor latent HSV-2, the usual cause of genital herpes.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Trigeminal ganglia are the latency site of HSV-1, which reactivates as cold sores.

questions.stem: A 10-month-old infant has 3 days of high fever followed by a rose-colored rash that appears as the fever breaks. The illness is attributed to human herpesvirus 6. This virus establishes latency in which of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: B lymphocytes and mucosal epithelial cells

choices.label: B
choices.text: CD4 T lymphocytes of the peripheral blood

choices.label: C
choices.text: Monocytes and bone marrow progenitor cells

choices.label: D
choices.text: Neurons of the dorsal root and cranial nerve ganglia

choices.label: E
choices.text: Neurons of the trigeminal sensory ganglia

explanation.summary: HHV-6 and HHV-7 cause roseola infantum and establish latency in CD4 T cells.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick identifies HHV-6 and HHV-7 as the agents of roseola infantum, a childhood illness of high fever followed by rash, and states that these viruses establish latency in CD4 T cells. This places them apart from the neurotropic alpha herpesviruses and from the myeloid reservoir used by CMV.

whyWrongByChoice.A: B lymphocytes and epithelial cells are the reservoir for Epstein-Barr virus.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Monocytes and bone marrow progenitors are the reservoir for cytomegalovirus.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Dorsal root and cranial nerve ganglia are the latency sites of varicella zoster virus.
whyWrongByChoice.E: HSV-1 uses the trigeminal ganglia; it causes oral lesions, not a febrile exanthem of infancy.

questions.stem: A newly isolated virus is assigned to the family Herpesviridae. Which of the following genome and particle descriptions should be expected?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Circular double-stranded DNA, naked, icosahedral capsid

choices.label: B
choices.text: Linear double-stranded DNA, enveloped, icosahedral capsid

choices.label: C
choices.text: Linear positive-sense RNA, enveloped, helical capsid

choices.label: D
choices.text: Linear single-stranded DNA, naked, icosahedral capsid

choices.label: E
choices.text: Segmented single-stranded RNA, enveloped, helical capsid

explanation.summary: All herpesviruses are enveloped, icosahedral virions carrying a linear double-stranded DNA genome.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that all herpesviruses store their genetic information as linear double-stranded DNA and have an enveloped, icosahedral capsid, with replication occurring in the host nucleus. These shared structural features are what unify an otherwise clinically diverse family.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Herpesvirus DNA is linear, not circular, and the virion is enveloped rather than naked.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Herpesviruses do not have an RNA genome, and their capsid symmetry is icosahedral rather than helical.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The herpesvirus genome is double-stranded, and herpesvirus particles carry an envelope.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Herpesviruses are DNA viruses; a segmented RNA genome with helical symmetry describes a different family entirely.

questions.stem: Electron microscopy of a cell infected with a herpesvirus shows budding nucleocapsids acquiring an envelope at a site unusual for enveloped viruses. From which membrane is the herpesvirus envelope derived?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The cisternal membrane of the Golgi apparatus

choices.label: B
choices.text: The limiting membrane of host cell lysosomes

choices.label: C
choices.text: The nuclear membrane of the infected host cell

choices.label: D
choices.text: The outer mitochondrial membrane of the host cell

choices.label: E
choices.text: The plasma membrane of the infected host cell

explanation.summary: Herpesvirus nucleocapsids become enveloped by pinching off a segment of the nuclear membrane.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick highlights this as the odd feature of herpesviruses: budding nucleocapsids of new virions become enveloped by pinching off a segment of the nuclear membrane, whereas most enveloped viruses take their envelope from the host cell membrane. The enveloped virions then accumulate in the endoplasmic reticulum and are transported out of the cell to infect surrounding cells.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The Golgi is part of the export route for many viral glycoproteins but is not where the herpesvirus envelope is acquired.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Lysosomal membranes are degradative compartments and are not a source of viral envelope.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Mitochondrial membranes are not used by any human virus as an envelope source.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The plasma membrane is the source of the envelope for most other enveloped viruses, which is precisely the contrast the brick draws.

questions.stem: An antiviral compound is designed to inhibit replication of the herpes simplex virus genome. To reach its target, the drug must be active in which of the following compartments?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Cytoplasmic membranous replication factories

choices.label: B
choices.text: Endosomal vesicles near the cell surface

choices.label: C
choices.text: The lumen of the rough endoplasmic reticulum

choices.label: D
choices.text: The matrix of host cell mitochondria

choices.label: E
choices.text: The nucleus of the infected host cell

explanation.summary: Herpesvirus replication occurs in the host cell nucleus.
explanation.whyCorrect: After the virus is transported to a nuclear pore, its DNA is released into the nucleus, and the brick states that replication of all herpesviruses occurs in the host nucleus. A drug targeting genome replication must therefore act on nuclear events. The endoplasmic reticulum is involved later, when assembled virions accumulate there before export.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Cytoplasmic replication complexes are used by many RNA viruses, not by herpesviruses.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Endosomes participate in entry for some viruses but are not where herpesvirus DNA is copied.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Virions accumulate in the endoplasmic reticulum after assembly, but the genome is not replicated there.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The mitochondrial matrix has no role in herpesvirus genome replication.

questions.stem: After replicating in oral epithelium, herpes simplex virus enters sensory nerve endings and travels to the neuronal cell body, where it becomes latent. Which receptor interaction and which direction of axonal transport best describe this step?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Neurokinin-1 receptor with anterograde transport

choices.label: B
choices.text: Neurokinin-1 receptor with retrograde transport

choices.label: C
choices.text: Nicotinic acetylcholine receptor with anterograde transport

choices.label: D
choices.text: Nicotinic acetylcholine receptor with retrograde transport

choices.label: E
choices.text: Transferrin receptor with retrograde transport

explanation.summary: HSV binds the neurokinin-1 receptor and moves up peripheral sensory nerves by retrograde transport to establish latency.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that herpes simplex virus establishes latent infection in neurons by binding the neurokinin-1 receptor and migrating up the peripheral sensory nerves from the site of initial exposure, which is retrograde transport. Once in the cell body, the virus is carried to a nuclear pore and its DNA is released into the nucleus, where it can remain latent for years.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The receptor is correct, but anterograde transport moves virus away from the ganglion toward the skin, which is what happens later during reactivation.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The nicotinic acetylcholine receptor is not the entry receptor described for HSV, and anterograde transport is the direction used on reactivation.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Retrograde transport is correct, but the nicotinic acetylcholine receptor is not the receptor the brick attributes to HSV neuronal entry.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The transferrin receptor mediates iron uptake and is not the receptor used by HSV to enter neurons.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old man develops a cold sore on his lower lip several days after a ski trip. Which of the following best describes how virus latent in his trigeminal ganglion produced this lesion?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It enters the blood and seeds the lip through dermal capillaries

choices.label: B
choices.text: It is carried to the lip within infected circulating monocytes

choices.label: C
choices.text: It is shed into saliva and reinfects the lip from outside

choices.label: D
choices.text: It moves down sensory nerves and infects flanking epithelial cells

choices.label: E
choices.text: It passes from neuron to neuron across the facial dermis

explanation.summary: Reactivated HSV travels back down peripheral sensory nerves and destroys the epithelial cells flanking the nerve endings.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick describes reactivation as the reverse of latency establishment: once reactivated, HSV travels back down the peripheral sensory nerves by anterograde transport and infects flanking epithelial cells, leading to their destruction. Because HSV-1 and HSV-2 replicate rapidly and are cytolytic, this epithelial destruction produces the visible vesicle and subsequent ulcer.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Viremic seeding of the lip is not the mechanism of recurrent herpes labialis; the virus travels within nerves.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Transport inside mononuclear cells is how varicella zoster virus reaches the skin during chicken pox, not how HSV recurs.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Recurrences arise from latent virus already in the ganglion, not from external reinoculation of the lip.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Spread from neuron to neuron through the dermis is not described; the virus moves within the axons of sensory nerves.

questions.stem: A 21-year-old medical student develops a cold sore during final examinations; a previous outbreak followed a severe sunburn. Which of the following best explains why her latent virus began replicating on both occasions?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Antibiotic therapy eliminated the protective normal oral flora

choices.label: B
choices.text: Complete loss of antibody allowed the virus to return to the lip

choices.label: C
choices.text: Mutation of the viral genome during latency restored replication

choices.label: D
choices.text: Reinfection from a new contact introduced a second viral strain

choices.label: E
choices.text: Stress, immunosuppression, and tissue damage trigger reactivation

explanation.summary: Herpesviruses reactivate when the host is stressed, immunocompromised, has another infection, or sustains tissue damage such as sunburn or trauma.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states directly that the virus can rapidly replicate when the host is stressed, immunocompromised, has other infections, or receives tissue damage from infections, sunburns, or trauma. Both of this student's triggers, examination stress and a sunburn, appear on that list. Nothing about the latent genome itself changes; what changes is the host state that had been containing it.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Loss of normal bacterial flora is not one of the reactivation triggers described for herpesviruses.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Antibody does not disappear between outbreaks, and its presence does not prevent recurrences.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Reactivation is not attributed to mutation of the latent viral genome.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Recurrences come from latent virus already established in the ganglion, not from acquiring a new strain.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old man with established genital HSV-2 infection asks how often he might be contagious when he has no symptoms at all. Approximately what proportion of the time do patients with HSV-2 shed virus asymptomatically?

choices.label: A
choices.text: About 5-10% of the time

choices.label: B
choices.text: About 10-20% of the time

choices.label: C
choices.text: About 30-40% of the time

choices.label: D
choices.text: About 50-60% of the time

choices.label: E
choices.text: About 70-80% of the time

explanation.summary: Patients with HSV-2 shed virus asymptomatically roughly 10-20% of the time; for HSV-1 the figure is about 5-10%.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick gives these two numbers side by side: HSV-1 is shed without symptoms approximately 5-10% of the time and HSV-2 roughly 10-20% of the time. This is why avoiding contact only with visible lesions does not prevent transmission, and why a patient who feels entirely well can still infect a partner.

whyWrongByChoice.A: About 5-10% is the asymptomatic shedding rate quoted for HSV-1, not HSV-2.
whyWrongByChoice.C: No herpes simplex virus type is described as shedding asymptomatically a third of the time.
whyWrongByChoice.D: This figure far exceeds the shedding rate reported for either HSV type.
whyWrongByChoice.E: About 70% is the proportion of genital herpes transmissions attributed to asymptomatic shedding, not the fraction of time virus is shed.

questions.stem: A physician counsels a couple who are discordant for genital herpes and explains that most transmission does not happen from visible sores. Studies show that approximately what percentage of genital herpes transmission occurs during asymptomatic viral shedding?

choices.label: A
choices.text: About 10% of transmissions

choices.label: B
choices.text: About 40% of transmissions

choices.label: C
choices.text: About 70% of transmissions

choices.label: D
choices.text: About 90% of transmissions

choices.label: E
choices.text: Essentially none of the transmissions

explanation.summary: Up to 70% of genital herpes transmission occurs during asymptomatic viral shedding.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that studies have shown up to 70% of genital herpes transmission occurs during asymptomatic viral shedding. It also notes that even when a symptom such as a cold sore does develop, virus can be shed for days before the lesion is felt or seen. Counseling therefore cannot rely on lesion avoidance alone.

whyWrongByChoice.A: This greatly underestimates the contribution of asymptomatic shedding to transmission.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Less than half is still an underestimate; the majority of transmissions occur without symptoms.
whyWrongByChoice.D: This overstates the figure given, which is up to about 70%.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Asymptomatic shedding is in fact the dominant route of genital herpes transmission.

questions.stem: A 22-year-old woman has a first episode of painful genital ulcers. PCR of a lesion swab identifies herpes simplex virus type 1. Which of the following best explains this result?

choices.label: A
choices.text: HSV-1 and HSV-2 are now classified as a single viral serotype

choices.label: B
choices.text: HSV-1 has mutated and acquired the tissue tropism of HSV-2

choices.label: C
choices.text: HSV-1 reached the genitals by spreading through the bloodstream

choices.label: D
choices.text: Laboratory cross-reaction between HSV-1 and HSV-2 is expected

choices.label: E
choices.text: Oral sex transmits HSV-1 to the genitals in up to 30% of cases

explanation.summary: HSV-1 and HSV-2 share enough tropism that oral sex can move either virus between sites, and HSV-1 accounts for up to 30% of genital herpes.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick notes that HSV-1 and HSV-2 share enough trophism that oral sex can transmit the viruses between locations, and that up to 30% of cases of genital herpes are caused by HSV-1. The useful but imperfect rule is above the waist HSV-1, below the waist HSV-2; a genital HSV-1 isolate is common rather than surprising.

whyWrongByChoice.A: HSV-1 and HSV-2 remain distinct viruses with different usual latency sites and disease patterns.
whyWrongByChoice.B: No mutation is required; HSV-1 already has sufficient tropism to infect genital epithelium.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Genital HSV-1 arises from direct inoculation at the site, not from hematogenous spread from the mouth.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Type-specific PCR distinguishes HSV-1 from HSV-2; the result is not a cross-reaction artifact.

questions.stem: A public health survey measures herpes simplex virus antibodies in a general adult population. Which of the following is closest to the expected seroprevalence?

choices.label: A
choices.text: About 10-20% for HSV-1 and about 70-90% for HSV-2

choices.label: B
choices.text: About 30% for HSV-1 and about 30% for HSV-2

choices.label: C
choices.text: About 50% for HSV-1 and about 40% for HSV-2

choices.label: D
choices.text: About 70-90% for HSV-1 and about 10-20% for HSV-2

choices.label: E
choices.text: About 70-90% for HSV-1 and about 40-50% for HSV-2

explanation.summary: By adulthood roughly 70-90% of people are infected with HSV-1 and 10-20% with HSV-2.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick estimates that by the time we become adults, 70-90% of people are infected with HSV-1 and 10-20% with HSV-2, consistent with its statement that more than half of all people on earth carry HSV-1. It adds that people in lower socioeconomic brackets are infected at much higher rates, with HSV-2 prevalence reaching 40% in some poor urban communities.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The two figures are reversed; HSV-1 is by far the more prevalent of the two.
whyWrongByChoice.B: This underestimates HSV-1, which infects the large majority of adults.
whyWrongByChoice.C: HSV-1 prevalence is higher than half, and HSV-2 prevalence in the general population is well below 40%.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The HSV-1 figure is right, but 40-50% for HSV-2 describes only the highest-risk communities, not the general population.

questions.stem: A 40-year-old woman reports recurrent painful vesicles at the border of her lip several times a year. Which virus accounts for the overwhelming majority of such lesions?

choices.label: A
choices.text: CMV, which causes about 50% of oropharyngeal lesions

choices.label: B
choices.text: EBV, which causes about 30% of oropharyngeal lesions

choices.label: C
choices.text: HSV-1, which causes about 99% of oropharyngeal lesions

choices.label: D
choices.text: HSV-2, which causes about 99% of oropharyngeal lesions

choices.label: E
choices.text: VZV, which causes about 70% of oropharyngeal lesions

explanation.summary: The vast majority of oropharyngeal herpes lesions, about 99%, are caused by HSV-1.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that the vast majority (99%) of oropharyngeal lesions, meaning cold sores or herpes labialis, are caused by HSV-1, while 70-80% of genital herpes is caused by HSV-2. This underlies the simplified rule that above the waist is usually HSV-1 and below the waist is usually HSV-2, even though either virus can cause either disease.

whyWrongByChoice.A: CMV is not described as a cause of recurrent perioral vesicles.
whyWrongByChoice.B: EBV is not described as a cause of recurrent herpes labialis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: HSV-2 can rarely cause oral lesions, but it is the usual cause of genital rather than oropharyngeal disease.
whyWrongByChoice.E: VZV causes chicken pox and shingles; oral mucosa may be involved in chicken pox but VZV does not cause recurrent cold sores.

questions.stem: A patient reports that his recurrent oral lesions always begin with an itching, tingling, burning sensation. Which of the following correctly orders the stages that follow?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Crust, then papule, then vesicle, then ulcer

choices.label: B
choices.text: Papule, then ulcer, then crust, then vesicle

choices.label: C
choices.text: Papule, then vesicle, then ulcer, then crust

choices.label: D
choices.text: Ulcer, then vesicle, then papule, then crust

choices.label: E
choices.text: Vesicle, then papule, then crust, then ulcer

explanation.summary: Herpes lesions progress from prodromal tingling to red papule, fluid-filled vesicle, shallow painful ulcer, and finally crust.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick describes the sequence precisely: lesions typically start as an itching, tingling, or burning sensation, then small red papules appear and progress to a fluid-filled vesicle. The vesicle ruptures, leaving a shallow, painful ulcer, which then crusts and scabs over as the tissue heals. Recognizing the prodrome matters clinically because treatment started at that stage can reduce severity and duration.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Crusting marks healing at the end of the sequence, not its beginning.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The intact fluid-filled vesicle forms before ulceration, not after crusting.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The ulcer follows rupture of the vesicle; it cannot precede the papule and vesicle.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The papule precedes the vesicle, and crusting is the final stage rather than a step before ulceration.

questions.stem: A 52-year-old man develops unilateral eye pain, redness, tearing, and blurred vision several days after an outbreak of cold sores. Examination shows inflammation of the cornea. Which of the following is the most likely cause?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Cytomegalovirus, a frequent cause of corneal scarring

choices.label: B
choices.text: Epstein-Barr virus, a frequent cause of corneal scarring

choices.label: C
choices.text: HSV-1, one of the most common causes of corneal blindness

choices.label: D
choices.text: HSV-2, one of the most common causes of corneal blindness

choices.label: E
choices.text: Human herpesvirus 6, a frequent cause of corneal damage

explanation.summary: Herpetic keratitis is inflammation of the cornea caused most commonly by HSV-1 and is a leading infectious cause of corneal blindness.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick lists herpetic keratitis in its disease table as caused by HSV-1 and describes keratitis as inflammation or irritation of the cornea, noting that herpetic keratitis is one of the most common causes of corneal blindness. Autoinoculation from an active oral lesion to the eye is one way the virus reaches the cornea.

whyWrongByChoice.A: CMV is not listed among the causes of herpetic keratitis in this brick.
whyWrongByChoice.B: EBV is a lymphotropic herpesvirus and is not described as causing keratitis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: HSV-2 causes mainly genital disease and aseptic meningitis; keratitis is attributed to HSV-1.
whyWrongByChoice.E: HHV-6 causes roseola infantum and is not associated with corneal disease here.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man presents with fever, confusion, and seizures. Cerebrospinal fluid PCR identifies herpes simplex virus type 1. Which of the following statements about this condition is correct?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It carries a mortality of less than 5% when left untreated

choices.label: B
choices.text: It is the most common cause of aseptic meningitis in adults

choices.label: C
choices.text: It is the most common cause of fatal sporadic viral encephalitis

choices.label: D
choices.text: It is usually caused by spread from genital HSV-2 lesions

choices.label: E
choices.text: It resolves with supportive care alone in nearly all patients

explanation.summary: HSV-1 encephalitis is the most common cause of fatal sporadic viral encephalitis in the United States and carries high mortality.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that although most cases of viral encephalitis resolve with supportive therapy alone, HSV-1 encephalitis is different: it is the most common cause of fatal sporadic viral encephalitis in the United States, roughly 70% of untreated patients die, and even with treatment mortality remains high and long-term neurological damage is very common. This is why rapid PCR diagnosis matters so much.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Untreated HSV-1 encephalitis kills roughly 70% of patients, not fewer than 5%.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Aseptic meningitis is a separate, far milder entity, and in the herpes family it is linked chiefly to HSV-2.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Encephalitis in the brick's disease table is attributed to HSV-1, not to genital HSV-2.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Supportive care alone suffices for most other viral encephalitides, but not for HSV-1 encephalitis.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old woman with a first episode of genital herpes develops headache, neck stiffness, and photophobia. Cerebrospinal fluid shows a lymphocytic pleocytosis with negative bacterial cultures. Approximately what proportion of genital herpes cases are complicated in this way?

choices.label: A
choices.text: About 1% of cases

choices.label: B
choices.text: About 10% of cases

choices.label: C
choices.text: About 30% of cases

choices.label: D
choices.text: About 50% of cases

choices.label: E
choices.text: About 70% of cases

explanation.summary: Aseptic meningitis complicates about 10% of genital herpes cases and is usually due to HSV-2.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick lists aseptic meningitis as a common complication of genital herpes occurring in 10% of cases, alongside extragenital lesions in 20% of cases. Its disease table attributes aseptic meningitis to HSV-2, usually as a complication of genital herpes, with HSV-1 a less common cause.

whyWrongByChoice.A: This understates a complication the brick describes as common.
whyWrongByChoice.C: About 20% is the figure for extragenital lesions; meningitis is less frequent than that.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Half of genital herpes cases are not complicated by meningitis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: About 70% describes the share of transmissions occurring during asymptomatic shedding, not the meningitis rate.

questions.stem: A neonate develops clustered vesicles around the eyes and mouth on the sixth day of life, and HSV-2 is identified. Which of the following best describes how neonates most often acquire this infection?

choices.label: A
choices.text: By transfusion of contaminated blood products

choices.label: B
choices.text: By transplacental spread during the first trimester

choices.label: C
choices.text: During delivery or after birth from a person shedding virus

choices.label: D
choices.text: From contaminated formula or hospital water supplies

choices.label: E
choices.text: Through breast milk during the first week of feeding
