explanation.summary: Neonatal herpes is usually acquired during delivery or after birth from a shedding contact, because HSV rarely crosses the placenta.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that the virus is typically transmitted during delivery, or after birth when a family member or hospital worker shedding the virus passes it to the child through close interactions. Unlike other herpesviruses, HSV rarely crosses the placental barrier, although vertical transmission is possible. About 1 in 3500 neonates contracts neonatal herpes.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Transfusion is not a described route for neonatal herpes.
whyWrongByChoice.B: HSV rarely crosses the placental barrier, which is exactly what distinguishes it from the other TORCH agents.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Contaminated formula or water is not a route of transmission for this enveloped, contact-spread virus.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Breast milk is not described as a route of neonatal HSV transmission.

questions.stem: A neonate is admitted to the intensive care unit with disseminated herpes simplex virus infection. Which of the following pairs of figures best describes the mortality of untreated neonatal herpes and of disseminated neonatal disease?

choices.label: A
choices.text: About 5% untreated and about 15% with dissemination

choices.label: B
choices.text: About 10% untreated and about 25% with dissemination

choices.label: C
choices.text: About 25% untreated and about 40% with dissemination

choices.label: D
choices.text: About 50% untreated and about 80% with dissemination

choices.label: E
choices.text: About 90% untreated and about 95% with dissemination

explanation.summary: Untreated neonatal herpes has a mortality as high as 50%, and disseminated neonatal herpes as high as 80%.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick gives both numbers: if left untreated, the mortality rate of neonatal herpes is as high as 50%, and the mortality of disseminated herpes infections in neonates is as high as 80%, with survivors frequently left with permanent neurological damage. Neonatal disease may present as lesions around the eyes and mouth, as encephalitis, or as disseminated infection.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Neonatal herpes is not a mild infection; untreated mortality approaches half of cases.
whyWrongByChoice.B: These figures are far too low for a disease the brick describes as frequently lethal.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Both figures understate the quoted mortality rates.
whyWrongByChoice.E: These figures overstate the numbers given in the brick.

questions.stem: A pregnant woman is counseled about infections that can cross the placenta or be transmitted to her infant at birth. Which of the following lists contains only TORCH pathogens?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Toxoplasma gondii, rotavirus, rubella, CMV, HSV

choices.label: B
choices.text: Toxoplasma gondii, rubella, CMV, HSV, norovirus

choices.label: C
choices.text: Toxoplasma gondii, rubella, Helicobacter pylori, CMV, HSV

choices.label: D
choices.text: Toxoplasma gondii, rubella, influenza virus, CMV, HSV

choices.label: E
choices.text: Toxoplasma gondii, syphilis, rubella, CMV, HSV

explanation.summary: TORCH stands for Toxoplasmosis, Other (including syphilis, VZV, mumps, parvovirus B19, Zika, HIV), Rubella, Cytomegalovirus, and Herpes simplex virus 1 and 2.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick spells out the acronym: T for toxoplasmosis, O for other agents such as syphilis, varicella zoster virus, mumps, parvovirus B19, Zika, and HIV, R for rubella, C for cytomegalovirus, and H for herpes simplex virus types 1 and 2. These pathogens can either cross the placenta directly or be transmitted during vaginal birth, and they cause miscarriages, birth defects, and life-threatening neonatal infections.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Rotavirus causes infantile gastroenteritis and is not part of the TORCH group.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Norovirus causes acute gastroenteritis and is not a congenital or perinatal TORCH pathogen.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Helicobacter pylori is a gastric pathogen and is not a TORCH agent.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Influenza virus is not included among the TORCH pathogens.

questions.stem: A dental hygienist who does not routinely wear gloves develops painful grouped vesicles on the distal pad of her index finger. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis and cause?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Disseminated herpes caused by HSV-2 in an immunocompetent host

choices.label: B
choices.text: Herpes gladiatorum caused by HSV-2 entering damaged skin

choices.label: C
choices.text: Herpetic gingivostomatitis caused by HSV-2 spreading to the hand

choices.label: D
choices.text: Herpetic keratitis caused by HSV-1 entering damaged skin

choices.label: E
choices.text: Herpetic whitlow caused by HSV-1 entering damaged skin

explanation.summary: Herpetic whitlow is HSV infection of the fingers, typically HSV-1, and was common in healthcare workers before routine glove use.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick defines herpetic whitlow as a herpes infection of the fingers, and rarely the toes, typically caused by HSV-1, and notes that before the practice of wearing gloves it was common in healthcare workers. It also warns that whitlow can be autoinoculated, so an infection at one site, even an asymptomatic one, can spread to other parts of the body such as the eyes or genitals.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Disseminated herpes occurs in severely immunocompromised hosts, not in a healthy worker with one finger lesion.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Herpes gladiatorum refers to HSV skin infection spread through mat burns in wrestlers, not a finger lesion in a hygienist.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Gingivostomatitis is an oral disease of primary HSV-1 infection, not a digital lesion.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Keratitis is corneal inflammation, not a lesion on the finger.

questions.stem: A high school wrestler develops clusters of vesicles on his face and shoulders several days after a tournament in which he sustained abrasions from the mat. Which term best describes this infection?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Disseminated herpes infection

choices.label: B
choices.text: Herpes gladiatorum

choices.label: C
choices.text: Herpetic gingivostomatitis

choices.label: D
choices.text: Herpetic keratitis

choices.label: E
choices.text: Herpetic whitlow

explanation.summary: HSV skin infection acquired through mat burns in wrestlers and mixed martial artists is called herpes gladiatorum.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick explains that wrestlers and mixed martial artists frequently get mat burns when pressed into the canvas, and the damaged skin facilitates the spread of HSV. Because these infections are so common in that group, HSV skin infection is called herpes gladiatorum, although the brick stresses that skin infections can occur in anyone with skin damage, not just athletes.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Disseminated herpes occurs in severely immunocompromised hosts, not in a healthy athlete with localized skin lesions.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Gingivostomatitis is primary HSV-1 disease of the gums and oral mucosa.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Keratitis is HSV inflammation of the cornea.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Herpetic whitlow specifically describes HSV infection of the fingers or, rarely, the toes.

questions.stem: A patient with suspected herpes simplex virus encephalitis requires rapid confirmation so that therapy is not delayed. Which of the following is the preferred diagnostic test?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Blood cultures incubated for seven full days

choices.label: B
choices.text: Gram stain and bacterial culture of the specimen

choices.label: C
choices.text: Paired acute and convalescent serologic titers

choices.label: D
choices.text: Polymerase chain reaction on the clinical specimen

choices.label: E
choices.text: Viral culture of the specimen in cell monolayers

explanation.summary: PCR is the preferred diagnostic tool when HSV is suspected because it is faster than culture.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that PCR is the preferred diagnostic tool when HSV is suspected because it is more rapid than cell culture techniques, and time is of the essence in severe invasive disease. HSV-1 encephalitis is exactly that situation: untreated, roughly 70% of patients die, so a same-day answer changes outcome.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Blood cultures detect bacteremia and would not identify herpes simplex virus in the central nervous system.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Gram stain and bacterial culture address septic meningitis, not a viral encephalitis.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Antibody titers appear only 4-7 days after onset and peak weeks later, so they are of little use early.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Cell culture can grow the virus but is slower than PCR, which matters in severe invasive disease.

questions.stem: A patient presents 2 days after the onset of a vesicular rash, and HSV serology is negative. Which of the following best explains this result?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Antibody becomes detectable only after a second recurrence

choices.label: B
choices.text: Antibody is suppressed while virus remains latent in ganglia

choices.label: C
choices.text: Antibody titers rise only in immunocompromised patients

choices.label: D
choices.text: Titers appear 4-7 days after infection begins and peak 2-4 weeks later

choices.label: E
choices.text: Titers fall rapidly within 24 hours of the first lesion

explanation.summary: HSV antibody titers appear 4-7 days after infection begins and peak 2-4 weeks later, so serology is unhelpful early.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that serology can determine whether a patient is infected with HSV, but antibody titers appear 4-7 days after the start of the infection and peak roughly 2-4 weeks later, so early in the infection antibody titers will be of little use. A patient sampled on day 2 is simply too early. PCR of the lesion, or an antigen detection kit, answers the question at that point.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A first infection generates antibody; a recurrence is not required for seroconversion.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Latency does not suppress existing antibody, and this patient has active lesions rather than latent infection.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Immunocompetent patients mount antibody responses to HSV; immune status is not the issue here.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Titers rise and then peak over weeks; they do not collapse within a day.

questions.stem: A scraping taken from the base of a fresh vesicle shows large multinucleated cells, referred to as Tzanck cells. This finding indicates infection with which of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Any one of the eight human herpesviruses

choices.label: B
choices.text: Cytomegalovirus and no other herpesvirus

choices.label: C
choices.text: Epstein-Barr virus and no other herpesvirus

choices.label: D
choices.text: HSV-1, HSV-2, or varicella zoster virus

choices.label: E
choices.text: Human herpesvirus 6 or human herpesvirus 7

explanation.summary: Tzanck cells, large multinucleated cells, indicate infection by a member of the alpha subfamily: HSV-1, HSV-2, or VZV.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that the presence of large, multinucleated cells from tissue samples, called Tzanck cells, indicates one of the members of the alpha subfamily, that is HSV-1, HSV-2, or varicella zoster virus. Because all three produce the same cytologic picture, the test narrows the field but does not identify which of the three is responsible, which is one reason PCR is preferred.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The finding is specific to the alpha subfamily rather than to all human herpesviruses.
whyWrongByChoice.B: CMV is not part of the alpha subfamily and is not what Tzanck cells indicate.
whyWrongByChoice.C: EBV infects B lymphocytes and does not produce this multinucleated epithelial giant cell picture.
whyWrongByChoice.E: HHV-6 and HHV-7 are not among the viruses the brick links to Tzanck cells.

questions.stem: Histologic examination of a biopsy from a herpesvirus skin lesion demonstrates Cowdry type A inclusions. These inclusions are best described as which of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Cytoplasmic basophilic inclusions within infected cells

choices.label: B
choices.text: Cytoplasmic eosinophilic inclusions within infected cells

choices.label: C
choices.text: Intranuclear basophilic inclusions within infected cells

choices.label: D
choices.text: Intranuclear eosinophilic inclusions within infected cells

choices.label: E
choices.text: Perinuclear clearing with no true inclusion bodies

explanation.summary: Cowdry type A inclusions are intranuclear eosinophilic inclusions induced by the alpha herpesviruses.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that the alpha herpesviruses, HSV-1, HSV-2, and VZV, can induce formation of Cowdry type A inclusions, which are intranuclear eosinophilic inclusions. Their location in the nucleus fits the biology of the family, since herpesvirus replication occurs in the host nucleus.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Cowdry type A inclusions are nuclear rather than cytoplasmic, and they stain eosinophilic.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The eosinophilic staining is correct but the location is wrong; these inclusions sit inside the nucleus.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The nuclear location is correct but Cowdry type A inclusions are eosinophilic, not basophilic.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Cowdry type A describes a true inclusion body, not simply a perinuclear halo.

questions.stem: An unvaccinated 5-year-old develops chicken pox about 2 weeks after a classmate became ill with the same illness. Which of the following is the most common route by which this virus entered his body?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Fecal-oral ingestion of contaminated drinking water

choices.label: B
choices.text: Ingestion of contaminated food at a shared school meal

choices.label: C
choices.text: Percutaneous inoculation by an arthropod vector bite

choices.label: D
choices.text: Respiratory droplets reaching the eyes and airway

choices.label: E
choices.text: Transfusion of contaminated blood or blood products

explanation.summary: The most common routes of entry for varicella zoster virus are the eyes and respiratory tract via respiratory droplets.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that the most common routes of entry for VZV are the eyes and respiratory tract by respiratory droplets, and that direct contact with lesions can also spread the virus. This respiratory route is why chicken pox moves so efficiently through classrooms, in contrast to HSV, which requires contact with infected body fluid or a lesion.

whyWrongByChoice.A: VZV is an enveloped virus spread by droplets and lesion contact, not by the fecal-oral route.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Foodborne transmission is not a route for this respiratory and contact-spread virus.
whyWrongByChoice.C: No arthropod vector transmits varicella zoster virus.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Transfusion is not a described route of VZV acquisition.

questions.stem: After varicella zoster virus replicates in local epithelial cells and spreads to regional lymph nodes, which of the following best describes the next steps that produce the widespread skin rash?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It infects erythrocytes, which carry it to skin capillary beds

choices.label: B
choices.text: It replicates in marrow, then reaches the skin in neutrophils

choices.label: C
choices.text: It seeds spleen and liver, then reaches skin in mononuclear cells

choices.label: D
choices.text: It spreads along lymphatic channels directly into the epidermis

choices.label: E
choices.text: It travels up peripheral sensory nerves directly into the dermis

explanation.summary: VZV disseminates from regional lymph nodes to the spleen and liver and is then carried to the skin by mononuclear cells.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick traces the pathway explicitly: viral replication starts in local epithelial cells and spreads to regional lymph nodes, the virus quickly disseminates to the spleen and liver, and it is also transported to the skin by mononuclear cells where it infects epithelial cells, causing fluid-filled vesicles that rupture and form ulcers. This cell-associated viremia is why chicken pox produces a diffuse rash rather than a lesion at one inoculation site.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Erythrocytes are not described as the vehicle carrying VZV to the skin.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Bone marrow replication and neutrophil transport are not part of the described VZV pathway.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Regional lymph nodes are an early step, but the virus reaches skin through the bloodstream within mononuclear cells.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Neuronal transport is how VZV reaches ganglia to establish latency, not how the primary rash is distributed.

questions.stem: A 6-year-old with fever, malaise, and headache develops a vesicular rash, and lesions are also noted on the buccal mucosa. Which of the following best describes the typical distribution of this rash?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It begins on the hands and spreads centrally toward the trunk

choices.label: B
choices.text: It begins on the lower legs and spreads upward to the trunk

choices.label: C
choices.text: It begins on the palms and soles and spreads to the trunk

choices.label: D
choices.text: It begins on the trunk and spreads to the limbs and face

choices.label: E
choices.text: It remains confined to one dermatome on one side of the body

explanation.summary: Chicken pox vesicles typically appear on the trunk first and then spread to the limbs and face, and may involve the buccal and pharyngeal mucosa.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that chicken pox vesicles typically appear on the trunk first and spread to the limbs and face, that the buccal and pharyngeal mucosa of the mouth may also be affected, and that early symptoms include fever, malaise, and headache. Individual lesions progress through the same papule-vesicle-ulcer-crust sequence seen with HSV.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Spread is centrifugal, from trunk outward, rather than starting on the hands.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The rash is described as starting centrally on the trunk rather than ascending from the legs.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A palms-and-soles onset is not the pattern described for varicella.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A single unilateral dermatome describes shingles, the reactivation syndrome, not primary chicken pox.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old man with advanced HIV infection develops chicken pox and then becomes dyspneic and hypoxemic; chest radiography shows diffuse speckled opacities throughout both lungs. Which of the following best explains this course?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Bacterial superinfection never complicates chicken pox in adults

choices.label: B
choices.text: Chicken pox is uniformly severe in adults regardless of immunity

choices.label: C
choices.text: Lung involvement by VZV occurs only in previously vaccinated patients

choices.label: D
choices.text: Pulmonary disease occurs only during reactivation of VZV as shingles

choices.label: E
choices.text: Severe complications such as pneumonia occur in the immunocompromised

explanation.summary: Chicken pox mortality is low overall, but encephalitis, pneumonia, bacterial superinfection, and dissemination occur in neonates and the severely immunocompromised.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that mortality is low for chicken pox but severe complications can occur in neonates and severely immunocompromised patients such as those with HIV and organ transplant recipients. Encephalitis, pneumonia, secondary bacterial infections, and disseminated infection are listed as potential complications of either primary infection or reactivation, and they can be lethal. The speckled appearance in the lungs is illustrated in the brick as VZV pneumonia.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Secondary bacterial infection is explicitly listed as a potential complication of chicken pox.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Chicken pox is usually mild; severity here is driven by the patient's immunosuppression, not by adult age alone.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Vaccination reduces disease; it is not a prerequisite for pulmonary involvement.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The listed complications can follow either primary infection or reactivation of VZV.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old man has a painful vesicular rash forming a band across the left side of his chest that stops abruptly at the midline. He had chicken pox as a child. Which of the following best explains this presentation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Allergic contact dermatitis from a newly applied topical agent

choices.label: B
choices.text: Autoinoculation of herpes simplex virus from an oral lesion

choices.label: C
choices.text: Disseminated herpes simplex virus infection involving the skin

choices.label: D
choices.text: Reactivation of varicella zoster virus in a single dermatome

choices.label: E
choices.text: Recently acquired primary infection with varicella zoster virus

explanation.summary: Shingles is reactivation of latent VZV, producing a painful vesicular rash in strips on one or a few dermatomes on one side of the body.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that reactivation of VZV presents as a particularly painful vesicular rash called shingles, or herpes zoster, and that the rash typically manifests on one side of the body, usually in strips on singular dermatomes. Inflammation of the sensory nerves and ganglia in which the virus was latent is what makes the rash so painful, and fever, headache, chills, and upset stomach may accompany it.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Contact dermatitis follows the area of exposure and would not respect a dermatome or produce a painful prodrome.
whyWrongByChoice.B: HSV autoinoculation produces localized lesions at the inoculated site, not a dermatomal stripe.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Disseminated HSV occurs in severely immunocompromised hosts and is widespread rather than dermatomal.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Primary VZV infection is chicken pox, a diffuse rash starting on the trunk, not a unilateral dermatomal band.

questions.stem: Six weeks after her shingles rash cleared, a 78-year-old woman still has severe burning pain confined to the flank where the rash had been. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Aseptic meningitis caused by the same virus

choices.label: B
choices.text: Bacterial superinfection of the healed skin

choices.label: C
choices.text: Herpetic whitlow spreading to the flank

choices.label: D
choices.text: Postherpetic neuralgia after the rash resolves

choices.label: E
choices.text: Recurrent chicken pox in the same dermatome

explanation.summary: Postherpetic neuralgia is severe pain persisting in the area of a shingles rash after the rash has cleared, and it is common in the elderly.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick describes postherpetic neuralgia as a common complication of shingles in the elderly, in which people have severe pain in the areas where they had the shingles rash even after the rash clears up. The pain may be severe and debilitating and can last weeks to months, and rarely for years.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Aseptic meningitis causes headache and meningeal signs, not localized dermatomal pain weeks after a rash.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Bacterial superinfection would produce local signs of infection rather than isolated neuropathic pain in healed skin.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Herpetic whitlow is an HSV infection of the fingers and does not explain flank pain.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Primary varicella does not recur; reactivation presents as shingles, and this patient's rash has already resolved.

questions.stem: A healthy 62-year-old woman who had chicken pox as a child asks whether she should be vaccinated against shingles. Which of the following best describes the appropriate product and its purpose?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A daily oral antiviral taken indefinitely to suppress reactivation

choices.label: B
choices.text: A live attenuated vaccine for children that prevents chicken pox

choices.label: C
choices.text: A more potent vaccine for adults over 50 that prevents reactivation

choices.label: D
choices.text: A vaccine given only once shingles symptoms have already begun

choices.label: E
choices.text: An antibody preparation given after exposure to a shingles rash

explanation.summary: Two VZV vaccines exist: a live attenuated childhood vaccine that prevents chicken pox and a more potent adult vaccine, Shingrix, that prevents reactivation as shingles.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick describes a live attenuated vaccine used in children that prevents 85% of chicken pox cases and 99% of severe chicken pox sequelae, and a more potent version, Shingrix, recommended for adults over 50 and patients with certain medical conditions, which prevents the reactivation of VZV and therefore prevents shingles. This woman already has latent virus, so the adult product aimed at reactivation is the relevant one; over half of shingles cases occur in people over 60, and waning immunity is strongly implicated in reactivation.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The brick describes vaccination, not indefinite antiviral suppression, as the means of preventing reactivation.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The live attenuated pediatric vaccine prevents primary chicken pox and is not the product aimed at preventing shingles in an adult who is already latently infected.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Shingrix is given for prevention before reactivation, not as a treatment after symptoms begin.
whyWrongByChoice.E: No post-exposure antibody preparation is described as the strategy for preventing shingles.

questions.stem: A 19-year-old college student recovers from an illness with fever, sore throat, and cervical adenopathy. Six years later, while receiving immunosuppressive therapy after a kidney transplant, the same virus reactivates. This virus establishes latency primarily in which of the following cell types?

choices.label: A
choices.text: B lymphocytes

choices.label: B
choices.text: Bone marrow progenitor cells

choices.label: C
choices.text: CD4+ T lymphocytes of the peripheral blood

choices.label: D
choices.text: Monocytes and tissue macrophages

choices.label: E
choices.text: Renal tubular epithelial cells

explanation.summary: Epstein-Barr virus establishes latency primarily in B lymphocytes.
explanation.whyCorrect: EBV, like other herpesviruses, causes latent infections that can reactivate when the host becomes immunosuppressed. Latency is established primarily in B lymphocytes, although the virus can also be found in epithelial cells and other cell types. This is why immunosuppression after transplantation can allow the virus to re-emerge.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Bone marrow progenitor cells are among the cells in which CMV establishes latency.
whyWrongByChoice.C: CD4+ T cells harbor latent human herpesvirus 6 and 7, not EBV.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Monocytes and macrophages are sites of cytomegalovirus latency, not EBV latency.
whyWrongByChoice.E: CMV latent infections are commonly established in the kidneys; EBV does not use renal tubular cells as its principal reservoir.

questions.stem: A laboratory studies how Epstein-Barr virus enters its principal host cell. A viral glycoprotein is shown to attach to a surface molecule that is also known as CR2. Binding to which of the following surface molecules allows the virus to enter the cell?

choices.label: A
choices.text: CD3

choices.label: B
choices.text: CD4

choices.label: C
choices.text: CD8

choices.label: D
choices.text: CD19

choices.label: E
choices.text: CD21

explanation.summary: EBV uses a viral glycoprotein to bind CD21 (CR2) on B cells.
explanation.whyCorrect: EBV attaches to its target cell through a viral glycoprotein that binds CD21, also known as CR2. CD21 is a surface marker commonly found on B cells, which explains why B lymphocytes are the principal site of EBV infection and latency.

whyWrongByChoice.A: CD3 is part of the T cell receptor complex and is not used by EBV for entry.
whyWrongByChoice.B: CD4 is not the EBV receptor; CD4+ T cells are the latency site for HHV-6 and HHV-7.
whyWrongByChoice.C: CD8 is a T cell molecule and plays no role in EBV attachment.
whyWrongByChoice.D: CD19 is a B cell marker, but the brick identifies CD21/CR2 as the molecule EBV binds.

questions.stem: A healthy 30-year-old man with no history of infectious mononucleosis asks whether he has ever been infected with Epstein-Barr virus. Approximately what proportion of adults have been infected with EBV and carry antibodies to the virus?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Fewer than 10%

choices.label: B
choices.text: About 25%

choices.label: C
choices.text: About 50%

choices.label: D
choices.text: About 75%

choices.label: E
choices.text: More than 90%

explanation.summary: By adulthood, more than 90% of individuals have been infected with EBV.
explanation.whyCorrect: Most people acquire several herpesviruses before adulthood, and latency is established early. By adulthood, more than 90% of individuals have been infected with EBV and have antibodies to the virus, and many were completely asymptomatic at the time of primary infection.

whyWrongByChoice.A: This drastically understates EBV seroprevalence, which is near-universal in adults.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A quarter of adults is far below the observed seroprevalence of EBV.
whyWrongByChoice.C: About half is closer to the seroprevalence of CMV by age 40, not EBV in adults.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Three-quarters still understates the greater than 90% figure for adults.

questions.stem: A 17-year-old girl feels entirely well and has no symptoms, but she is known to be EBV seropositive. Her boyfriend develops infectious mononucleosis three weeks after they begin dating. Which of the following best explains how she transmitted the virus?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Aerosol spread of virus from the lower respiratory tract

choices.label: B
choices.text: Bloodborne spread of virus from latently infected B lymphocytes

choices.label: C
choices.text: Sexual transmission of virus present in semen and cervical fluid

choices.label: D
choices.text: Shedding of virus in oral secretions

choices.label: E
choices.text: Shedding of virus in urine from chronically infected renal tubules

explanation.summary: EBV is spread predominantly by oral secretions, and asymptomatic carriers still shed virus.
explanation.whyCorrect: EBV infects the epithelium of the oropharynx and the salivary glands and is shed from these cells, which is why mononucleosis is called the kissing disease. Even asymptomatic patients shed virus to some degree in oral secretions, so they remain infectious and can readily spread the disease to others.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The brick describes spread by oral secretions, not by aerosols from the lower airway.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Latently infected B cells are the viral reservoir, but person-to-person spread is by oral secretions rather than blood.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Semen is listed as a body fluid that transmits cytomegalovirus, not EBV.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Urine is a recognized vehicle for cytomegalovirus transmission, not for EBV.

questions.stem: A 5-year-old boy and his 22-year-old aunt are both infected with Epstein-Barr virus during the same household outbreak. Compared with his aunt, the boy is most likely to have which of the following presentations?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Blueberry muffin rash with hepatosplenomegaly

choices.label: B
choices.text: Classic mononucleosis with weeks of disabling fatigue

choices.label: C
choices.text: High fever followed by a rash that begins on the trunk

choices.label: D
choices.text: Mild pharyngitis with or without tonsillitis

choices.label: E
choices.text: Oral hairy leukoplakia on the lateral borders of the tongue

explanation.summary: EBV in children usually causes mild pharyngitis, while adults get classic mononucleosis.
explanation.whyCorrect: The clinical manifestations of EBV depend on the patient's age. In children, most cases present as a mild pharyngitis with or without tonsillitis, whereas in adults the presentation is most commonly the classic symptoms of mononucleosis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A blueberry muffin rash with hepatosplenomegaly describes congenital cytomegalovirus infection in a neonate.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Classic mononucleosis is the adult presentation, which is what his aunt would be expected to develop.
whyWrongByChoice.C: High fever followed by a truncal rash as the fever breaks is roseola infantum caused by HHV-6/7.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Oral hairy leukoplakia occurs in patients with AIDS and the severely immunosuppressed, not in healthy children.

questions.stem: A 20-year-old woman with serologically confirmed infectious mononucleosis is otherwise healthy and asks how long she will feel ill. Which of the following is the most accurate counseling?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Most symptoms resolve in 2 to 4 weeks, but fatigue may last for months

choices.label: B
choices.text: Most symptoms resolve within 48 hours of starting antiviral therapy

choices.label: C
choices.text: Symptoms last 3 to 5 days and end abruptly as a rash appears

choices.label: D
choices.text: Symptoms recur predictably every few weeks for the rest of her life

choices.label: E
choices.text: Symptoms usually persist for 6 to 12 months in healthy patients

explanation.summary: Mononucleosis symptoms usually persist 2 to 4 weeks, though fatigue can linger for months.
explanation.whyCorrect: In the majority of patients with mononucleosis, symptoms persist for 2 to 4 weeks. Some symptoms, especially fatigue, may persist for months. Complications of EBV are rare in otherwise healthy patients.

whyWrongByChoice.B: The brick describes no antiviral therapy that truncates mononucleosis to two days.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A 3 to 5 day fever ending as a rash appears describes roseola infantum, not mononucleosis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Predictable lifelong recurrences are not a feature of EBV infection in a healthy host.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Six to twelve months overstates the usual course; only fatigue tends to linger.

questions.stem: A 41-year-old man with untreated HIV infection and a CD4 count of 90/uL has raised, white, corrugated lesions along the lateral borders of his tongue. Biopsy of the lesions contains herpesvirus DNA. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Cytomegalovirus esophagitis

choices.label: B
choices.text: Nasopharyngeal carcinoma

choices.label: C
choices.text: Oral hairy leukoplakia

choices.label: D
choices.text: Roseola infantum

choices.label: E
choices.text: Thrush

explanation.summary: Oral hairy leukoplakia is an EBV lesion of the lateral tongue seen in AIDS and severe immunosuppression.
explanation.whyCorrect: In patients with AIDS and the severely immunosuppressed, oral hairy leukoplakia is a common clinical presentation caused by EBV. Patients present with raised, white, corrugated lesions on the lateral sides of the tongue, and occasionally the buccal mucosa, and these lesions contain EBV DNA.

whyWrongByChoice.A: CMV esophagitis presents with esophageal symptoms rather than corrugated tongue plaques.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Nasopharyngeal carcinoma is an EBV-associated malignancy of the nasopharynx, not a tongue plaque.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Roseola infantum is a febrile exanthem of young children caused by HHV-6/7.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Thrush is a fungal infection caused by Candida species and would not contain herpesvirus DNA.

questions.stem: A physician examines a severely immunosuppressed patient with white plaques on the tongue and wants to distinguish oral hairy leukoplakia from thrush at the bedside. Which of the following findings would most strongly favor thrush?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Lesions confined strictly to the lateral borders of the tongue

choices.label: B
choices.text: Lesions shown to contain viral DNA when a biopsy is taken

choices.label: C
choices.text: Lesions that appeared only as the patient's immunity declined

choices.label: D
choices.text: Lesions that are easily removed from the tongue by light scraping

choices.label: E
choices.text: Lesions with a raised, white, corrugated plaque-like surface

explanation.summary: Thrush scrapes off the tongue easily, whereas oral hairy leukoplakia does not.
explanation.whyCorrect: Thrush and oral hairy leukoplakia have a very similar clinical appearance, so a quick scrape test is used to distinguish them before laboratory testing. Thrush can easily be removed from the tongue with light scraping, while the plaque-like lesion of oral hairy leukoplakia is much more difficult to scrape off.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The lateral borders of the tongue are the classic site of oral hairy leukoplakia.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Lesions containing viral DNA point to oral hairy leukoplakia, since thrush is fungal.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Both lesions can be caused by a weakening immune system, so this does not separate them.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A raised, white, corrugated surface describes the appearance of oral hairy leukoplakia.

questions.stem: Two immunosuppressed patients present with white oral lesions, and one of them has just finished a 10-day course of broad-spectrum antibiotics. Which of the following statements about antibiotic use and these two lesions is correct?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Antibiotic therapy reliably clears both lesions within several days

choices.label: B
choices.text: Both thrush and oral hairy leukoplakia frequently follow antibiotic use

choices.label: C
choices.text: Neither lesion is related to antibiotic use or to the patient's immune status

choices.label: D
choices.text: Oral hairy leukoplakia frequently follows antibiotic use, but thrush does not

choices.label: E
choices.text: Thrush frequently follows antibiotic use, but oral hairy leukoplakia does not

explanation.summary: Thrush often follows antibiotic use; oral hairy leukoplakia has no such correlation.
explanation.whyCorrect: Both thrush and oral hairy leukoplakia can be caused by a weakening immune system, but thrush also frequently occurs after antibiotic use because antibiotics disturb the normal flora that hold Candida in check. There is no correlation between oral hairy leukoplakia and antibiotic use.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Antibiotics predispose to thrush rather than curing it, and they have no effect on an EBV lesion.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Only thrush shows the antibiotic association; oral hairy leukoplakia does not.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Both lesions are linked to a weakening immune system, and thrush is additionally linked to antibiotics.
whyWrongByChoice.D: This reverses the relationship described in the brick.

questions.stem: A 9-year-old boy in the United States is diagnosed with Burkitt's lymphoma, a B cell cancer, and the tumor cells are tested for Epstein-Barr virus. In the United States, approximately what percentage of Burkitt's lymphoma cases are associated with EBV?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Less than 1%

choices.label: B
choices.text: About 5%

choices.label: C
choices.text: About 9%

choices.label: D
choices.text: About 15%

choices.label: E
choices.text: About 40%

explanation.summary: In the U.S., about 15% of Burkitt's lymphoma cases are EBV-associated.
explanation.whyCorrect: Burkitt's lymphoma is a B cell cancer that is one of the malignancies linked to EBV. In the United States, 15% of Burkitt's lymphoma cases are associated with EBV, a much smaller fraction than is seen in Africa.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Less than 1% would make the association negligible, which is not the case.
whyWrongByChoice.B: About 5% understates the U.S. association with Burkitt's lymphoma.
whyWrongByChoice.C: About 9% is the figure for EBV-associated gastric carcinoma worldwide.
whyWrongByChoice.E: About 40% approaches the upper end of the figure for EBV-positive Hodgkin's lymphomas.

questions.stem: In equatorial Africa, roughly 90% of Burkitt's lymphoma cases are associated with Epstein-Barr virus, a far higher proportion than in the United States. Coinfection with which of the following is thought to contribute to this difference by causing EBV-infected B cells to proliferate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Candida species

choices.label: B
choices.text: Helicobacter pylori

choices.label: C
choices.text: Human herpesvirus 6

choices.label: D
choices.text: Mycobacterium tuberculosis

choices.label: E
choices.text: Plasmodium species

explanation.summary: Malaria coinfection drives proliferation of EBV-infected B cells and promotes Burkitt's lymphoma in Africa.
explanation.whyCorrect: In Africa, 90% of Burkitt's lymphoma cases are associated with EBV. Coinfection with malaria may cause EBV-infected B cells to proliferate, enhancing viral spread and promoting tumorigenesis. HIV infection likewise increases the risk of EBV-associated Burkitt's lymphoma.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Candida causes thrush and has no described role in driving B cell proliferation.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Helicobacter pylori is a gastric pathogen and is not the cofactor described for Burkitt's lymphoma.
whyWrongByChoice.C: HHV-6 causes roseola infantum and is not implicated in Burkitt's lymphoma.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Tuberculosis is not described as a cofactor for EBV-associated lymphomagenesis.

questions.stem: A pathologist surveys gastric carcinoma specimens collected worldwide and tests each tumor for Epstein-Barr virus. Approximately what proportion of gastric carcinomas worldwide are associated with EBV?

choices.label: A
choices.text: About 1%

choices.label: B
choices.text: About 5%

choices.label: C
choices.text: About 9%

choices.label: D
choices.text: About 20%

choices.label: E
choices.text: About 35%

explanation.summary: About 9% of gastric carcinomas worldwide are EBV-associated.
explanation.whyCorrect: Gastric carcinoma is one of several malignancies linked to EBV infection. Worldwide, about 9% of gastric carcinoma cases are associated with EBV, making it a substantial but minority share of this common cancer.

whyWrongByChoice.A: About 1% would make the link trivial, which understates the association.
whyWrongByChoice.B: About 5% is below the reported worldwide figure for gastric carcinoma.
whyWrongByChoice.D: About 20% is the lower end of the range for EBV-positive Hodgkin's lymphomas.
whyWrongByChoice.E: About 35% substantially overstates the association with gastric carcinoma.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old man with HIV infection develops painless cervical lymphadenopathy, night sweats, and weight loss. Lymph node biopsy shows Hodgkin's disease. Which of the following viruses is most strongly associated with this malignancy, particularly in HIV-positive patients?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Cytomegalovirus

choices.label: B
choices.text: Epstein-Barr virus

choices.label: C
choices.text: Herpes simplex virus type 2

choices.label: D
choices.text: Human herpesvirus 7

choices.label: E
choices.text: Varicella-zoster virus

explanation.summary: EBV is strongly associated with Hodgkin's disease, especially in HIV-positive patients.
explanation.whyCorrect: EBV is strongly associated with Hodgkin's disease, and the association is particularly pronounced in HIV-positive patients. About 20 to 40% of Hodgkin's lymphomas are EBV-positive. EBV-associated cancers in general are more prevalent in HIV-positive populations.

whyWrongByChoice.A: CMV causes mononucleosis-like illness and end-organ disease, but is not linked to lymphomas.
whyWrongByChoice.C: HSV-2 is not among the herpesviruses associated with lymphoma in this brick.
whyWrongByChoice.D: HHV-7 causes a roseola-like illness in young children and is not linked to Hodgkin's disease.
whyWrongByChoice.E: VZV has no described association with Hodgkin's disease.

questions.stem: A 52-year-old man develops a nasopharyngeal mass, and biopsy shows a carcinoma that contains Epstein-Barr virus genome within the tumor cells. This EBV-associated malignancy is described as endemic in which of the following groups of regions?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Central Europe, Japan, and the Caribbean

choices.label: B
choices.text: Northern Europe, Australia, and New Zealand

choices.label: C
choices.text: South America, India, and the Middle East

choices.label: D
choices.text: Southeast Asia, North Africa, and the Arctic

choices.label: E
choices.text: The United States, Canada, and Mexico

explanation.summary: EBV-associated nasopharyngeal carcinoma is endemic in Southeast Asia, North Africa, and the Arctic.
explanation.whyCorrect: EBV is strongly associated with nasopharyngeal carcinoma, particularly in endemic regions such as Southeast Asia, North Africa, and the Arctic. EBV-associated cancer risk varies across the globe and reflects a complex combination of genetics, diet, comorbidities, and socioeconomic factors.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Central Europe, Japan, and the Caribbean are not the endemic regions described.
whyWrongByChoice.B: These regions are not listed among the endemic areas for nasopharyngeal carcinoma.
whyWrongByChoice.C: South America, India, and the Middle East are not the endemic regions described.
whyWrongByChoice.E: North America is not an endemic region for EBV-associated nasopharyngeal carcinoma.

questions.stem: A 23-year-old woman has had fever, pharyngitis, and cervical adenopathy for 8 days, and severe illness prompts serologic testing. Which of the following results would best confirm that her Epstein-Barr virus infection was acquired recently?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A negative monospot test on the patient's serum

choices.label: B
choices.text: Anti-VCA IgG alone at a stable titer

choices.label: C
choices.text: Anti-VCA IgM in the patient's serum

choices.label: D
choices.text: Atypical lymphocytes on the peripheral blood smear

choices.label: E
choices.text: Owl's eye intranuclear inclusions on tissue histology

explanation.summary: IgM antibodies to viral capsid antigen appear early and confirm recent EBV infection.
explanation.whyCorrect: Rarely are labs needed to diagnose mononucleosis, but in severe cases serology is useful. IgM antibodies against viral capsule antigens (VCA) appear early in infection and can be used to confirm a recent infection with EBV. Anti-VCA IgM usually disappears 2 to 4 weeks after infection, although it may persist in some patients.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A negative monospot does not confirm anything about recency and is common in some demographics.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Anti-VCA IgG stays with the patient for life, so a stable titer cannot date the infection.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Atypical lymphocytes support a mononucleosis syndrome but do not establish timing or the specific agent.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Owl's eye inclusions indicate cytomegalovirus rather than recent EBV infection.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old man is found to have anti-VCA IgG during a workup for fatigue, with no other serologic abnormalities. Which of the following best describes the behavior of anti-VCA IgG after Epstein-Barr virus infection?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It appears only during reactivation in immunosuppressed patients

choices.label: B
choices.text: It appears within 24 hours and is gone by the end of the first week

choices.label: C
choices.text: It is detectable only in patients who develop an EBV-associated cancer

choices.label: D
choices.text: It is directed against animal red blood cells rather than viral antigens

choices.label: E
choices.text: It peaks 2 to 4 weeks after infection and persists for the rest of life

explanation.summary: Anti-VCA IgG peaks 2 to 4 weeks after infection and persists for life.
explanation.whyCorrect: Anti-VCA IgG peaks 2 to 4 weeks after infection and stays with a patient for the rest of their life. Used together, anti-VCA IgM and anti-VCA IgG allow a clinician to determine whether a patient was infected recently or in the past.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Anti-VCA IgG is produced after primary infection in immunocompetent hosts, not only on reactivation.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A rapid rise and fall within one week does not describe either anti-VCA antibody.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Most adults carry anti-VCA IgG, and the vast majority never develop an EBV-associated cancer.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Antibodies reactive across animal species are heterophile antibodies, which are not anti-VCA.

questions.stem: A laboratory performs a monospot test by adding dilutions of a patient's serum to horse erythrocytes, and agglutination of the erythrocytes is observed. This result indicates the presence of which of the following in the patient's serum?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Anti-VCA IgM directed at the viral capsid antigen

choices.label: B
choices.text: Antibodies specific for EBV nuclear antigens

choices.label: C
choices.text: Complement components activated by viral antigen

choices.label: D
choices.text: Heterophile antibodies reactive across animal species

choices.label: E
choices.text: Viral DNA amplified from circulating B lymphocytes

explanation.summary: The monospot test detects heterophile antibodies by agglutination of animal red blood cells.
explanation.whyCorrect: The monospot test checks for the presence of heterophile antibodies, which react with antigens across multiple animal species. Detection is done by adding patient serum to animal red blood cells, commonly sheep, horse, or cow erythrocytes. Agglutination indicates the presence of heterophile antibodies, and serial dilutions of serum establish the titer.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Anti-VCA IgM is measured by specific serology, not by agglutinating animal erythrocytes.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Antibodies against EBV antigens are not what the agglutination reaction demonstrates.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The monospot reaction depends on antibody cross-reactivity, not on complement activation.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Viral DNA is detected by PCR, which is a separate laboratory method.

questions.stem: A student asks why heterophile antibodies are considered only an indirect indicator of Epstein-Barr virus infection. Which of the following best answers the question?

choices.label: A
choices.text: They are detected in essentially every patient who is infected with EBV

choices.label: B
choices.text: They are produced only weeks after the acute illness has fully resolved

choices.label: C
choices.text: They are secreted by EBV-infected B lymphocytes rather than by the host

choices.label: D
choices.text: They bind the EBV capsid antigen, but only with a very low binding affinity

choices.label: E
choices.text: They do not bind EBV antigens and are simply made alongside anti-EBV antibodies

explanation.summary: Heterophile antibodies do not bind EBV antigens; they are simply made alongside the anti-EBV response.
explanation.whyCorrect: Heterophile antibodies react with antigens across multiple animal species but do not bind EBV antigens at all. The host's immune response just happens to produce them alongside the anti-EBV antibodies. For that reason, their presence only indirectly indicates an EBV infection.

whyWrongByChoice.A: They are frequently absent in children, the elderly, and the severely immunosuppressed.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Heterophile antibodies are detectable during acute illness, which is when the monospot is used.
whyWrongByChoice.C: They are host antibodies produced by the patient's immune response, not by infected B cells.
whyWrongByChoice.D: They do not bind EBV antigens even with low affinity; they are directed elsewhere.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old woman with systemic lupus erythematosus has a positive monospot test but no clinical evidence of mononucleosis and no lymphocytosis. Which of the following best explains this result?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Lupus autoantibodies bind EBV viral capsid antigen directly

choices.label: B
choices.text: Lupus causes reactivation of latent EBV in the salivary epithelium

choices.label: C
choices.text: Other conditions, including lupus, can raise heterophile antibody titers

choices.label: D
choices.text: The monospot test cross-reacts with cytomegalovirus surface antigens

choices.label: E
choices.text: The monospot test detects anti-VCA IgM, which persists for life

explanation.summary: The monospot is imperfect because other diseases raise heterophile antibody titers.
explanation.whyCorrect: The monospot test is not perfect, since other diseases and infections can cause a rise in heterophile antibody titers. False-positive monospot results are more common among people with connective tissue disease, lymphoma, viral hepatitis, lupus, and malaria. This is one reason the CDC no longer recommends the test.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Heterophile antibodies do not bind EBV antigens at all, so direct binding does not explain the result.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The brick attributes false positives to elevated heterophile titers, not to EBV reactivation in lupus.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The false positive reflects nonspecific heterophile antibodies rather than cross-reaction with CMV antigens.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The monospot detects heterophile antibodies, not anti-VCA IgM, and IgG is the lifelong marker.

questions.stem: A 4-year-old boy and an 80-year-old woman each have serologically confirmed Epstein-Barr virus infection, yet both have negative monospot tests. Which of the following best explains these results?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Children and the elderly clear EBV before any antibody can be produced

choices.label: B
choices.text: Children, the elderly, and the immunosuppressed are often heterophile negative

choices.label: C
choices.text: Heterophile antibodies are neutralized by anti-VCA IgG in these age groups

choices.label: D
choices.text: Heterophile antibodies are produced only when EBV reactivates from latency

choices.label: E
choices.text: The monospot test requires atypical lymphocytes to be present in the blood

explanation.summary: Children, the elderly, and the severely immunosuppressed with EBV are frequently heterophile antibody negative.
explanation.whyCorrect: Children, the elderly, and the severely immunosuppressed who have EBV are frequently heterophile antibody negative, so the monospot test has little use in these demographics. In such patients, EBV-specific serology or other testing is needed rather than relying on a heterophile assay.

whyWrongByChoice.A: EBV establishes lifelong latency and elicits antibodies; it is not cleared before seroconversion.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Anti-VCA IgG does not neutralize heterophile antibodies; the two responses are unrelated.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Heterophile antibodies arise during primary infection, not exclusively with reactivation.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The monospot is a serum agglutination assay and does not depend on circulating atypical lymphocytes.

questions.stem: A 21-year-old man is in the third week of an illness caused by Epstein-Barr virus, and a complete blood count is obtained. Which of the following white blood cell counts is most consistent with this illness?

explanation.summary: In EBV infection the white blood cell count peaks at 12,000 to 25,000/uL in the second or third week.
explanation.whyCorrect: In patients with EBV, the white blood cell count is usually elevated and peaks at 12,000 to 25,000/uL during the second or third week of illness. Lymphocytosis is usually demonstrable, with more than 10% atypical lymphocytes on the smear.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Leukopenia is not the expected finding; EBV typically raises the white blood cell count.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A normal count of 4,500/uL would be unexpected at the peak of an EBV illness.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A count of 35,000/uL exceeds the range described for EBV and suggests another process.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A count of 60,000/uL is far above the peak described for infectious mononucleosis.

questions.stem: A peripheral blood smear from a patient with mononucleosis shows that more than 10% of the lymphocytes are enlarged, with abundant cytoplasm, vacuoles, and indentations of the cell membrane. These cells are best described as which of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Blast cells of a B cell lymphoma

choices.label: B
choices.text: Downey cells

choices.label: C
choices.text: Giant multinucleated cells

choices.label: D
choices.text: Owl's eye inclusion cells

choices.label: E
choices.text: Tzanck cells

explanation.summary: Atypical lymphocytes in mononucleosis are called Downey cells.
explanation.whyCorrect: Lymphocytosis is usually demonstrable in EBV infection, with more than 10% atypical lymphocytes called Downey cells. These cells tend to be enlarged, with abundant cytoplasm, vacuoles, and indentations of the cell membrane. CMV can occasionally produce the same cells when it causes a mononucleosis-like illness.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The smear shows reactive lymphocytes of an acute infection, not malignant blasts.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Giant multinucleated cells describe the Tzanck preparation rather than atypical lymphocytes.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Owl's eye inclusion cells are the enlarged cells with intranuclear inclusions caused by CMV.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Tzanck cells are the large multinucleated cells produced by HSV-1, HSV-2, and VZV.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old woman has 2 weeks of fever, fatigue, and lymphadenopathy with a lymphocytosis, but her heterophile antibody test is repeatedly negative. Epstein-Barr virus causes roughly 90% of mononucleosis cases. Which of the following is the most likely cause of her heterophile antibody negative illness?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Cytomegalovirus

choices.label: B
choices.text: Herpes simplex virus type 1

choices.label: C
choices.text: Human herpesvirus 6

choices.label: D
choices.text: Human herpesvirus 7

choices.label: E
choices.text: Varicella-zoster virus

explanation.summary: Cytomegalovirus is the most common cause of heterophile antibody negative mononucleosis.
explanation.whyCorrect: EBV is the most common cause of mononucleosis, accounting for roughly 90% of cases. The most common cause of heterophile antibody negative mononucleosis is cytomegalovirus, which accounts for 5 to 10% of mononucleosis-like cases and is clinically indistinguishable from EBV mononucleosis by symptoms alone.

whyWrongByChoice.B: HSV-1 is not described as a cause of heterophile-negative mononucleosis.
whyWrongByChoice.C: HHV-6 causes roseola infantum in young children rather than a mononucleosis-like syndrome in adults.
whyWrongByChoice.D: HHV-7 causes a milder roseola-like illness, not heterophile-negative mononucleosis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: VZV is not among the causes of a mononucleosis-like illness described here.

questions.stem: A tissue biopsy from an immunocompromised patient shows massively enlarged cells, each containing a dense intracellular inclusion surrounding the nucleus that gives an owl's eye appearance. Which of the following viruses is most likely responsible?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Cytomegalovirus

choices.label: B
choices.text: Epstein-Barr virus

choices.label: C
choices.text: Herpes simplex virus type 1

choices.label: D
choices.text: Human herpesvirus 6

choices.label: E
choices.text: Human herpesvirus 7

explanation.summary: Massively enlarged cells with owl's eye inclusions are characteristic of cytomegalovirus.
explanation.whyCorrect: Cytomegalovirus takes its name from the morphology of infected cells: they are massively enlarged, from the Greek cyto for cell and megalo for large. In addition to their large size, cells infected with CMV have an owl's eye appearance created by an inclusion surrounding the nucleus.

whyWrongByChoice.B: EBV produces atypical lymphocytes called Downey cells rather than owl's eye inclusions.
whyWrongByChoice.C: HSV-1 produces Tzanck cells, which are large multinucleated cells.
whyWrongByChoice.D: HHV-6 causes roseola infantum and is not identified by owl's eye inclusions.
whyWrongByChoice.E: HHV-7 causes a milder roseola-like illness and has no such histologic hallmark.

questions.stem: A woman who is shedding cytomegalovirus asks how the virus can be passed to other people. Transmission of CMV occurs through close contact and through which of the following groups of body fluids?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Aerosolized respiratory droplets only, with no fluid-borne spread

choices.label: B
choices.text: Amniotic fluid and synovial fluid, but not saliva or semen

choices.label: C
choices.text: Bile, gastric juice, and pancreatic secretions, but not urine

choices.label: D
choices.text: Sweat, tears, and cerebrospinal fluid, but not saliva or blood

choices.label: E
choices.text: Urine, saliva, blood, breast milk, and semen

explanation.summary: CMV spreads by close contact and through urine, saliva, blood, breast milk, and semen.
explanation.whyCorrect: CMV is spread from person to person through close contact or transmission of body fluids: urine, saliva, blood, breast milk, and semen. CMV is frequently present in the salivary glands, although the virus can be found systemically in multiple organs and also in leukocytes.

whyWrongByChoice.A: CMV spreads through body fluids and close contact rather than by aerosols alone.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Saliva and semen are both listed routes of CMV transmission.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Gastrointestinal secretions are not the described route, and urine is a major vehicle.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Saliva and blood are important vehicles for CMV, so excluding them is incorrect.

questions.stem: After a primary cytomegalovirus infection resolves, the virus persists in the host for life. CMV most characteristically establishes latency in which of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: B lymphocytes bearing the CD21 surface molecule

choices.label: B
choices.text: CD4+ T lymphocytes of the peripheral blood

choices.label: C
choices.text: Epithelial cells of the oropharynx and the tonsils

choices.label: D
choices.text: Monocytes, macrophages, and bone marrow progenitor cells

choices.label: E
choices.text: Squamous epithelium of the lateral border of the tongue

explanation.summary: CMV establishes latency in monocytes, macrophages, and bone marrow progenitor cells.
explanation.whyCorrect: CMV establishes latency in various cells, including monocytes, macrophages, and bone marrow progenitor cells. Latent infections by CMV are also commonly established in glands, kidneys, and lymphoid tissue, which is consistent with how widely the virus is distributed in the body.

whyWrongByChoice.A: CD21-bearing B cells are the principal latency site for EBV, not CMV.
whyWrongByChoice.B: CD4+ T cells are where HHV-6 and HHV-7 establish lifelong latency.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Oropharyngeal epithelium is where EBV replicates and is shed into saliva.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The lateral tongue epithelium is the site of the EBV lesion oral hairy leukoplakia.

questions.stem: A public health officer reviews cytomegalovirus seroprevalence in the general population. By 40 years of age, approximately what proportion of the population has been infected with CMV?

explanation.summary: Roughly 50 to 80% of the population is infected with CMV by 40 years of age.
explanation.whyCorrect: CMV is one of the most common infections in humans. Roughly 50 to 80% of the population are infected with CMV by 40 years of age, and most of these infections are asymptomatic and harmless in immunocompetent hosts.

whyWrongByChoice.A: This is far below the observed CMV seroprevalence in middle-aged adults.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A quarter of the population understates how common CMV infection is by age 40.
whyWrongByChoice.C: This range approximates the proportion of U.S. women who have never been infected with CMV.
whyWrongByChoice.D: This range still understates the proportion infected by 40 years of age.

questions.stem: A 27-year-old woman who has never been infected with cytomegalovirus acquires a primary infection during the second trimester of pregnancy. Approximately what is the chance that she will pass the infection to her fetus?

choices.label: A
choices.text: About 10%

choices.label: B
choices.text: About 5%

choices.label: C
choices.text: About one-third

choices.label: D
choices.text: Essentially none

choices.label: E
choices.text: Nearly all

explanation.summary: About one-third of women with primary CMV infection during pregnancy transmit it to the infant.
explanation.whyCorrect: In the United States, approximately 30 to 50% of women have never been infected with CMV. If a woman is infected with CMV for the first time during a pregnancy, one-third will pass the infection to their infant. Vertical transmission is a very common mode of transmission for CMV.

whyWrongByChoice.A: About 10% understates the risk; roughly 10% is the share of infected infants symptomatic at birth.
whyWrongByChoice.B: About 5% greatly understates the transmission risk with primary maternal infection.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Vertical transmission is common with CMV, so the risk is far from negligible.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Most infants are not infected, since transmission occurs in about a third of primary infections.

questions.stem: A neonatologist reviews the epidemiology of congenital cytomegalovirus infection in the United States. Which of the following best describes the frequency and severity of this infection?

choices.label: A
choices.text: About 1 in 2,000 babies is born with it, and about half are symptomatic at birth

choices.label: B
choices.text: About 1 in 20 babies is born with it, and nearly all are symptomatic at birth

choices.label: C
choices.text: About 1 in 20,000 babies is born with it, and none are symptomatic at birth

choices.label: D
choices.text: About 1 in 200 babies is born with it, and roughly 10% are symptomatic at birth

choices.label: E
choices.text: About 1 in 200,000 babies is born with it, and all are symptomatic at birth

explanation.summary: About 1 in 200 babies is born with congenital CMV, and roughly 10% are symptomatic at birth.
explanation.whyCorrect: About 1 in 200 babies is born with congenital CMV. Roughly 10% are symptomatic at birth, and among all infected infants about 20% go on to develop long-term sequelae such as hearing loss. CMV is the most common viral infection that infants are born with in the United States.

whyWrongByChoice.A: One in 2,000 understates the incidence, and half of infants are not symptomatic at birth.
whyWrongByChoice.B: One in 20 vastly overstates the incidence, and most infected infants are asymptomatic at birth.
whyWrongByChoice.C: One in 20,000 is far too rare, and some infected infants are symptomatic at birth.
whyWrongByChoice.E: One in 200,000 is far too rare, and most infected infants have no symptoms at birth.

questions.stem: A 3-week-old male infant born at 38 weeks' gestation is brought in for poor feeding, jaundice, and abdominal distention. Examination shows hepatosplenomegaly and a petechial rash with lesions resembling blueberries. Cranial ultrasonography shows periventricular calcifications. Which of the following is the most likely cause?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Cytomegalovirus

choices.label: B
choices.text: Epstein-Barr virus

choices.label: C
choices.text: Herpes simplex virus type 2

choices.label: D
choices.text: Human herpesvirus 6

choices.label: E
choices.text: Varicella-zoster virus

explanation.summary: Jaundice, a blueberry muffin rash, hepatosplenomegaly, and periventricular calcification indicate congenital CMV.
explanation.whyCorrect: Some infants born with CMV develop cytomegalic inclusion disease, a severe form that may present months after birth. It is characterized by jaundice, petechial or purple blueberry muffin rash, low birth weight, chorioretinitis, enlarged spleen and liver, periventricular calcification, hearing loss, and seizures. CMV is one of the TORCH pathogens and is the most common congenital viral infection in the United States.

whyWrongByChoice.B: EBV causes mononucleosis and several cancers, not this congenital syndrome.
whyWrongByChoice.C: HSV-2 is not the herpesvirus described as producing this constellation of congenital findings.
whyWrongByChoice.D: HHV-6 causes roseola infantum in young children, typically after 6 months of age.
whyWrongByChoice.E: VZV is not the pathogen associated with periventricular calcification and blueberry muffin rash here.

questions.stem: A transplant center reviews all of the acute cytomegalovirus illnesses that occurred among its immunocompromised patients over 5 years. Which of the following is the most common disease caused by CMV in such patients?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Colitis

choices.label: B
choices.text: Encephalitis

choices.label: C
choices.text: Esophagitis

choices.label: D
choices.text: Pneumonia

choices.label: E
choices.text: Retinitis

explanation.summary: Pneumonia is the most common CMV disease in immunocompromised patients.
explanation.whyCorrect: HIV patients, other immunocompromised patients, organ transplant recipients, and cancer patients are at risk for acute illness caused by CMV, and pneumonia is the most common of these. Lung samples contain multiple giant cells with characteristic owl's eye nuclear inclusions, sometimes referred to as giant cell pneumonia.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Colitis occurs in the immunocompromised but is less common than CMV pneumonia.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Encephalitis is among the CMV illnesses of the immunocompromised but is not the most common.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Esophagitis is a recognized CMV illness but not the most frequent presentation.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Retinitis is an important CMV illness in AIDS but is not the most common one overall.

questions.stem: Before effective antiretroviral therapy was available, one herpesvirus was a common cause of blindness in patients with AIDS. Which of the following viruses was responsible?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Cytomegalovirus

choices.label: B
choices.text: Epstein-Barr virus

choices.label: C
choices.text: Herpes simplex virus type 1

choices.label: D
choices.text: Human herpesvirus 6

choices.label: E
choices.text: Human herpesvirus 7

explanation.summary: CMV retinitis was a common cause of blindness in AIDS before antiretroviral therapy.
explanation.whyCorrect: Retinitis is one of the CMV illnesses seen in the immunocompromised. Prior to the development of anti-retroviral drugs, CMV was a common cause of blindness in patients with AIDS, because uncontrolled HIV infection allowed latent CMV to reactivate and involve the retina.

whyWrongByChoice.B: EBV in AIDS causes oral hairy leukoplakia and lymphomas rather than retinitis.
whyWrongByChoice.C: HSV-1 is not the herpesvirus described as a common cause of blindness in AIDS.
whyWrongByChoice.D: HHV-6 causes roseola infantum and reactivates as encephalitis or marrow suppression.
whyWrongByChoice.E: HHV-7 causes a milder roseola-like illness and is not a cause of AIDS blindness.

questions.stem: A physician must confirm an active cytomegalovirus infection in a bone marrow transplant recipient whose antibody titers are low and who is too unstable to wait weeks for a result. Which of the following is the most appropriate test?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A light scrape preparation taken from the patient's buccal mucosa

choices.label: B
choices.text: A monospot test performed on the patient's serum using horse erythrocytes

choices.label: C
choices.text: PCR of a blood sample, which also quantifies viral load

choices.label: D
choices.text: Serology for anti-CMV antibodies performed on a single serum sample

choices.label: E
choices.text: Viral culture of a urine sample, which returns a result within 24 hours

explanation.summary: PCR is the gold standard for identifying CMV and can distinguish active infection from asymptomatic shedding.
explanation.whyCorrect: PCR is the gold standard in identifying CMV, and throat washings, blood, and urine samples are commonly tested. Viral titers can also be determined by PCR, and high titers indicate an active infection as opposed to asymptomatic shedding of the virus.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A scrape preparation is used to distinguish thrush from oral hairy leukoplakia, not to diagnose CMV.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The monospot detects heterophile antibodies and is an indirect indicator of EBV, not CMV.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Antibody titers can be low in immunocompromised individuals, so serology is of little value here.
whyWrongByChoice.E: CMV is relatively slow growing, so culture results can take 2 to 3 weeks rather than a day.

questions.stem: An 11-month-old girl has 4 days of temperatures up to 40 degrees Celsius. The fever then breaks, and a rash appears on her trunk that spreads to her neck and extremities. Which of the following is the most likely cause?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Cytomegalovirus

choices.label: B
choices.text: Epstein-Barr virus

choices.label: C
choices.text: Herpes simplex virus type 1

choices.label: D
choices.text: Human herpesvirus 6

choices.label: E
choices.text: Varicella-zoster virus

explanation.summary: Roseola infantum, caused mainly by HHV-6, is high fever for 3 to 5 days followed by a truncal rash.
explanation.whyCorrect: Human herpesviruses 6 and 7 most commonly infect young children and cause roseola infantum, a disease with 3 to 5 days of very high fever followed by a sudden rash that starts on the trunk and spreads to the neck and extremities as the fever breaks. HHV-6 is the primary cause, while HHV-7 causes a similar but often milder illness.

whyWrongByChoice.A: CMV causes a mononucleosis-like illness or congenital infection rather than roseola.
whyWrongByChoice.B: EBV causes mild pharyngitis in children and classic mononucleosis in adults.
whyWrongByChoice.C: HSV-1 is not described as a cause of roseola infantum.
whyWrongByChoice.E: VZV is not the cause of the roseola fever-then-rash pattern described here.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old man develops encephalitis and marrow suppression after a stem cell transplant, and PCR of his blood detects human herpesvirus 6. Human herpesviruses 6 and 7 establish lifelong latency in which of the following cells?

choices.label: A
choices.text: B lymphocytes

choices.label: B
choices.text: Bone marrow progenitor cells

choices.label: C
choices.text: CD4+ T lymphocytes

choices.label: D
choices.text: Monocytes and macrophages

choices.label: E
choices.text: Oropharyngeal epithelial cells

explanation.summary: HHV-6 and HHV-7 establish lifelong latency in CD4+ T cells and reactivate in the immunocompromised.
explanation.whyCorrect: HHV-6 and HHV-7 establish lifelong latency in CD4+ T cells and can reactivate in immunocompromised patients, leading to encephalitis, marrow suppression, and post-transplant fevers. Diagnosis is clinical in typical childhood cases, but PCR is used in immunocompromised hosts such as this patient.

whyWrongByChoice.A: B lymphocytes are the principal latency site for EBV.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Bone marrow progenitor cells are among the cells in which CMV establishes latency.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Monocytes and macrophages harbor latent cytomegalovirus.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Oropharyngeal epithelium is where EBV replicates and is shed, not an HHV-6 latency site.

questions.stem: A 14-month-old girl had 3 days of fever up to 40 degrees Celsius complicated by a brief febrile seizure. She is now afebrile, and a rash has just appeared. Which of the following features best distinguishes her illness from measles and rubella?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The fever and the rash begin on the same day of the illness

choices.label: B
choices.text: The fever is gone or diminished by the time the rash appears

choices.label: C
choices.text: The illness is diagnosed by detecting heterophile antibodies

choices.label: D
choices.text: The rash appears while the fever is at its highest point

choices.label: E
choices.text: The rash begins on the face and spreads downward to the trunk

explanation.summary: In HHV-6/7 the fever resolves before the rash appears, unlike in measles and rubella.
explanation.whyCorrect: With HHV-6/7 the fever can be high enough, above 39 to 40 degrees Celsius, to provoke febrile seizures. Unlike measles and rubella, the fever is usually gone or diminished before the rash appears with HHV-6/7. The rash then starts on the trunk and spreads to the neck and extremities.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Simultaneous onset does not capture the sequence, in which fever precedes and then breaks.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Heterophile antibodies are an indirect marker of EBV infection, not of roseola.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The defining feature is that the rash follows defervescence rather than peak fever.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The roseola rash starts on the trunk and spreads outward rather than beginning on the face.

questions.stem: A 46-year-old man who received a kidney transplant 3 years ago and remains on chronic immunosuppressive therapy develops generalized lymphadenopathy and hypercalcemia. A peripheral blood smear shows malignant T lymphocytes. His physician explains that the responsible agent is a retrovirus, but one that causes T cell cancer rather than acquired immunodeficiency. Which of the following is the most likely causal organism?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Epstein-Barr virus

choices.label: B
choices.text: Human herpesvirus 8

choices.label: C
choices.text: Human immunodeficiency virus type 1

choices.label: D
choices.text: Human immunodeficiency virus type 2

choices.label: E
choices.text: Human T-cell lymphotropic virus type 1

explanation.summary: Retroviridae contains two medically significant human viruses: HIV, which causes AIDS, and HTLV-1, which causes T cell cancers.
explanation.whyCorrect: HTLV-1 is the second medically significant member of Retroviridae. It causes T cell malignancies, most commonly in immunosuppressed patients such as this transplant recipient. The stem specifies a retrovirus producing T cell cancer rather than immunodeficiency, which identifies HTLV-1.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Epstein-Barr virus is a herpesvirus, not a retrovirus, and it enters cells by binding CD21.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Human herpesvirus 8 is a herpesvirus that causes Kaposi sarcoma, a vascular tumor of endothelial cells.
whyWrongByChoice.C: HIV-1 is a retrovirus, but it causes acquired immunodeficiency syndrome rather than T cell cancer.
whyWrongByChoice.D: HIV-2 is a retrovirus, but like HIV-1 it causes progressive immunodeficiency, not T cell cancer.

questions.stem: A student compares HIV with influenza virus and poliovirus. She notes that the latter two viruses complete their entire replication cycle within the cytoplasm of the host cell, whereas HIV behaves differently once a DNA copy of its genome has been produced. Which of the following best describes where HIV replicates?

choices.label: A
choices.text: At the plasma membrane, using a membrane-bound viral polymerase

choices.label: B
choices.text: In mitochondria, using enzymes borrowed from the host organelle

choices.label: C
choices.text: In the cytoplasm, in the same way as most other RNA viruses

choices.label: D
choices.text: In the nucleus, after its DNA copy is incorporated into the host genome

choices.label: E
choices.text: In the rough endoplasmic reticulum, before budding from the cell

explanation.summary: Retroviruses are unusual among RNA viruses in that they replicate in the nucleus after their DNA copy is integrated into the host genome.
explanation.whyCorrect: Reverse transcriptase converts the viral RNA into DNA, and that DNA copy is incorporated into the host cell genome, where it remains. Because the viral genetic material now resides in host chromosomal DNA, HIV replication occurs in the nucleus. Most other RNA viruses never enter the nucleus and replicate in the cytoplasm.
