whyWrongByChoice.A: New virions bud from the plasma membrane, but genome replication does not occur there.
whyWrongByChoice.B: HIV does not replicate in mitochondria or use mitochondrial enzymes.
whyWrongByChoice.C: This describes most other RNA viruses; retroviruses are the exception to that rule.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The endoplasmic reticulum is not the site of retroviral genome replication.

questions.stem: A researcher purifies virions from the plasma of a patient with AIDS and characterizes the nucleic acid packaged inside the capsid, as well as the virion-associated enzyme required for the first step of replication after entry. Which of the following findings would be expected?

choices.label: A
choices.text: One molecule of double-stranded DNA, copied by a viral DNA polymerase

choices.label: B
choices.text: One molecule of single-stranded RNA, translated directly by host ribosomes

choices.label: C
choices.text: Two copies of double-stranded RNA, copied by a viral RNA polymerase

choices.label: D
choices.text: Two copies of single-stranded DNA, copied into RNA by reverse transcriptase

choices.label: E
choices.text: Two copies of single-stranded RNA, copied into DNA by reverse transcriptase

explanation.summary: Retroviruses package two copies of single-stranded RNA and carry reverse transcriptase to convert that RNA into DNA.
explanation.whyCorrect: Retroviruses encode their genetic information as two copies of single-stranded RNA. After entry, the enzyme reverse transcriptase converts viral RNA into DNA, and this DNA copy is then incorporated into the host cell genome, where it remains permanently.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Retroviruses do not package DNA; their genome is RNA that must first be reverse transcribed.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The genome is present in two copies, and replication requires reverse transcription rather than direct translation alone.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The retroviral genome is single-stranded RNA, and the enzyme carried converts RNA into DNA, not RNA into RNA.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Reverse transcriptase works in the opposite direction, copying RNA into DNA.

questions.stem: Electron microscopy of newly released HIV virions shows that each particle is surrounded by a lipid bilayer studded with viral glycoproteins. Which of the following is the source of this lipid bilayer?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A lipid layer synthesized de novo by viral enzymes

choices.label: B
choices.text: The endoplasmic reticulum membrane of the infected host cell

choices.label: C
choices.text: The Golgi apparatus membrane of the infected host cell

choices.label: D
choices.text: The nuclear membrane of the infected host cell

choices.label: E
choices.text: The plasma membrane of the infected host cell

explanation.summary: Retroviridae are enveloped viruses, and the HIV envelope is derived from the host cell plasma membrane.
explanation.whyCorrect: Retroviridae viruses have an envelope, and that envelope is derived from the host plasma membrane as the virion buds from the infected cell. Viral glycoproteins encoded by the virus are inserted into this host-derived membrane.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Viruses do not synthesize their own lipid bilayers; envelopes are acquired from host membranes.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The endoplasmic reticulum membrane is not the source of the HIV envelope.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The Golgi membrane is not the source of the retroviral envelope.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The envelope is taken from the plasma membrane, not the nuclear membrane.

questions.stem: A virologist annotates the complete genome of an HIV-1 isolate. She identifies the three genes carried by all retroviruses, plus additional open reading frames that are not present in other retroviruses. How many genes does the HIV genome contain in total?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Eight

choices.label: B
choices.text: Four

choices.label: C
choices.text: Nine

choices.label: D
choices.text: Seven

choices.label: E
choices.text: Six

explanation.summary: All retroviruses carry env, gag, and pol; HIV carries 6 additional genes for a total of 9.
explanation.whyCorrect: Every retrovirus has three genes: env, gag, and pol. HIV contains 6 additional genes beyond these three, giving a total of 9 genes. The extra genes encode proteins that help the virus evade and suppress the host immune system.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Eight understates the HIV gene count.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Four would mean only one gene beyond the three shared retroviral genes.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Seven understates the HIV gene count.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Six is the number of additional genes HIV carries, not its total.

questions.stem: HIV carries six genes that are not found in other retroviruses. A researcher deletes all six from a laboratory strain and finds that the virus still assembles infectious particles in cell culture but is rapidly cleared when introduced into an animal host with an intact immune system. Which of the following best describes the normal function of these six genes?

choices.label: A
choices.text: They encode proteins that allow the virus to evade and suppress host immunity.

choices.label: B
choices.text: They encode the enzymes that copy viral RNA into DNA and integrate it.

choices.label: C
choices.text: They encode the glycoproteins that mediate fusion with the target cell.

choices.label: D
choices.text: They encode the lipids of the envelope acquired during viral budding.

choices.label: E
choices.text: They encode the structural proteins of the capsid, nucleocapsid, and matrix.

explanation.summary: Beyond env, gag, and pol, HIV's six additional genes encode proteins that evade and suppress the host immune system.
explanation.whyCorrect: HIV contains 6 genes in addition to the 3 shared by all retroviruses. These extra genes encode proteins that allow the virus to evade and suppress the host immune system, which is consistent with a deletion mutant that assembles normally in culture but is cleared by an intact immune response.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Reverse transcriptase, integrase, and protease are encoded by pol, one of the three core retroviral genes.
whyWrongByChoice.C: gp120 and gp41, which mediate fusion, are encoded by env.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Envelope lipids are not encoded at all; they come from the host plasma membrane.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The capsid, nucleocapsid, and matrix proteins p24, p7, and p17 are encoded by gag.

questions.stem: An immunoblot of disrupted HIV virions identifies three structural proteins: one forming the conical core shell, one bound to the viral RNA inside it, and one lining the inner face of the envelope. Which of the following proteins are encoded by the HIV gag gene?

choices.label: A
choices.text: CD4 and CCR5, the cell-surface entry proteins

choices.label: B
choices.text: CXCR4 and CD4, the coreceptor and primary receptor

choices.label: C
choices.text: gp120 and gp41, the fusion glycoproteins

choices.label: D
choices.text: p24, p7, and p17, the capsid, nucleocapsid, and matrix proteins

choices.label: E
choices.text: Reverse transcriptase, integrase, and protease

explanation.summary: The gag gene codes for the HIV structural proteins of the capsid, nucleocapsid, and outer matrix: p24, p7, and p17.
explanation.whyCorrect: Gag encodes the structural proteins used in the capsid, nucleocapsid, and outer matrix, identified as p24, p7, and p17. These are the proteins detected in the described immunoblot.

whyWrongByChoice.A: CD4 and CCR5 are host cell surface proteins, not virally encoded products.
whyWrongByChoice.B: CXCR4 and CD4 are host cell surface proteins used for entry, not gag products.
whyWrongByChoice.C: gp120 and gp41 are encoded by env and mediate fusion with target cells.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Reverse transcriptase, integrase, and protease are encoded by the polymerase gene, pol.

questions.stem: A candidate antiviral is designed to bind the HIV docking glycoprotein so that the transmembrane glycoprotein can no longer drive fusion of the viral envelope with the target cell membrane. The two glycoproteins targeted by this drug are products of which HIV gene, and what are they called?

choices.label: A
choices.text: env, which encodes gp120 and gp41

choices.label: B
choices.text: gag, which encodes p24 and p17

choices.label: C
choices.text: gag, which encodes p7 and p24

choices.label: D
choices.text: pol, which encodes protease and integrase

choices.label: E
choices.text: pol, which encodes reverse transcriptase and integrase

explanation.summary: The env gene encodes gp120 and gp41, which mediate viral fusion with target cells.
explanation.whyCorrect: Env encodes gp120 and gp41. gp120 is the docking glycoprotein and gp41 is the transmembrane glycoprotein, and together they mediate fusion of the virus with target cells. A drug blocking these proteins blocks entry.

whyWrongByChoice.B: gag encodes structural proteins of the capsid and matrix, not the fusion glycoproteins.
whyWrongByChoice.C: p7 and p24 are gag-encoded structural proteins that do not mediate fusion.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Protease and integrase are pol products that act inside the cell, not at the membrane.
whyWrongByChoice.E: pol encodes replication enzymes that act after entry, not surface glycoproteins.

questions.stem: A 43-year-old man with HIV has taken antiretroviral therapy without missing doses for 4 years. On routine monitoring, his HIV viral titer has risen 4-fold. Resistance testing shows that the virus is no longer susceptible to inhibition of reverse transcriptase. A mutation in which of the following genes best explains this result?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A host gene encoding CCR5

choices.label: B
choices.text: A host gene encoding CD4

choices.label: C
choices.text: The viral env gene

choices.label: D
choices.text: The viral gag gene

choices.label: E
choices.text: The viral pol gene

explanation.summary: Reverse transcriptase, integrase, and protease are all encoded by the HIV polymerase gene, pol.
explanation.whyCorrect: The polymerase gene pol encodes reverse transcriptase, integrase, and protease, all of which are critical for viral replication. Because resistance has developed specifically to reverse transcriptase inhibition in an adherent patient, the mutation must lie in pol.

whyWrongByChoice.A: CCR5 is a host coreceptor and is not the target of reverse transcriptase inhibitors.
whyWrongByChoice.B: CD4 is a host receptor; drug resistance arises from mutation in the virus, not the host receptor.
whyWrongByChoice.C: env encodes gp120 and gp41, which mediate fusion rather than reverse transcription.
whyWrongByChoice.D: gag encodes the structural proteins p24, p7, and p17, not reverse transcriptase.

questions.stem: An investigational antiretroviral blocks cleavage of the large polyprotein translated from HIV transcripts. Virions still bud from treated cells, but they contain uncleaved precursor proteins and are non-infectious. Which of the following HIV proteins does this drug inhibit?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Integrase

choices.label: B
choices.text: Protease

choices.label: C
choices.text: Reverse transcriptase

choices.label: D
choices.text: The gp120 docking glycoprotein

choices.label: E
choices.text: The gp41 transmembrane glycoprotein

explanation.summary: HIV protease cleaves the polyprotein transcribed from viral DNA, a step required for virion maturation.
explanation.whyCorrect: Protease, encoded by pol, cleaves the polyprotein that is produced from viral DNA transcripts. Blocking this cleavage yields particles that still assemble and bud but contain uncleaved precursors and cannot establish infection.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Integrase incorporates the viral DNA copy into the host genome rather than cleaving proteins.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Reverse transcriptase converts viral RNA into DNA early in the cycle, before any polyprotein is made.
whyWrongByChoice.D: gp120 is the docking glycoprotein that binds the target cell and has no proteolytic role.
whyWrongByChoice.E: gp41 is the transmembrane glycoprotein that drives fusion and does not cleave polyproteins.

questions.stem: A drug under study allows HIV to enter a CD4 T cell and allows a DNA copy of the viral genome to be produced, but prevents that DNA copy from being inserted into host chromosomal DNA. Which of the following enzymes does this drug inhibit?

choices.label: A
choices.text: gp120

choices.label: B
choices.text: Integrase

choices.label: D
choices.text: Protease

choices.label: E
choices.text: Reverse transcriptase

explanation.summary: Integrase, a pol gene product, incorporates the DNA copy of the HIV genome into the host cell genome.
explanation.whyCorrect: After reverse transcriptase makes a DNA copy of the viral RNA, integrase incorporates that viral DNA into the host genome, where it remains permanently. A drug that permits reverse transcription but blocks insertion into host DNA is acting on integrase.

whyWrongByChoice.A: gp120 is a surface glycoprotein used for docking, and entry is stated to be intact.
whyWrongByChoice.C: p17 is a gag-encoded matrix structural protein with no role in integration.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Protease cleaves the viral polyprotein and acts later, during virion maturation.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Reverse transcriptase makes the DNA copy, which the stem states is still produced.

questions.stem: A man who has had an undetectable viral load on antiretroviral therapy for 10 years asks why he cannot simply stop his medication and why no curative treatment exists. Which of the following best explains why HIV infection is so difficult to cure?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Reverse transcriptase causes a high mutation rate and viral DNA is permanently integrated.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The host-derived envelope prevents the immune system from recognizing the virus at all.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The virus replicates only in the cytoplasm, where drugs cannot reach it.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The virus spreads only by cell-to-cell contact that antibodies are unable to block.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The virus stores its genetic information as DNA that host repair enzymes protect.

explanation.summary: HIV resists cure because reverse transcriptase generates a high mutation rate and the viral DNA becomes a permanent part of the host genome.
explanation.whyCorrect: Reverse transcriptase is error-prone, producing a high mutation rate that fuels escape from drugs and immunity. In addition, the DNA copy of the viral genome is incorporated into the host cell genome and remains there permanently, so suppressed virus can rebound when therapy stops.

whyWrongByChoice.B: The envelope is host derived, but this is not the reason cure is impossible.
whyWrongByChoice.C: HIV actually replicates in the nucleus once its DNA is integrated, unlike most RNA viruses.
whyWrongByChoice.D: HIV is a bloodborne pathogen transmitted by blood, sexual contact, and vertically, not solely cell to cell.
whyWrongByChoice.E: HIV stores its genetic information as RNA and must convert it to DNA inside host cells.

questions.stem: A laboratory creates cell lines that each express a single human surface molecule and exposes them to HIV in the presence of an appropriate coreceptor. Only one line becomes infected. Which of the following molecules must HIV bind in order to enter a target cell?

choices.label: A
choices.text: CD4

choices.label: B
choices.text: CXCR4

choices.label: C
choices.text: CCR5

choices.label: D
choices.text: CD21

choices.label: E
choices.text: gp120

explanation.summary: HIV targets cells by binding CD4 together with a coreceptor.
explanation.whyCorrect: HIV enters cells by binding CD4, which is why CD4 T cells are the major cell type infected. CD4 engagement is required in addition to a coreceptor for successful entry.

whyWrongByChoice.B: CXCR4 serves as a coreceptor, which the stem states is already provided.
whyWrongByChoice.C: CCR5 also serves as a coreceptor rather than the primary receptor.
whyWrongByChoice.D: CD21 is the receptor used by Epstein-Barr virus, not HIV.
whyWrongByChoice.E: gp120 is the viral docking glycoprotein, not a host cell molecule.

questions.stem: HIV entry into a target cell requires engagement of CD4 plus a second host cell surface protein. Which of the following pairs contains the molecules that can serve as that coreceptor?

choices.label: A
choices.text: CD4 and CD21

choices.label: B
choices.text: CXCR4 and CCR5

choices.label: C
choices.text: gp120 and gp41

choices.label: D
choices.text: p7 and p17

choices.label: E
choices.text: Reverse transcriptase and integrase

explanation.summary: HIV targets cells by binding CD4 and a coreceptor, either CXCR4 or CCR5.
explanation.whyCorrect: Entry requires CD4 plus a coreceptor, and the coreceptors HIV uses are CXCR4 and CCR5. Both are host cell surface molecules, and either can complete the entry complex with CD4.

whyWrongByChoice.A: CD4 is the primary receptor rather than the coreceptor, and CD21 is used by Epstein-Barr virus.
whyWrongByChoice.C: gp120 and gp41 are viral envelope glycoproteins, not host coreceptors.
whyWrongByChoice.D: p7 and p17 are gag-encoded viral structural proteins.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Reverse transcriptase and integrase are viral enzymes that act after entry.

questions.stem: CD4 T lymphocytes are the major cell type infected by HIV, but the virus also infects other cells that display CD4 together with a coreceptor. Which of the following additional cell types does HIV infect?

choices.label: A
choices.text: B lymphocytes and plasma cells

choices.label: B
choices.text: Erythrocytes and platelets

choices.label: C
choices.text: Hepatocytes and biliary epithelium

choices.label: D
choices.text: Macrophages and dendritic cells

choices.label: E
choices.text: Neutrophils and eosinophils

explanation.summary: CD4 T cells are the major HIV target, but macrophages and dendritic cells are also infected.
explanation.whyCorrect: HIV infects cells that express CD4 and a coreceptor. CD4 T cells are the dominant target and account for the profound CD4 lymphopenia of advanced disease, but macrophages and dendritic cells are also infected by the virus.

whyWrongByChoice.A: B cells and plasma cells are not listed among the cells HIV infects; HHV-8 is the virus that stays latent in B cells.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Erythrocytes and platelets are not infected by HIV.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Hepatocytes and biliary epithelium are not HIV target cells.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Granulocytes are not HIV target cells.

questions.stem: In 1981, clusters of previously healthy young men in Los Angeles, San Francisco, and New York were diagnosed with a rare opportunistic cancer and with an opportunistic respiratory infection. The cancer in these patients is itself caused by a herpesvirus. Which of the following is the causal organism of that cancer?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Epstein-Barr virus, also called human herpesvirus 4

choices.label: B
choices.text: Human herpesvirus 8

choices.label: C
choices.text: Human immunodeficiency virus type 1

choices.label: D
choices.text: Human immunodeficiency virus type 2

choices.label: E
choices.text: Human T-cell lymphotropic virus type 1

explanation.summary: Kaposi sarcoma, one of the sentinel illnesses of the 1981 clusters, is caused by the herpesvirus HHV-8.
explanation.whyCorrect: The 1981 clusters featured Kaposi sarcoma, a rare opportunistic cancer, and Pneumocystis jirovecii infection. Kaposi sarcoma is caused by a herpesvirus, HHV-8, which mainly causes disease in immunocompromised people, especially those with HIV.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Epstein-Barr virus is a herpesvirus, but it is not the cause of Kaposi sarcoma.
whyWrongByChoice.C: HIV-1 produced the underlying immunosuppression but is not the cause of the tumor itself.
whyWrongByChoice.D: HIV-2 is a retrovirus found mostly in West Africa and does not cause Kaposi sarcoma.
whyWrongByChoice.E: HTLV-1 is a retrovirus associated with T cell cancers, not Kaposi sarcoma.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old man with untreated HIV infection has multiple red-purple macules and nodules on his lower legs, and similar lesions are visible on his hard palate. Biopsy of a skin lesion is most likely to show a tumor arising from which of the following cell types?

choices.label: A
choices.text: B lymphocytes within the dermis

choices.label: B
choices.text: Dermal fibroblasts

choices.label: C
choices.text: Endothelial cells

choices.label: D
choices.text: Keratinocytes of the epidermis

choices.label: E
choices.text: Melanocytes of the basal layer

explanation.summary: Kaposi sarcoma is a vascular tumor that arises from endothelial cells.
explanation.whyCorrect: HHV-8 most commonly leads to Kaposi sarcoma, a vascular tumor that arises from endothelial cells. It appears as red-purple spots or nodules on the skin or in the mouth, often starting on the legs or face, and can also affect internal organs.

whyWrongByChoice.A: HHV-8 remains latent in B cells, but the tumor itself arises from endothelial cells.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Kaposi sarcoma is described as a vascular tumor of endothelial origin, not a fibroblastic one.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Keratinocyte-derived tumors are not vascular and do not produce these red-purple nodules.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Melanocytic lesions are pigmented tumors of a different lineage.

questions.stem: HHV-8 persists for life after infection, and transmission occurs through saliva and sexual contact. In which of the following cells does this virus remain latent?

choices.label: A
choices.text: B cells and endothelial cells

choices.label: B
choices.text: CD4 T cells and macrophages

choices.label: C
choices.text: Dendritic cells and neutrophils

choices.label: D
choices.text: Hepatocytes and Kupffer cells

choices.label: E
choices.text: Keratinocytes and melanocytes

explanation.summary: HHV-8 stays latent in B cells and endothelial cells and is transmitted via saliva and sexual contact.
explanation.whyCorrect: HHV-8, also called KSHV, remains latent in B cells and endothelial cells. Endothelial latency is consistent with Kaposi sarcoma being a vascular tumor arising from endothelium in immunocompromised hosts.

whyWrongByChoice.B: CD4 T cells and macrophages are targets of HIV, not latency sites for HHV-8.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Dendritic cells can be infected by HIV, but they are not where HHV-8 remains latent.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Hepatic cells are not the described latency site for HHV-8.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Keratinocytes and melanocytes are not the latency reservoir for this virus.

questions.stem: One of the two sentinel opportunistic illnesses that signaled the beginning of the AIDS epidemic in 1981 was infection with Pneumocystis jirovecii. This organism is best classified as which of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A bacterium causing skin and soft tissue infection

choices.label: B
choices.text: A fungus causing respiratory infection

choices.label: C
choices.text: A herpesvirus causing a vascular tumor

choices.label: D
choices.text: A protozoan causing diarrheal illness

choices.label: E
choices.text: A retrovirus causing immunodeficiency

explanation.summary: Pneumocystis jirovecii is an opportunistic respiratory fungal infection seen in severely immunosuppressed patients.
explanation.whyCorrect: Pneumocystis jirovecii is an opportunistic respiratory fungal infection. Along with Kaposi sarcoma, it appeared in previously healthy young men in 1981, a pattern that was highly unusual because these conditions were previously seen only with severe immunosuppression or advanced age.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Pneumocystis is not a bacterium and does not cause skin and soft tissue infection.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The herpesvirus in this setting is HHV-8, which causes Kaposi sarcoma.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Pneumocystis causes respiratory disease, not a protozoal diarrheal illness.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The retrovirus responsible for the underlying immunodeficiency is HIV.

questions.stem: The illness first recognized in 1981 was initially named on the basis of the demographic in which the earliest clusters occurred. As cases were identified in people who inject drugs, hemophiliacs receiving blood products, infants born to infected people, and heterosexual partners of infected people, the name was changed to acquired immunodeficiency syndrome. What was the original name?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Gay-Related Immune Deficiency

choices.label: B
choices.text: Human immunodeficiency virus disease

choices.label: C
choices.text: Kaposi sarcoma-associated immune deficiency

choices.label: D
choices.text: Pneumocystis-related immune deficiency

choices.label: E
choices.text: Transfusion-associated immune deficiency

explanation.summary: The syndrome was originally called Gay-Related Immune Deficiency before being renamed acquired immunodeficiency syndrome.
explanation.whyCorrect: Because the earliest clusters were predominantly among men who have sex with men, the illness was first called Gay-Related Immune Deficiency. The name was inaccurate, since the disease was rapidly identified in other demographics, and it fueled misinformation and stigma that persists today.

whyWrongByChoice.B: The virus itself was not discovered until 1983, so disease naming did not reference HIV at first.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Kaposi sarcoma was one of the sentinel illnesses, but it was not used in the original name.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Pneumocystis infection was a sentinel illness, but the original name did not reference it.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Transfusion recipients were recognized as at risk, but this was not the original designation.

questions.stem: The human immunodeficiency virus was identified in 1983 by researchers led by Luc Montagnier and Francoise Barre-Sinoussi. Because testing was not available immediately, the virus spread extensively before routine screening and preventive measures could be implemented. In which year did widespread screening tests for HIV become available?

explanation.summary: HIV was discovered in 1983, but widespread screening tests were not available until 1985.
explanation.whyCorrect: Researchers led by Montagnier and Barre-Sinoussi discovered HIV by 1983. Widespread screening tests for HIV were not available until 1985, which meant the virus had already spread extensively before routine testing and prevention could be implemented.

whyWrongByChoice.A: 1981 is when the first clusters of Kaposi sarcoma and Pneumocystis infection were recognized.
whyWrongByChoice.B: 1983 is the year the virus itself was discovered, not the year testing became widespread.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Screening became available earlier than this.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Screening became available well before 1990.

questions.stem: A global health agency is selecting a single diagnostic assay for an HIV program that will operate across all world regions. Which type of HIV is responsible for the majority of infections globally?

choices.label: A
choices.text: HIV-1

choices.label: B
choices.text: HIV-1 and HIV-2 in equal proportions

choices.label: C
choices.text: HTLV-1

choices.label: D
choices.text: HIV-2

choices.label: E
choices.text: HHV-8

explanation.summary: HIV-1 is the most common and widespread type of HIV and causes the majority of infections globally.
explanation.whyCorrect: HIV is categorized into two types. HIV-1 is the most common and widespread type and is responsible for the majority of infections worldwide, so a global program must detect HIV-1.

whyWrongByChoice.B: The two types are not equally distributed; HIV-1 predominates.
whyWrongByChoice.C: HTLV-1 is a different retrovirus that causes T cell cancers.
whyWrongByChoice.D: HIV-2 is less common and is mostly found in West Africa.
whyWrongByChoice.E: HHV-8 is a herpesvirus that causes Kaposi sarcoma, not an HIV type.

questions.stem: A 40-year-old woman who emigrated from West Africa is found to be infected with a retrovirus that is less transmissible than the type responsible for most global infections and that progresses to AIDS more slowly, making her infection more manageable. Which of the following is the most likely infecting virus?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Epstein-Barr virus

choices.label: B
choices.text: HHV-8

choices.label: C
choices.text: HIV-1

choices.label: D
choices.text: HIV-2

choices.label: E
choices.text: HTLV-1

explanation.summary: HIV-2 is less common and less transmissible than HIV-1, is mostly found in West Africa, and progresses more slowly to AIDS.
explanation.whyCorrect: HIV-2 is less common and less transmissible than HIV-1 and is mostly found in West Africa. HIV-2 infection also progresses more slowly to AIDS, which makes it more manageable. All three features in this stem point to HIV-2.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Epstein-Barr virus is a herpesvirus that binds CD21 and is not a cause of AIDS.
whyWrongByChoice.B: HHV-8 is a herpesvirus that causes Kaposi sarcoma, not a retroviral immunodeficiency.
whyWrongByChoice.C: HIV-1 is the most common and widespread type and does not fit the slower, less transmissible description.
whyWrongByChoice.E: HTLV-1 causes T cell cancers rather than progressive immunodeficiency.

questions.stem: Both types of HIV are believed to have originated in Central Africa and to have entered humans in separate events, most probably through hunting and consumption of bushmeat that exposed people to infected blood and tissues. HIV-2 is believed to have originated in which of the following animals?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Chimpanzees

choices.label: B
choices.text: Domestic swine

choices.label: C
choices.text: Fruit bats

choices.label: D
choices.text: Gorillas

choices.label: E
choices.text: Sooty mangabey monkeys

explanation.summary: HIV-1 is believed to have originated in chimpanzees and HIV-2 in sooty mangabey monkeys.
explanation.whyCorrect: HIV-1 and HIV-2 were transmitted to humans independently. HIV-1 is believed to have originated in chimpanzees, while HIV-2 originated in sooty mangabey monkeys, with bushmeat hunting and consumption the most probable route of transmission.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Chimpanzees are the believed origin of HIV-1, not HIV-2.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Domestic animals are not implicated; exposure came from hunting and eating bushmeat.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Bats are not implicated in the origin of HIV.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Gorillas are not identified as the source of either human HIV type.

questions.stem: Starting around the 1920s, HIV-1 began spreading outward from a large Central African city where rapid urbanization, the sex trade, and increased population density contributed to the virus adapting to and spreading among humans. By the 1960s the virus had reached Haiti. From which city did HIV-1 spread?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Johannesburg, South Africa

choices.label: B
choices.text: Kinshasa, DR Congo

choices.label: C
choices.text: Lagos, Nigeria

choices.label: D
choices.text: Nairobi, Kenya

choices.label: E
choices.text: Port-au-Prince, Haiti

explanation.summary: HIV-1 began spreading around the 1920s from Kinshasa, the largest city in what is now the Democratic Republic of the Congo.
explanation.whyCorrect: Kinshasa, the largest city in what is now the Democratic Republic of the Congo, is where HIV-1 began spreading outward starting around the 1920s. Rapid urbanization, the sex trade, and increased population density contributed to the virus adapting to and transmitting among humans.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Johannesburg is not the described origin of HIV-1 spread.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Lagos is not identified as the origin point of HIV-1 spread.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Nairobi is not the city from which HIV-1 spread outward.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Haiti was reached by the 1960s but was not the origin of the spread.

questions.stem: The roommate of a man newly diagnosed with HIV asks whether he is at risk from sharing meals, hugging, or being coughed on. Which of the following is the most appropriate response?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Any contact transmits HIV once the viral load becomes detectable in blood.

choices.label: B
choices.text: HIV is bloodborne; casual contact and respiratory secretions do not transmit it.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Hugging transmits HIV whenever either person has any break in the skin.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Respiratory secretions transmit HIV, so a mask should be worn when indoors.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Sharing utensils transmits HIV, so separate dishware should be used at home.

explanation.summary: HIV is a bloodborne pathogen, so casual contact and respiratory secretions do not transmit the virus.
explanation.whyCorrect: HIV is a bloodborne pathogen. Casual contact and respiratory secretions do not transmit the virus. The main routes are sexual contact, parenteral exposure, occupational exposure, and vertical transmission.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Transmission requires a recognized bloodborne or sexual route, not any contact.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Hugging is casual contact and is not a route of HIV transmission.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Respiratory secretions do not transmit HIV, so masking is not a relevant precaution here.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Sharing utensils is casual contact and does not transmit HIV.

questions.stem: A pregnant woman with untreated HIV infection asks how the virus could reach her child. HIV is a TORCH pathogen. Which of the following describes the routes by which she could transmit HIV to her infant?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Across the placenta during pregnancy, during delivery, and through breastfeeding

choices.label: B
choices.text: Only across the placenta, and only during the first trimester of pregnancy

choices.label: C
choices.text: Only during delivery, with no risk during pregnancy or after birth

choices.label: D
choices.text: Only through breastfeeding, beginning after the first month of life

choices.label: E
choices.text: Through maternal respiratory secretions during routine care of the infant

explanation.summary: As a TORCH pathogen, HIV can cross the placenta during pregnancy and can also be transmitted during delivery or through breastfeeding.
explanation.whyCorrect: HIV is a TORCH pathogen and can cross the placenta during pregnancy. It can also be transmitted during delivery or through breastfeeding, so all three routes must be addressed when counseling a pregnant patient.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Placental transmission is one route, but delivery and breastfeeding are also routes.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Delivery is one route, but transplacental and breastfeeding transmission also occur.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Breastfeeding is one route, but transmission can occur in pregnancy and at delivery.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Respiratory secretions do not transmit HIV, which is a bloodborne pathogen.

questions.stem: A woman with newly diagnosed HIV infection is 12 weeks pregnant and has not yet started antiretroviral therapy. If she remains untreated through delivery and breastfeeding, what is the approximate risk that she will transmit HIV to her infant?

choices.label: A
choices.text: 1 in 10

choices.label: C
choices.text: 1 in 3

choices.label: D
choices.text: 2 in 3

choices.label: E
choices.text: Nearly 100 percent

explanation.summary: Without antiretroviral therapy the risk of transmitting HIV to an infant is about 1 in 3; with therapy it is near zero.
explanation.whyCorrect: Without antiretroviral therapy, the risk of transmitting HIV to an infant is 1 in 3, occurring at delivery or through feeding. If the pregnant person is on ART, the risk of transmission is near zero, which is why screening and access to treatment are critical.

whyWrongByChoice.A: This underestimates the untreated risk, which is about one third.
whyWrongByChoice.B: This substantially underestimates the untreated vertical transmission risk.
whyWrongByChoice.D: This overestimates the untreated vertical transmission risk.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Transmission is not near universal even without treatment.

questions.stem: A public health officer reviews estimated per-act probabilities of acquiring HIV from an infected source, expressed as risk per 10,000 exposures. Which of the following exposures carries the highest risk?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Blood transfusion

choices.label: B
choices.text: Needle-sharing during injection drug use

choices.label: C
choices.text: Percutaneous needle-stick injury

choices.label: D
choices.text: Receptive anal intercourse

choices.label: E
choices.text: Receptive penile-vaginal intercourse

explanation.summary: Blood transfusion from an infected source carries by far the highest per-act risk of HIV transmission, about 9,250 per 10,000 exposures.
explanation.whyCorrect: Per 10,000 exposures, blood transfusion carries a risk of about 9,250, far exceeding every other route. This is why blood transfusions are now screened for HIV and other bloodborne pathogens.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Needle-sharing during injection drug use carries about 63 per 10,000 exposures.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Percutaneous needle-stick injury carries about 23 per 10,000 exposures.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Receptive anal intercourse carries about 138 per 10,000 exposures, the highest sexual risk but far below transfusion.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Receptive penile-vaginal intercourse carries about 8 per 10,000 exposures.

questions.stem: A clinician counsels a patient about the relative risk of different sexual behaviors. Among sexual exposures to an infected source, which of the following carries the highest estimated per-act risk of acquiring HIV?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Insertive anal intercourse

choices.label: B
choices.text: Insertive penile-vaginal intercourse

choices.label: C
choices.text: Receptive anal intercourse

choices.label: D
choices.text: Receptive oral intercourse

choices.label: E
choices.text: Receptive penile-vaginal intercourse

explanation.summary: Receptive anal intercourse carries the highest per-act HIV risk of any sexual exposure, about 138 per 10,000.
explanation.whyCorrect: Receptive anal intercourse carries about 138 infections per 10,000 exposures, the highest of any sexual act. Anal intercourse carries higher risk than other sexual practices because of mucosal vulnerability.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Insertive anal intercourse carries about 11 per 10,000 exposures.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Insertive penile-vaginal intercourse carries about 4 per 10,000 exposures.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Receptive oral intercourse is estimated as low risk.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Receptive penile-vaginal intercourse carries about 8 per 10,000 exposures.

questions.stem: A nurse sustains a percutaneous needle-stick injury while drawing blood from a patient known to be HIV positive. Using estimated per-act probabilities of acquiring HIV from an infected source, what is the approximate risk from this single exposure?

choices.label: A
choices.text: About 138 per 10,000 exposures

choices.label: B
choices.text: About 23 per 10,000 exposures

choices.label: C
choices.text: About 63 per 10,000 exposures

choices.label: D
choices.text: About 9,250 per 10,000 exposures

choices.label: E
choices.text: Negligible and not well documented

explanation.summary: A percutaneous needle-stick from an HIV-positive source carries a risk of about 23 per 10,000 exposures.
explanation.whyCorrect: Percutaneous needle-stick exposure is listed at about 23 per 10,000 exposures. Occupational exposure occurs when healthcare workers contact blood or body fluids during procedures without proper precautions, and its per-act risk is lower than needle-sharing.

whyWrongByChoice.A: About 138 per 10,000 is the estimate for receptive anal intercourse.
whyWrongByChoice.C: About 63 per 10,000 is the estimate for needle-sharing during injection drug use.
whyWrongByChoice.D: About 9,250 per 10,000 is the estimate for blood transfusion.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Negligible applies to routes such as biting, spitting, and sharing sex toys.

questions.stem: A man is bitten and spat upon during an altercation with a person known to be HIV positive. He has no puncture wound and no exposure to blood. Which of the following best describes the risk of HIV transmission from these exposures?

choices.label: A
choices.text: About 63 per 10,000 exposures, as with shared needles

choices.label: B
choices.text: Equivalent to that of a percutaneous needle-stick injury

choices.label: C
choices.text: Higher than that of receptive penile-vaginal intercourse

choices.label: D
choices.text: Negligible, and not well documented as a route of transmission

choices.label: E
choices.text: The highest of all exposures other than blood transfusion

explanation.summary: Biting, spitting, throwing body fluids, and sharing sex toys carry negligible HIV transmission risk.
explanation.whyCorrect: Biting and spitting are listed among the exposures whose risk is negligible. HIV transmission through these routes is technically possible but unlikely and not well documented, which is consistent with HIV being a bloodborne pathogen not spread by casual contact or saliva.

whyWrongByChoice.A: That figure applies to needle-sharing during injection drug use.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A needle-stick carries about 23 per 10,000 exposures, far above a negligible estimate.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Receptive penile-vaginal intercourse carries about 8 per 10,000, which still exceeds negligible.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Receptive anal intercourse, not biting or spitting, carries the highest non-transfusion risk.

questions.stem: A 25-year-old HIV-negative man whose partner is HIV positive asks about a daily medication he could take to prevent infection. When taken consistently as prescribed, pre-exposure prophylaxis reduces his risk of acquiring HIV by approximately how much?

choices.label: A
choices.text: About 20 percent

choices.label: B
choices.text: About 40 percent

choices.label: C
choices.text: About 60 percent

choices.label: D
choices.text: More than 90 percent

choices.label: E
choices.text: 100 percent, with no residual risk

explanation.summary: Pre-exposure prophylaxis taken consistently reduces the risk of acquiring HIV by more than 90 percent.
explanation.whyCorrect: PrEP is a medication that helps prevent HIV infection in people at high risk. Taken consistently as prescribed, it reduces the risk of acquiring HIV by more than 90 percent. Abstaining from risky behavior would be ideal, but where that is not possible PrEP is an excellent alternative.

whyWrongByChoice.A: This greatly understates the protection PrEP provides when taken consistently.
whyWrongByChoice.B: This understates the effectiveness of consistently taken PrEP.
whyWrongByChoice.C: This understates the effectiveness of consistently taken PrEP.
whyWrongByChoice.E: PrEP is highly effective but does not eliminate risk entirely.

questions.stem: A health department reviews the 37,981 new HIV diagnoses reported in the United States and dependent areas in 2022. Which of the following transmission categories accounted for the largest share of these diagnoses?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Blood transfusion, about 5 percent

choices.label: B
choices.text: Heterosexual contact, about 22 percent

choices.label: C
choices.text: Injection drug use, about 7 percent

choices.label: D
choices.text: Male-to-male sexual contact, about 70 percent

choices.label: E
choices.text: Perinatal transmission, about 15 percent

explanation.summary: Of the 37,981 new U.S. HIV diagnoses in 2022, about 70 percent were among men who reported male-to-male sexual contact.
explanation.whyCorrect: Among the 37,981 new diagnoses in 2022, 70 percent (26,749) were among gay, bisexual, and other men who reported male-to-male sexual contact. Black and Hispanic/Latino MSM carry the highest burden of HIV in the United States.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Blood transfusion is not a leading category, since the blood supply is now screened.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Heterosexual contact accounted for about 22 percent (8,495), which is roughly one in four but not the largest share.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Injection drug use accounted for about 7 percent (2,651) of new diagnoses.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Perinatal transmission is not one of the leading reported transmission categories in these data.

questions.stem: A planner reviewing 2022 estimates of new HIV infections in the United States notes that nearly half of all new infections occurred in a single region, which also has the highest HIV mortality and where fewer people living with HIV are aware of their status. Which region is this?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Midwest

choices.label: B
choices.text: Northeast

choices.label: C
choices.text: Pacific territories

choices.label: D
choices.text: South

choices.label: E
choices.text: West

explanation.summary: The South accounts for roughly half of new U.S. HIV infections and has the highest HIV mortality.
explanation.whyCorrect: Nearly half of new HIV infections, 49 percent or about 15,700, occurred in the South, which also experiences the highest mortality rates. Structural barriers such as poverty, stigma, and lack of Medicaid expansion, along with rural healthcare challenges, drive these disparities, and awareness of HIV status there is substantially below the national figure.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The Midwest accounted for about 14 percent of new infections.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The Northeast accounted for about 14 percent of new infections.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Pacific territories are not reported as a leading region for new infections.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The West accounted for about 23 percent of new infections.

questions.stem: In impoverished regions of the world where access to healthcare is poor, HIV infection rates remain high. Sub-Saharan Africa has an extremely high rate of HIV infection along with a high rate of co-infection by a second organism whose reactivation and spread is facilitated by HIV-induced immunosuppression. Which of the following is that organism?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Epstein-Barr virus

choices.label: B
choices.text: Human herpesvirus 8

choices.label: C
choices.text: Human T-cell lymphotropic virus type 1

choices.label: D
choices.text: Mycobacterium tuberculosis

choices.label: E
choices.text: Pneumocystis jirovecii

explanation.summary: Sub-Saharan Africa has very high rates of HIV and of HIV co-infection with Mycobacterium tuberculosis, whose reactivation is facilitated by HIV-induced immunosuppression.
explanation.whyCorrect: Sub-Saharan Africa has an incredibly high rate of HIV infection as well as co-infection with M. tuberculosis. The immunosuppression caused by HIV facilitates the reactivation and spread of tuberculosis and other diseases.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Epstein-Barr virus is not the organism identified as driving co-infection in this setting.
whyWrongByChoice.B: HHV-8 causes Kaposi sarcoma in immunocompromised patients rather than the reactivating co-infection described.
whyWrongByChoice.C: HTLV-1 is a retrovirus causing T cell cancers and is not the described co-infection.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Pneumocystis jirovecii is an opportunistic fungal respiratory infection, but it is not the co-infection emphasized in this region.

questions.stem: A 29-year-old man with HIV has taken a single antiretroviral agent for 8 months. His plasma HIV RNA level, previously undetectable, has risen to 45,000 copies/mL, and sequencing of the circulating virus shows several new mutations not present at diagnosis. Which of the following properties of HIV best explains this finding?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Its capsid shields the genome from host nucleases

choices.label: B
choices.text: Its envelope is acquired from the host nuclear membrane

choices.label: C
choices.text: Its genome is transcribed only within the host nucleolus

choices.label: D
choices.text: Its protease degrades host DNA repair enzymes

choices.label: E
choices.text: Its reverse transcriptase cannot proofread the DNA it makes

explanation.summary: Reverse transcriptase has no proofreading ability, so HIV mutates rapidly and quickly adapts to a single drug.
explanation.whyCorrect: Reverse transcriptase cannot recognize and correct errors as it copies viral RNA into DNA. HIV makes billions of copies of itself in a single day, so even though most of those mutations harm the virus, a few by random chance benefit it. Those mutant viruses spread through the host and become the dominant strain, which is how HIV escapes both the immune response and antiviral therapy.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The p24 capsid packages the viral genome, but it has nothing to do with how faithfully the genome is copied.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The viral envelope is taken from host cell membrane, and its origin does not affect replication fidelity.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Viral DNA is integrated into host chromosomes, and the site of transcription is not what generates new mutations.
whyWrongByChoice.D: HIV protease cleaves the viral polyprotein into functional proteins after translation; it does not act on host DNA repair enzymes.

questions.stem: Zidovudine (AZT) was the first drug approved to treat HIV, but patients given AZT alone continued to progress to AIDS. Modern regimens combine several antiretroviral agents. Which of the following best explains the advantage of combination therapy?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Combined drugs let the host clear integrated viral DNA

choices.label: B
choices.text: Combined drugs restore proofreading by reverse transcriptase

choices.label: C
choices.text: Each drug raises the plasma concentration of the others

choices.label: D
choices.text: Multiple drugs block viral entry into resting CD4 cells

choices.label: E
choices.text: The virus must acquire several mutations at once to escape

explanation.summary: Multi-drug therapy works because HIV would have to accumulate several resistance mutations simultaneously.
explanation.whyCorrect: AZT monotherapy failed because the high mutation rate of HIV let the virus adapt to a single drug quickly and become resistant. When several drugs act at once, the virus must mutate around all of them at the same time, which is far less likely, so viral titers stay suppressed for years.

whyWrongByChoice.A: No antiretroviral regimen removes proviral DNA from the host genome; therapy only suppresses viral titers.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Reverse transcriptase has no proofreading function, so there is nothing for a drug to restore.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Raising drug levels is not the reason multi-drug therapy succeeded; resistance, not inadequate drug concentration, defeated AZT alone.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Therapy does not prevent the reservoir of already-infected cells from persisting, and that reservoir is the problem.

questions.stem: A 37-year-old man with HIV has had undetectable plasma viral loads for 6 years while taking antiretroviral therapy. He asks his physician whether he has been cured of the infection. Which of the following best explains why he has not?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Antibodies to gp120 neutralize but do not kill the virus

choices.label: B
choices.text: Free virions persist just below the assay detection limit

choices.label: C
choices.text: The drugs suppress only virus replicating in lymph nodes

choices.label: D
choices.text: Viral DNA is integrated into the genome of host cells

choices.label: E
choices.text: Viral reverse transcriptase stays active within the cytoplasm

explanation.summary: Once reverse transcriptase makes viral DNA, integrase inserts it into the host genome, where it persists for the life of the cell.
explanation.whyCorrect: After viral RNA is converted into DNA, that DNA is incorporated into the host cell genome, and every daughter cell made from that cell carries the viral DNA too. Curing the infection would require destroying every cell holding HIV DNA or cutting the viral DNA back out. Therapy can suppress plasma titers below the limit of detection without touching this reservoir.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Antibody responses are not the reason therapy fails to cure; integrated proviral DNA is.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The barrier to cure is archived proviral DNA inside cells, not a small residue of circulating virions.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Antiretroviral therapy suppresses virus throughout the body rather than sparing tissues outside lymph nodes.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Enzyme activity in the cytoplasm is not what persists; the integrated provirus in host chromosomes is.

questions.stem: A 41-year-old woman with HIV has had an undetectable viral load on antiretroviral therapy for 3 years. She loses her insurance and stops all medication. Which of the following is most likely to occur over the next several weeks?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Cytotoxic T cells will clear her integrated proviral DNA

choices.label: B
choices.text: Her CD4 count and viral load will both remain stable

choices.label: C
choices.text: Her plasma viral load will rise rapidly

choices.label: D
choices.text: Her viral load will fall further as drug pressure is removed

choices.label: E
choices.text: She will become permanently resistant to all antiretrovirals

explanation.summary: Antiretroviral therapy suppresses HIV replication but does not remove the virus, so stopping it causes viral titers to rebound.
explanation.whyCorrect: The virus is still present in the patient's DNA even when it cannot be detected in blood. When therapy is withdrawn, the integrated provirus resumes producing virions and plasma viral titers begin to rise rapidly again. This is the reason continuity of care matters so much in HIV.

whyWrongByChoice.A: No immune mechanism removes integrated proviral DNA from infected cells.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Suppression depends entirely on continued drug pressure, so neither value remains stable off therapy.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Removing the drugs removes the block on replication, so titers climb rather than fall.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Resistance arises from mutation under drug pressure, not from stopping treatment altogether.

questions.stem: A man with HIV and leukemia underwent a bone marrow transplant to treat his cancer. Years later he has no detectable HIV despite having stopped antiretroviral therapy, making him one of only a handful of people ever cured of the infection. Which of the following features of the donor cells best accounts for this outcome?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A donor immune system that excises proviral DNA

choices.label: B
choices.text: Absence of CD4 on the donor lymphocytes

choices.label: C
choices.text: Homozygous CCR5 delta-32 mutation

choices.label: D
choices.text: Homozygous deletion of the CXCR4 gene

choices.label: E
choices.text: Preformed IgG against the p24 capsid protein

explanation.summary: The handful of cured patients received marrow from donors homozygous for the CCR5 delta-32 mutation, which blocks efficient viral entry.
explanation.whyCorrect: HIV engages CD4 and then a coreceptor, most commonly CCR5. Donor stem cells carrying a homozygous CCR5 delta-32 mutation cannot be entered efficiently by the virus, so the recipient's reconstituted immune system was resistant and the infection was cured. The other cured patients received similar transplants from donors with the same mutation.

whyWrongByChoice.A: No immune system removes integrated proviral DNA from cells on its own.
whyWrongByChoice.B: CD4 is the primary receptor for HIV, and healthy donor lymphocytes express it normally.
whyWrongByChoice.D: CXCR4 is an alternative coreceptor, and losing it was not the change present in the donor cells.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Antibodies against the capsid protein do not block viral entry and cannot cure an established infection.

questions.stem: A 33-year-old man who is homozygous for the CCR5 delta-32 allele, and therefore considered highly resistant to HIV, is found on screening to have acquired HIV infection. Which of the following best explains how the virus was able to enter his cells?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It entered his cells without first binding CD4

choices.label: B
choices.text: It used CXCR4 as its coreceptor

choices.label: C
choices.text: It was carried in by integrase rather than by membrane fusion

choices.label: D
choices.text: Its protease restored function to the mutant CCR5 protein

choices.label: E
choices.text: Its reverse transcriptase copied the virus into the CCR5 gene

explanation.summary: CCR5 mutations make a person very resistant to HIV, but the virus can still enter using the alternative coreceptor CXCR4.
explanation.whyCorrect: Some people carry naturally occurring CCR5 mutations that make them very resistant to HIV infection. The virus is crafty, however, and strains that bind the CXCR4 coreceptor instead can still engage CD4 and fuse with the cell, establishing infection in a person who lacks functional CCR5.

whyWrongByChoice.A: CD4 is the primary receptor for HIV and binding it is required regardless of which coreceptor is used.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Integrase acts inside the cell to insert viral DNA into host DNA; it plays no role in entry.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Protease cleaves viral polyprotein into functional proteins and does not modify host receptors.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Reverse transcriptase copies the viral genome into DNA and does not repair or target the host CCR5 gene.

questions.stem: A 26-year-old man acquires HIV through condomless intercourse. Which of the following best describes what happens during the first days to weeks after transmission?

choices.label: A
choices.text: CD4 counts fall below 200/uL and opportunistic infections begin

choices.label: B
choices.text: Cytotoxic T cells eliminate every infected cell at the entry site

choices.label: C
choices.text: Host antibodies bind virions and drive titers to undetectable

choices.label: D
choices.text: It establishes latency in neurons without replicating

choices.label: E
choices.text: It replicates locally, then seeds lymphoid organs throughout the body

explanation.summary: In the acute phase HIV replicates locally, spreads to draining lymph nodes, and seeds lymphoid organs systemically, producing high viremia.
explanation.whyCorrect: After exposure the virus replicates in local tissue antigen-presenting cells and CD4 cells. The infection then spreads to local lymph nodes where rapid replication begins, and the virus travels through the blood to distal sites and seeds the lymphoid organs systemically. The result is acute viremia with very high viral titers in the blood.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Profound CD4 depletion defines AIDS and develops years later; in acute infection the count rarely drops below 400/uL.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The immune response never clears HIV completely at any stage of the infection.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Antibody production against HIV surface antigens begins only several weeks later, in the chronic phase.
whyWrongByChoice.D: HIV does not establish a silent, non-replicating neuronal latency after transmission.

questions.stem: A 22-year-old woman has fever, pharyngitis, and diffuse lymphadenopathy 4 weeks after a high-risk exposure. Plasma HIV RNA is 1.2 million copies/mL. Which of the following is most likely true of her CD4 T-cell count at this time?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It drops below 50/uL within days

choices.label: B
choices.text: It falls significantly but rarely below 400/uL

choices.label: C
choices.text: It falls to an undetectable level

choices.label: D
choices.text: It rises well above the normal range

choices.label: E
choices.text: It stays exactly at her pre-infection value

explanation.summary: During acute HIV the CD4 count may drop noticeably, but it rarely falls below 400/uL.
explanation.whyCorrect: The acute phase is marked by rapid viral replication and very high plasma titers, and the CD4 T cell count may fall significantly. Even so, it rarely drops below 400 CD4 T cells/uL at this stage. The severe depletion seen in AIDS takes years to develop in an untreated adult.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Counts below 50/uL are seen in very advanced disease, not within weeks of infection.
whyWrongByChoice.C: CD4 cells are never driven to undetectable levels, even in advanced AIDS.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Acute HIV drives CD4 counts down rather than above the normal range of 500 to 1500/uL.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A significant fall in CD4 count is expected with the acute viremia, so the count does not stay unchanged.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old man develops fever, sore throat, myalgias, and diffuse lymphadenopathy. He reports condomless sex with a new partner about 1 month ago. Heterophile antibody testing is negative. Which of the following best describes the expected course of his current symptoms?

choices.label: A
choices.text: They persist until antiretroviral therapy is started

choices.label: B
choices.text: They progress directly into opportunistic infection

choices.label: C
choices.text: They recur every 3 to 6 weeks for several years

choices.label: D
choices.text: They resolve on their own in 2 to 4 weeks

choices.label: E
choices.text: They worsen steadily over the next 12 months

explanation.summary: Acute HIV viremia causes a self-limited mononucleosis-like illness that resolves in 2 to 4 weeks.
explanation.whyCorrect: The acute viremia of HIV can present as a mononucleosis-like illness that is clinically indistinct from EBV or CMV infection. It typically appears 3 to 6 weeks after infection and the symptoms usually resolve in 2 to 4 weeks. Roughly 40 to 90 percent of patients have such an illness, while some have no signs of infection at all.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The symptoms subside on their own as the chronic phase begins, whether or not therapy is started.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Opportunistic infections appear only after years of CD4 decline, not at the end of the acute phase.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The acute illness is a single self-limited episode, not a relapsing one.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Progressive worsening over a year is not the pattern of acute retroviral syndrome.

questions.stem: A 31-year-old man at high risk for HIV presents with a 5-day history of fever, rash, and lymphadenopathy that began about 5 weeks after a high-risk sexual exposure. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial test?

choices.label: A
choices.text: CD4 count with viral resistance culture

choices.label: B
choices.text: Deferral of all testing for 3 months

choices.label: C
choices.text: HIV antigen/antibody combination assay

choices.label: D
choices.text: HIV-1/HIV-2 antibody differentiation immunoassay

choices.label: E
choices.text: Western blot for antibodies against HIV

explanation.summary: The antigen/antibody combination assay is the usual first-line HIV screen because it detects both p24 antigen and host antibody.
explanation.whyCorrect: The combination assay detects early infection through the p24 antigen and established infection through host IgM or IgG, so it throws the broadest net and catches the most cases regardless of where a patient is in the infection. At roughly 5 weeks after exposure, p24 and usually IgM are already detectable, so this assay will identify the infection.

whyWrongByChoice.A: CD4 count and resistance testing are follow-up studies performed once the diagnosis has been established.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Deferral applies to exposures within about 10 days; 5 weeks is well within the detectable window.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The antibody differentiation immunoassay is the confirmatory second test performed after a positive screen.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Western blot is no longer used for HIV testing.

questions.stem: About 8 weeks after acquiring HIV, a patient's plasma viral load falls from 2 million copies/mL to 30,000 copies/mL and his fever and rash resolve. Which of the following best accounts for this decline?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Antibodies bind virions and cytotoxic T cells kill infected cells

choices.label: B
choices.text: CD4 cells resist infection by shedding their CCR5 coreceptors

choices.label: C
choices.text: Integrated proviral DNA is excised from infected cells

choices.label: D
choices.text: Reverse transcriptase is inhibited by host interferons

choices.label: E
choices.text: The virus stops replicating and enters a dormant state

explanation.summary: Falling viral titers at the start of the chronic phase reflect antibody production plus an expanding cytotoxic T cell response.
explanation.whyCorrect: Several weeks after infection the patient begins producing antibodies against HIV surface antigens. Those antibodies bind free-floating virions and target them for destruction by phagocytes. At the same time cytotoxic T cell numbers increase and begin hunting down and destroying infected cells. Together these responses lower viral titers and the patient's symptoms, if present, subside.

whyWrongByChoice.B: CD4 cells do not shed coreceptors to escape infection; resistance to entry is a fixed genetic trait.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Nothing removes integrated proviral DNA from infected cells, which is why the infection cannot be cleared.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The decline is driven by antibody and cytotoxic T cell responses rather than by inhibition of the viral enzyme.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The virus continues to replicate actively throughout the chronic phase even though the patient feels well.

questions.stem: A 35-year-old woman with untreated HIV diagnosed 7 years ago feels well and has no symptoms. Which of the following is most likely true of her infection at this time?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Her CD4 count has risen above the normal range

choices.label: B
choices.text: Her viral load is undetectable without any therapy

choices.label: C
choices.text: The virus has been cleared from her lymphoid tissue

choices.label: D
choices.text: The virus is actively replicating

choices.label: E
choices.text: The virus persists as DNA but makes no new virions

explanation.summary: The chronic phase of HIV is asymptomatic but not quiescent: the virus replicates actively while the immune system fights it.
explanation.whyCorrect: Although antibody and cytotoxic T cell responses bring viral titers down and symptoms subside, the immune system cannot clear the virus completely. Despite the patient having no symptoms, the virus is actively replicating as the immune system fights the infection, and this phase can last a decade or more.

whyWrongByChoice.A: CD4 counts drift downward over the chronic phase rather than rising above normal.
whyWrongByChoice.B: An undetectable viral load requires antiretroviral therapy and is not a feature of untreated chronic HIV.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The immune system never clears HIV from lymphoid tissue, which is seeded during the acute phase.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Ongoing production of new virions is exactly what characterizes the chronic phase.

questions.stem: In a phase I trial, a novel antiretroviral agent prevents incorporation of viral DNA into the host genome, and treated participants show a greater reduction in blood HIV titers than controls. Which of the following viral proteins does this drug most likely target?

choices.label: A
choices.text: gp120/gp41

choices.label: B
choices.text: Integrase

choices.label: C
choices.text: p24 capsid protein

choices.label: D
choices.text: Protease

choices.label: E
choices.text: Reverse transcriptase

explanation.summary: Integrase is the enzyme that incorporates HIV DNA into host DNA.
explanation.whyCorrect: Reverse transcriptase first converts viral RNA into DNA, and integrase then inserts that DNA into the host cell genome. A drug that prevents viral DNA from entering the host genome must therefore act on integrase, and blocking this step also limits the reservoir of cells carrying HIV DNA that makes the infection so hard to cure.

whyWrongByChoice.A: gp120 and gp41 facilitate viral entry by binding CD4 and a coreceptor such as CXCR4 or CCR5.
whyWrongByChoice.C: p24 is the capsid protein detected by screening assays and is not an enzyme acting on host DNA.
whyWrongByChoice.D: HIV protease cleaves the viral polyprotein into functional proteins after translation of viral DNA.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Reverse transcriptase converts viral RNA into DNA, a step that occurs before integration.

questions.stem: A 52-year-old man has been known to be HIV positive for 22 years, has never taken antiretroviral therapy, and has a CD4 count of 780/uL with a low viral load. He has had no opportunistic infections. Which of the following best explains his clinical course?

choices.label: A
choices.text: He carries a host genetic mutation such as one in CCR5

choices.label: B
choices.text: He was given zidovudine at the moment of transmission

choices.label: C
choices.text: He was infected with HIV-2 rather than with HIV-1

choices.label: D
choices.text: His antibodies have eliminated all integrated proviral DNA

choices.label: E
choices.text: His reverse transcriptase makes no errors during replication

explanation.summary: Long-term non-progressors typically carry host mutations, such as in CCR5, that make them naturally resistant to HIV.
explanation.whyCorrect: Progression from chronic HIV to AIDS is highly variable. A small percentage progress within 2 to 3 years, while some people are long-term non-progressors who do not develop AIDS for decades even without therapy. Genetic mutations that make the host naturally resistant to the virus, like those affecting CCR5, are common in these patients.

whyWrongByChoice.B: He has never received antiretroviral therapy, and a single early dose would not produce lifelong control.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Both HIV-1 and HIV-2 cause progressive infection, and the virus type does not explain decades without progression.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Antibodies do not remove integrated proviral DNA; no immune mechanism can.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Reverse transcriptase has no proofreading ability in any strain, so it always makes errors.

questions.stem: An infant acquires HIV perinatally and, because the diagnosis is missed, receives no treatment. Compared with an untreated adult who acquires HIV, this infant's infection is most likely to do which of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Be limited to mucocutaneous disease

choices.label: B
choices.text: Progress to AIDS only after 8 to 10 years

choices.label: C
choices.text: Progress to AIDS within 1 to 2 years

choices.label: D
choices.text: Remain in the acute phase for a decade

choices.label: E
choices.text: Resolve spontaneously during infancy

explanation.summary: HIV is far more aggressive in infants infected perinatally, who often progress to AIDS within 1 to 2 years untreated.
explanation.whyCorrect: Untreated adults typically take 8 to 10 years to progress from the chronic stage to AIDS. HIV can be extremely aggressive in children, and infants infected around the time of birth tend to progress much more rapidly, often reaching AIDS within 1 to 2 years if they are not treated.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Untreated perinatal HIV causes systemic immunodeficiency, not disease confined to skin and mucosa.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Eight to ten years is the adult figure; perinatally infected infants progress considerably faster.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The acute phase lasts weeks, not a decade, at any age.
whyWrongByChoice.E: HIV infection does not resolve on its own in infants or in adults.

questions.stem: A 38-year-old man with HIV feels well and has had no infections or malignancies. His physician reviews serial laboratory results. At which of the following CD4 T-cell counts would he first meet criteria for a diagnosis of AIDS?

explanation.summary: One of the two criteria for AIDS in an adult is a CD4 T-cell count below 200/uL.
explanation.whyCorrect: There are two criteria for a diagnosis of AIDS, and the first is a T cell count below 200/uL against a normal range of 500 to 1500/uL. At 150/uL this patient is below that threshold and is severely immunosuppressed, putting him at risk for serious, lethal infections and cancers.

whyWrongByChoice.B: 250/uL is still above 200/uL, so it does not satisfy the count-based criterion.
whyWrongByChoice.C: 350/uL indicates immunosuppression but does not meet the AIDS threshold.
whyWrongByChoice.D: 480/uL is below normal but well above the 200/uL threshold that defines AIDS.
whyWrongByChoice.E: 750/uL falls within the normal range of 500 to 1500/uL.

questions.stem: A 44-year-old woman with HIV is admitted with hypoxemia and diffuse ground-glass opacities on chest imaging, and is diagnosed with Pneumocystis pneumonia. Her CD4 T-cell count is 310/uL. Which of the following statements about her diagnosis is most accurate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: She cannot have AIDS until her CD4 count is below 200/uL

choices.label: B
choices.text: She has AIDS on the basis of an AIDS-defining condition

choices.label: C
choices.text: She has AIDS only if a repeat CD4 count is below 200/uL

choices.label: D
choices.text: She has chronic HIV, and the pneumonia is unrelated to it

choices.label: E
choices.text: She has chronic HIV, since her CD4 count is above 200/uL

explanation.summary: Either a CD4 count below 200/uL or an AIDS-defining condition establishes a diagnosis of AIDS.
explanation.whyCorrect: The second criterion for AIDS is any patient with HIV diagnosed with an infection or cancer that indicates severe immunodeficiency, and these are the AIDS-defining conditions. Pneumocystis pneumonia is one of them, so a patient can have AIDS even when the T cell count is above 200/uL. Some infections associated with HIV do occur at CD4 levels higher than 200/uL.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The diagnosis does not require the count to drop, because an AIDS-defining condition is enough.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Repeating the count is unnecessary once an AIDS-defining condition has been diagnosed.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Pneumocystis pneumonia in an HIV-positive patient is an opportunistic infection of severe immunodeficiency.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The count-based criterion is only one of two; meeting either one is sufficient for the diagnosis.

questions.stem: A 29-year-old woman presents for a routine physical examination. She is in a monogamous relationship, does not inject drugs, and has never been tested for HIV. Which of the following is the most appropriate recommendation regarding HIV testing?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Annual testing is recommended for every adult

choices.label: B
choices.text: She should be tested for HIV at least once

choices.label: C
choices.text: Testing is indicated only if she reports a specific risk factor

choices.label: D
choices.text: Testing should be deferred until she plans a pregnancy

choices.label: E
choices.text: Testing should be repeated every 3 to 6 months

explanation.summary: Everyone aged 13 to 64 should be tested for HIV at least once, regardless of stated risk.
explanation.whyCorrect: One-time testing is recommended for everyone aged 13 to 64 so that infections are found early, which both protects the patient's health and reduces the risk of onward spread. More frequent testing, at least yearly, is reserved for people with ongoing risk such as men who have sex with men, people with multiple partners since their last test, or people who share injection equipment.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Yearly testing is aimed at people with specific ongoing risk behaviors rather than all adults.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Routine one-time testing applies to everyone in this age range, not only to those reporting risk factors.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Pregnancy is one reason to test early, but it is not the only indication for testing.
whyWrongByChoice.E: That interval is suggested for sexually active gay and bisexual men, not for the general population.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old man presents with painless, white, corrugated lesions along the lateral borders of his tongue that have been present for several weeks. He reports that he cannot remove them even when he scrubs vigorously with a toothbrush. He has taken no antibiotics. Which of the following organisms is the most likely cause?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Candida albicans

choices.label: B
choices.text: Cytomegalovirus

choices.label: C
choices.text: Epstein-Barr virus

choices.label: D
choices.text: Human herpesvirus 8

choices.label: E
choices.text: Human papillomavirus

explanation.summary: Oral hairy leukoplakia is an unscrapable white plaque on the lateral tongue caused by EBV, and it should prompt HIV testing.
explanation.whyCorrect: Hairy leukoplakia is caused by EBV and produces an unscrapable white plaque on the lateral tongue. The fact that the lesion cannot be scraped off is what distinguishes it from thrush. Because hairy leukoplakia is commonly seen in immunocompromised patients, an HIV antigen/antibody assay is warranted, and it is one of the conditions seen once CD4 counts fall below 500/mm3.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Candida causes oral thrush, a scrapable white plaque that shows pseudohyphae on microscopy.
whyWrongByChoice.B: CMV in advanced HIV causes colitis, retinitis, esophagitis, encephalitis, and pneumonitis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: HHV-8 causes Kaposi sarcoma, which produces violaceous vascular tumors rather than white plaques.
whyWrongByChoice.E: HPV causes squamous cell carcinoma at sites of sexual contact such as the cervix, anus, and oropharynx.

questions.stem: A 40-year-old woman with HIV and a CD4 count of 430/uL has white plaques on her buccal mucosa that are easily scraped off with a tongue blade, leaving an erythematous base. Which of the following findings is most likely on microscopy of the scraped material?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Acid-fast oocysts

choices.label: B
choices.text: Cells with owl-eye inclusions

choices.label: C
choices.text: Encapsulated yeast on India ink

choices.label: D
choices.text: Perivascular spindle cells

choices.label: E
choices.text: Yeast with pseudohyphae

explanation.summary: A scrapable oral white plaque is thrush from Candida albicans, which shows yeast and pseudohyphae on microscopy.
explanation.whyCorrect: Candida albicans causes oral thrush in HIV-positive adults once CD4 counts fall below 500/mm3, and the plaque is scrapable, in contrast to the unscrapable plaque of EBV hairy leukoplakia. Microscopy shows yeast forms with pseudohyphae. At counts below 100/mm3 the same organism causes esophagitis with white plaques seen on endoscopy.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Acid-fast oocysts in stool indicate Cryptosporidium causing chronic watery diarrhea.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Intranuclear owl-eye inclusion bodies are seen on biopsy in CMV disease.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Encapsulated yeast on India ink stain indicates Cryptococcus neoformans meningitis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Perivascular spindle cells forming vascular tumors are the histologic hallmark of Kaposi sarcoma from HHV-8.

questions.stem: A 39-year-old man with HIV has several violaceous cutaneous plaques on his trunk. Biopsy of one lesion shows perivascular spindle cells invading tissue and forming vascular tumors. Which of the following organisms is most likely responsible?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Bartonella spp

choices.label: B
choices.text: Epstein-Barr virus

choices.label: C
choices.text: Human herpesvirus 8

choices.label: D
choices.text: Human papillomavirus

choices.label: E
choices.text: JC virus

explanation.summary: Kaposi sarcoma is caused by HHV-8 and shows perivascular spindle cells forming vascular tumors on histology.
explanation.whyCorrect: HHV-8 causes Kaposi sarcoma, whose biopsy shows perivascular spindle cells invading and forming vascular tumors. With CD4 counts below 500/mm3 the disease is usually localized cutaneous involvement, and once counts fall below 200/mm3 it can disseminate to pulmonary, gastrointestinal, and lymphatic sites.
