whyWrongByChoice.A: Bartonella causes bacillary angiomatosis, which also gives red-purple lesions but shows neutrophilic inflammation on biopsy.
whyWrongByChoice.B: EBV causes oral hairy leukoplakia and B-cell lymphomas rather than cutaneous vascular tumors.
whyWrongByChoice.D: HPV causes squamous cell carcinoma at sites of sexual contact, not spindle cell vascular lesions.
whyWrongByChoice.E: JC virus reactivation causes progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy in the central nervous system.

questions.stem: A 36-year-old woman with HIV and a CD4 count of 460/uL is found on cervical screening to have invasive squamous cell carcinoma. She has no other lesions. Which of the following organisms is most likely responsible for her malignancy?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Candida albicans

choices.label: B
choices.text: Cytomegalovirus

choices.label: C
choices.text: Epstein-Barr virus

choices.label: D
choices.text: Human herpesvirus 8

choices.label: E
choices.text: Human papillomavirus

explanation.summary: HPV causes squamous cell carcinoma at sites of sexual contact in HIV-positive adults once CD4 counts fall below 500/mm3.
explanation.whyCorrect: Human papillomavirus drives squamous cell carcinoma at the sites of sexual contact, including the cervix, anus, and oropharynx. This is one of the diseases that becomes more common in HIV-positive adults as CD4 counts drop below 500/mm3, which fits this patient's count of 460/uL.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Candida causes thrush and esophagitis and is not associated with carcinoma.
whyWrongByChoice.B: CMV in advanced HIV causes colitis, retinitis, esophagitis, encephalitis, and pneumonitis.
whyWrongByChoice.C: EBV causes oral hairy leukoplakia and B-cell lymphomas including CNS lymphoma.
whyWrongByChoice.D: HHV-8 causes Kaposi sarcoma, a vascular tumor with spindle cells, not squamous cell carcinoma.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old man with newly diagnosed HIV and a CD4 count of 420/uL has a positive interferon-gamma release assay. His chest radiograph is normal and he has no respiratory symptoms. At this CD4 count he is at greatest risk for which of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Cryptococcal meningitis

choices.label: B
choices.text: Disseminated Mycobacterium avium complex

choices.label: C
choices.text: Pneumocystis pneumonia

choices.label: D
choices.text: Progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy

choices.label: E
choices.text: Reactivation of latent tuberculosis

explanation.summary: Falling CD4 counts reactivate past infections, and increased risk of latent TB reactivation appears once counts drop below 500/mm3.
explanation.whyCorrect: As the CD4 count falls, past infections reactivate, bacterial and fungal infections disseminate, and non-Hodgkin lymphomas appear. Mycobacterium tuberculosis is listed among the common diseases of HIV-positive adults at counts below 500/mm3, where the main feature is an increased risk of reactivating a latent TB infection, exactly the situation in this patient.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Cryptococcal meningitis is typically seen at counts below 100/mm3.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Disseminated MAC appears below 100/mm3 and is most common below 50/mm3.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Pneumocystis pneumonia is characteristic of counts below 200/mm3.
whyWrongByChoice.D: JC virus reactivation causing PML is seen once counts fall below 200/mm3.

questions.stem: A 33-year-old man with HIV and a CD4 count of 140/uL has several weeks of fever, weight loss, fatigue, cough, dyspnea, nausea, and diarrhea. Bone marrow biopsy shows oval yeast cells within macrophages. Which of the following is the most likely organism?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Candida albicans

choices.label: B
choices.text: Cryptococcus neoformans

choices.label: C
choices.text: Cryptosporidium spp

choices.label: D
choices.text: Histoplasma capsulatum

choices.label: E
choices.text: Pneumocystis jirovecii

explanation.summary: Disseminated histoplasmosis in advanced HIV shows oval yeast cells inside macrophages.
explanation.whyCorrect: Histoplasma capsulatum is one of the pathogens seen once CD4 counts fall below 200/mm3, and it presents with fever, weight loss, fatigue, cough, dyspnea, nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea. The characteristic finding is oval yeast cells within macrophages, which fits this patient's biopsy.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Candida albicans causes thrush and esophagitis, showing yeast with pseudohyphae rather than intracellular yeast.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Cryptococcus neoformans causes meningitis and appears as encapsulated yeast on India ink stain.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Cryptosporidium causes chronic watery diarrhea with acid-fast oocysts in stool.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Pneumocystis jirovecii causes pneumonia with ground-glass opacities on chest imaging.

questions.stem: A 47-year-old man with HIV and a CD4 count of 90/uL has 2 months of progressive right-sided weakness, visual field loss, and confusion. MRI of the brain shows non-enhancing areas of demyelination in the subcortical white matter. Which of the following is the most likely cause?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Cryptococcus neoformans

choices.label: B
choices.text: Cytomegalovirus

choices.label: C
choices.text: Epstein-Barr virus

choices.label: D
choices.text: JC virus

choices.label: E
choices.text: Toxoplasma gondii

explanation.summary: Reactivated JC virus causes progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy, seen on MRI as non-enhancing demyelination.
explanation.whyCorrect: JC virus reactivation in HIV-positive patients with CD4 counts below 200/mm3 causes progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy. The imaging hallmark is non-enhancing areas of demyelination on MRI, which distinguishes it from the enhancing mass lesions of toxoplasmosis and CNS lymphoma.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Cryptococcus causes meningitis diagnosed by encapsulated yeast on India ink or capsular antigen.
whyWrongByChoice.B: CMV disease presents as colitis, retinitis, esophagitis, encephalitis, and pneumonitis with owl-eye inclusions on biopsy.
whyWrongByChoice.C: EBV drives CNS lymphoma, which is ring-enhancing and may be solitary.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Toxoplasma gondii causes brain abscesses that appear as multiple ring-enhancing lesions on MRI.

questions.stem: A 29-year-old man with untreated HIV has 3 weeks of dry cough and progressive exertional dyspnea. His CD4 count is 90/uL and chest CT shows diffuse bilateral ground-glass opacities. Which of the following is the most likely causal organism?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Cytomegalovirus

choices.label: B
choices.text: Histoplasma capsulatum

choices.label: C
choices.text: Mycobacterium avium complex

choices.label: D
choices.text: Mycobacterium tuberculosis

choices.label: E
choices.text: Pneumocystis jirovecii

explanation.summary: Pneumocystis pneumonia produces ground-glass opacities on chest imaging in patients with CD4 counts below 200/mm3.
explanation.whyCorrect: Pneumocystis jirovecii causes Pneumocystis pneumonia once CD4 counts fall below 200/mm3, and the characteristic imaging finding is ground-glass opacities on chest imaging. This patient's count of 90/uL and subacute hypoxemic presentation fit that pattern.

whyWrongByChoice.A: CMV causes colitis, retinitis, esophagitis, encephalitis, and pneumonitis, diagnosed by owl-eye inclusion bodies.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Histoplasmosis presents with systemic symptoms and shows oval yeast cells within macrophages.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Disseminated MAC causes nonspecific fever, night sweats, and weight loss rather than a ground-glass pneumonitis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Reactivation tuberculosis becomes a risk at counts below 500/mm3 and does not typically give diffuse ground-glass opacities.

questions.stem: A 38-year-old man with AIDS and a CD4 count of 60/uL has multiple red to purple papules and nodules scattered over his arms and trunk. Biopsy of a nodule shows vascular proliferation with neutrophilic inflammation. Which of the following is the most likely cause?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Bartonella spp

choices.label: B
choices.text: Cryptococcus neoformans

choices.label: C
choices.text: Human herpesvirus 8

choices.label: D
choices.text: Human papillomavirus

choices.label: E
choices.text: Mycobacterium avium complex

explanation.summary: Bacillary angiomatosis from Bartonella gives red-purple papules whose biopsy shows neutrophilic inflammation.
explanation.whyCorrect: Bartonella species cause bacillary angiomatosis in HIV-positive patients with CD4 counts below 100/mm3. The lesions are multiple red to purple papules or nodules, and biopsy shows neutrophilic inflammation, which is the feature that separates it from Kaposi sarcoma.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Cryptococcus neoformans in advanced HIV presents as meningitis with encapsulated yeast on India ink stain.
whyWrongByChoice.C: HHV-8 causes Kaposi sarcoma, whose biopsy shows perivascular spindle cells forming vascular tumors rather than neutrophils.
whyWrongByChoice.D: HPV causes squamous cell carcinoma at sites of sexual contact, not vascular skin nodules.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Disseminated MAC gives fever, night sweats, weight loss, or focal lymphadenitis rather than vascular skin lesions.

questions.stem: A 42-year-old woman with AIDS and a CD4 count of 40/uL reports painless loss of vision in one eye and pain on swallowing. Fundoscopy shows cotton-wool spots with hemorrhage, and endoscopy shows linear esophageal ulcers whose biopsy reveals enlarged cells with intranuclear owl-eye inclusion bodies. Which of the following is the most likely organism?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Candida albicans

choices.label: B
choices.text: Cytomegalovirus

choices.label: C
choices.text: Epstein-Barr virus

choices.label: D
choices.text: Herpes simplex virus

choices.label: E
choices.text: Toxoplasma gondii

explanation.summary: CMV disease in advanced AIDS causes colitis, retinitis, esophagitis, encephalitis, and pneumonitis, with owl-eye inclusions on biopsy.
explanation.whyCorrect: At CD4 counts below 100/mm3, CMV produces the CREEP pattern of colitis, retinitis, esophagitis, encephalitis, and pneumonitis. The diagnostic findings are linear ulcers on endoscopy, cotton-wool spots on fundoscopy, and biopsy showing cells with intranuclear owl-eye inclusion bodies, all present in this patient.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Candida esophagitis shows white plaques on endoscopy with yeast and pseudohyphae on biopsy, not owl-eye inclusions.
whyWrongByChoice.C: EBV causes oral hairy leukoplakia and B-cell lymphomas rather than retinitis and esophageal ulcers.
whyWrongByChoice.D: HSV reactivation occurs as CD4 counts fall, but it does not produce retinal cotton-wool spots with owl-eye inclusion bodies.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Toxoplasma gondii causes brain abscesses seen as multiple ring-enhancing lesions on MRI.

questions.stem: A 36-year-old man with AIDS has 2 weeks of worsening headache, fever, and neck stiffness. Lumbar puncture is performed, and an India ink preparation of the cerebrospinal fluid shows encapsulated yeast. Which of the following is the most likely organism?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Candida albicans

choices.label: B
choices.text: Cryptococcus neoformans

choices.label: C
choices.text: Histoplasma capsulatum

choices.label: D
choices.text: Pneumocystis jirovecii

choices.label: E
choices.text: Toxoplasma gondii

explanation.summary: Cryptococcus neoformans causes meningitis in advanced HIV and appears as encapsulated yeast on India ink stain.
explanation.whyCorrect: Cryptococcus neoformans is among the pathogens seen once CD4 counts fall below 100/mm3, and it presents as meningitis. The diagnosis rests on encapsulated yeast seen on India ink stain of cerebrospinal fluid or on detection of cryptococcal capsular antigen.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Candida albicans causes thrush and esophagitis and shows yeast with pseudohyphae rather than a thick capsule.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Histoplasma capsulatum presents with systemic symptoms and oval yeast cells within macrophages.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Pneumocystis jirovecii causes pneumonia with ground-glass opacities rather than meningitis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Toxoplasma gondii causes brain abscesses with multiple ring-enhancing lesions, not a yeast on India ink.

questions.stem: A 31-year-old man with AIDS and a CD4 count of 55/uL has 6 weeks of profuse watery diarrhea and a 9-kg weight loss. Stool examination with an acid-fast stain shows oocysts. Which of the following is the most likely organism?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Candida albicans

choices.label: B
choices.text: Cryptosporidium spp

choices.label: C
choices.text: Cytomegalovirus

choices.label: D
choices.text: Histoplasma capsulatum

choices.label: E
choices.text: Mycobacterium avium complex

explanation.summary: Cryptosporidium causes chronic watery diarrhea in advanced AIDS and is identified by acid-fast oocysts in stool.
explanation.whyCorrect: Cryptosporidium species are seen once CD4 counts fall below 100/mm3 and produce chronic, watery diarrhea. The organism is identified by acid-fast oocysts in the stool, which is exactly the finding reported here.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Candida in advanced HIV causes esophagitis with white plaques, not a chronic watery diarrhea.
whyWrongByChoice.C: CMV causes colitis with linear ulcers on endoscopy and owl-eye inclusion bodies on biopsy.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Histoplasmosis can cause diarrhea but is identified by oval yeast cells within macrophages.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Disseminated MAC causes fever, night sweats, and weight loss or focal lymphadenitis rather than acid-fast oocysts in stool.

questions.stem: A 40-year-old man with AIDS has 10 days of headache and new right-sided weakness. MRI of the brain shows multiple ring-enhancing lesions at the gray-white junction and in the basal ganglia. Which of the following is the most likely cause?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Cerebral toxoplasmosis

choices.label: B
choices.text: Cryptococcal meningitis

choices.label: C
choices.text: Epstein-Barr virus-driven CNS lymphoma

choices.label: D
choices.text: HIV-associated dementia

choices.label: E
choices.text: JC virus reactivation

explanation.summary: Multiple ring-enhancing brain lesions in AIDS point to Toxoplasma abscesses, whereas EBV-driven CNS lymphoma tends to be solitary.
explanation.whyCorrect: Toxoplasma gondii causes brain abscesses in patients with CD4 counts below 100/mm3 and characteristically produces multiple ring-enhancing lesions on MRI. Multiplicity is the feature used to separate toxoplasmosis from CNS lymphoma, which is also ring-enhancing but may be solitary.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Cryptococcal disease presents as meningitis with encapsulated yeast on India ink, not focal abscesses.
whyWrongByChoice.C: EBV-driven CNS lymphoma is ring-enhancing but tends to be solitary rather than multifocal.
whyWrongByChoice.D: HIV-associated dementia shows cerebral atrophy on neuroimaging rather than discrete enhancing lesions.
whyWrongByChoice.E: PML from JC virus produces non-enhancing areas of demyelination, not ring-enhancing masses.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old man with AIDS and a CD4 count of 30/uL has 2 months of fever, drenching night sweats, and weight loss. Examination shows cervical lymphadenopathy but no localizing signs, and chest imaging is unremarkable. Which of the following organisms is most likely responsible?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Bartonella henselae bacilli

choices.label: B
choices.text: Cryptosporidium parvum, a protozoan

choices.label: C
choices.text: JC virus, a polyomavirus

choices.label: D
choices.text: Mycobacterium avium complex

choices.label: E
choices.text: Pneumocystis jirovecii, a fungus

explanation.summary: Disseminated Mycobacterium avium complex causes nonspecific systemic symptoms and is most common at CD4 counts below 50/mm3.
explanation.whyCorrect: Mycobacterium avium-intracellulare and the Mycobacterium avium complex appear once CD4 counts fall below 100/mm3 and are most common when the count is below 50/mm3. The presentation is nonspecific systemic symptoms such as fever, night sweats, and weight loss, or focal lymphadenitis, which matches this patient at 30/uL.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Bartonella causes bacillary angiomatosis with red-purple skin papules and nodules.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Cryptosporidium causes chronic watery diarrhea with acid-fast oocysts in stool.
whyWrongByChoice.C: JC virus reactivation causes progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy with focal neurologic deficits.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Pneumocystis causes pneumonia with dyspnea and ground-glass opacities, absent on this patient's imaging.

questions.stem: A 25-year-old man requests HIV testing 4 days after a condomless encounter with a partner whose status he does not know. He is asymptomatic and has never been tested. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Advise abstaining from risky behavior and return later for testing

choices.label: B
choices.text: Perform a nucleic acid amplification test and call the result conclusive

choices.label: C
choices.text: Perform a Western blot to detect the earliest antibody response

choices.label: D
choices.text: Perform an antigen/antibody assay and call a negative result conclusive

choices.label: E
choices.text: Start antiretroviral therapy and defer all testing for 6 months

explanation.summary: Earlier than about 10 days after infection, no HIV test detects the virus consistently, so the patient must return for repeat testing.
explanation.whyCorrect: In the first days after exposure the virus has not replicated and spread enough to be detected by any assay. Neither the antigen/antibody assay nor NAT is reliable this early, so a patient with a recent potential exposure should be advised to avoid risky behavior in the interim and return to be tested once enough time has passed.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Viral RNA becomes detectable only after roughly 10 days, so NAT is not conclusive at 4 days either.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Western blot is no longer used for HIV and is the last marker to become positive, not the earliest.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A negative antigen/antibody result 4 days after exposure does not exclude infection.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Treatment is not started on the basis of a possible exposure, and deferring testing for 6 months is far too long.

questions.stem: Blood is drawn from a patient 12 days after a documented HIV transmission event. Which of the following markers of infection is the first to become detectable in the blood?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A CD4 count below 200/uL

choices.label: B
choices.text: HIV RNA

choices.label: C
choices.text: IgG against HIV envelope proteins

choices.label: D
choices.text: IgM against HIV

choices.label: E
choices.text: p24 antigen

explanation.summary: Viral RNA is the first detectable sign of HIV infection, which is why NAT is the earliest usable test.
explanation.whyCorrect: After about 10 days, viral RNA rises rapidly and becomes the first detectable marker, so nucleic acid amplification testing by RT-PCR is the earliest test that can detect an HIV infection. The order of appearance is RNA, then the p24 capsid protein, then IgM roughly 20 to 30 days after infection, and finally IgG. The appearance of antibodies is called seroconversion.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Severe CD4 depletion takes years to develop and is not a marker of recent infection.
whyWrongByChoice.C: IgG rises slowly after IgM and is the last of these markers to appear.
whyWrongByChoice.D: IgM titers begin to rise roughly 20 to 30 days after infection, well after viral RNA.
whyWrongByChoice.E: p24 becomes detectable shortly after viral RNA rises, not before it.

questions.stem: A neonate is delivered at term to a woman known to have HIV. The pediatric team must determine whether the infant is infected. Which of the following is the most appropriate approach?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Antigen/antibody combination assay drawn at birth

choices.label: B
choices.text: CD4 count with viral resistance culture drawn at birth

choices.label: C
choices.text: HIV-1/HIV-2 antibody differentiation immunoassay at 1 month

choices.label: D
choices.text: IgG serology repeated at 6 months and at 12 months

choices.label: E
choices.text: Nucleic acid amplification testing at 14 to 21 days of life

explanation.summary: Maternal IgG crosses the placenta, so newborns of HIV-positive mothers are screened with NAT rather than antibody-based assays.
explanation.whyCorrect: IgG from a pregnant person with HIV crosses the placenta and can produce a false positive antigen/antibody screen in an uninfected newborn. Babies born to people with HIV should therefore be screened with NAT, which detects viral nucleic acid, at 14 to 21 days of life, again at 1 to 2 months, and again at 4 to 6 months.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The antigen/antibody assay detects transplacental maternal IgG and will be falsely positive in an uninfected infant.
whyWrongByChoice.B: CD4 count and resistance culture are follow-up studies for a patient already known to be infected.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The differentiation immunoassay is also antibody based, so maternal IgG confounds it in the same way.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Serial IgG serology cannot distinguish maternal from infant antibody and delays diagnosis for months.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old man has a positive HIV-1/2 antigen/antibody immunoassay. The follow-up HIV-1/HIV-2 antibody differentiation immunoassay is indeterminate for HIV-1 and negative for HIV-2, and an HIV-1 nucleic acid test is positive. Which of the following is the most accurate interpretation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: He has acute HIV-1 infection

choices.label: B
choices.text: He has chronic HIV-1 infection

choices.label: C
choices.text: He has HIV-2 infection

choices.label: D
choices.text: He is negative for both HIV-1 and HIV-2

choices.label: E
choices.text: The screening assay result was a false positive

explanation.summary: A positive screen with an indeterminate antibody differentiation assay and a positive HIV-1 NAT indicates acute HIV-1 infection.
explanation.whyCorrect: Because no test has perfect sensitivity and specificity, diagnosis requires two positive tests: first the antigen/antibody assay, then an immunoassay that differentiates antibodies to HIV-1 and HIV-2. When the differentiation assay is indeterminate or negative, an HIV-1 NAT is performed, and a positive NAT at that point establishes acute HIV-1 infection, since viral RNA appears before antibodies fully develop.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Chronic infection would show fully reactive HIV-1 antibodies on the differentiation assay rather than an indeterminate result.
whyWrongByChoice.C: HIV-2 antibodies were not detected, so HIV-2 infection is not supported.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A negative result requires a negative screening assay for HIV-1 and HIV-2 antibodies and for p24 antigen.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The positive nucleic acid test confirms true infection rather than a false positive screen.

questions.stem: A virology laboratory characterizes the agent isolated from nasopharyngeal specimens during a winter surge of respiratory illness. The particle is readily inactivated by lipid solvents, its genome is translated directly by host ribosomes without a prior transcription step, and electron microscopy shows a coiled internal nucleoprotein filament with club-shaped surface projections. Which of the following best describes this virus?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Enveloped virus with a double-stranded DNA genome and an icosahedral capsid

choices.label: B
choices.text: Enveloped virus with a negative-sense single-stranded RNA genome and an icosahedral capsid

choices.label: C
choices.text: Enveloped virus with a positive-sense single-stranded RNA genome and a helical capsid

choices.label: D
choices.text: Naked virus with a double-stranded RNA genome and a helical capsid

choices.label: E
choices.text: Naked virus with a single-stranded RNA genome and an icosahedral capsid

explanation.summary: Coronaviruses are enveloped, positive-sense single-stranded RNA viruses with a helical nucleocapsid.
explanation.whyCorrect: Coronaviruses are enveloped and store their genetic information as (+)ssRNA, which is why the genome can be translated directly by host ribosomes. They also have a helical nucleocapsid, and the spiked protrusions on the surface give the crown-like appearance that names the family. Susceptibility to lipid solvents reflects the lipid envelope.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Coronaviruses carry an RNA genome; a double-stranded DNA genome with an icosahedral capsid describes an unrelated family.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A negative-sense genome could not be translated directly by ribosomes, and the coronavirus capsid is helical, not icosahedral.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The genome is single stranded, not double stranded, and coronaviruses are enveloped rather than naked.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Although the genome is single-stranded RNA, coronaviruses are enveloped and have a helical rather than icosahedral capsid.

questions.stem: Electron micrographs of a coronavirus isolate show club-shaped projections radiating from the surface of each particle, giving it a crown-like silhouette. Which of the following best describes the function of these surface projections?

choices.label: A
choices.text: They bind receptors on the host cell surface and facilitate viral entry

choices.label: B
choices.text: They cleave sialic acid from the cell surface to release progeny virions

choices.label: C
choices.text: They coil around the genome to build the internal nucleocapsid structure

choices.label: D
choices.text: They copy the viral genome into a complementary negative-sense RNA template

choices.label: E
choices.text: They form the pore through which viral RNA is extruded into the cytoplasm

explanation.summary: The coronavirus spike protein binds host cells and mediates entry.
explanation.whyCorrect: Coronaviruses are named for the spiked protrusions on their surface, which make the particle look like a crown ('corona' is Latin for crown). The spike protein that protrudes from the virus surface binds host cells and facilitates entry. For SARS-CoV-2 this binding is to the ACE2 receptor.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Cleaving sialic acid to release progeny virions is the job of a neuraminidase, which coronaviruses do not use for this purpose.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The internal helical nucleocapsid is built from nucleocapsid protein, not from the external spike protein.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Copying the genome into a complementary template is performed by the RNA-dependent RNA polymerase, an internal enzyme.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The spike is an attachment and entry protein, not a channel for extruding genomic RNA into the cytoplasm.

questions.stem: A 67-year-old man is admitted with 5 days of fever, dry cough, and progressive dyspnea after his grandson had a 'cold.' Oxygen saturation is 88% on room air, and chest imaging shows bilateral peripheral ground-glass opacities. A nasopharyngeal nucleic acid amplification test is positive for SARS-CoV-2. Which of the following host cell receptors does this virus use to enter cells?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Angiotensin-converting enzyme 2 (ACE2)

choices.label: B
choices.text: CD21 (complement receptor 2) on B lymphocytes

choices.label: C
choices.text: CD4, together with the CXCR4 and CCR5 coreceptors

choices.label: D
choices.text: Heparan sulfate proteoglycans on epithelial cells

choices.label: E
choices.text: Sialic acid residues on surface glycoproteins

explanation.summary: SARS-CoV-2 enters cells by binding ACE2 with its spike glycoprotein.
explanation.whyCorrect: When SARS-CoV-2 reaches the distal respiratory tract it infects type II pneumocytes via the receptor for angiotensin-converting enzyme 2 (ACE2). ACE2 is also expressed in the cardiovascular system, brain, kidneys, and gastrointestinal tract, which is why patients may develop findings beyond the respiratory system.

whyWrongByChoice.B: CD21 (CR2) is the entry receptor used by Epstein-Barr virus on B lymphocytes.
whyWrongByChoice.C: CD4 with the CXCR4 and CCR5 coreceptors is used by HIV to enter cells.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Herpes simplex virus uses heparan sulfate proteoglycans for attachment.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Influenza virus attaches to sialic acid residues on host surface glycoproteins.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old woman with COVID-19 becomes hypoxemic on hospital day 8. Studies of patients with similar disease show that once the virus reaches the distal respiratory tract it completes its life cycle in an alveolar cell population that expresses high levels of the viral entry receptor. Which of the following cells is infected?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Alveolar macrophages

choices.label: B
choices.text: Bronchial smooth muscle cells

choices.label: C
choices.text: Goblet cells of the bronchial mucosa

choices.label: D
choices.text: Type I pneumocytes

choices.label: E
choices.text: Type II pneumocytes

explanation.summary: In the distal lung SARS-CoV-2 completes its life cycle inside ACE2-bearing type II pneumocytes.
explanation.whyCorrect: When the virus reaches the distal respiratory tract it infects type II pneumocytes via the ACE2 receptor and completes its virus life cycle there. Infection of these surfactant-producing cells contributes to surfactant dysfunction, alveolar collapse, and impaired gas exchange in severe disease.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Alveolar macrophages are recruited and activated during the inflammatory response but are not the cells in which the virus completes its life cycle.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Bronchial smooth muscle regulates airway caliber and is not a site of viral replication in this infection.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Goblet cells secrete mucus in the conducting airways and are not the distal alveolar target described.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Type I pneumocytes form the thin gas-exchange surface but are not identified as the ACE2-bearing cells in which the virus replicates.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old man develops nasal congestion, sore throat, and hoarseness 4 days after a household exposure to SARS-CoV-2. He notes that secretions feel difficult to clear from his nose and throat. Which of the following best explains this finding?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Antibody-mediated lysis of nasal epithelium strips the mucosal barrier

choices.label: B
choices.text: Bacterial superinfection enzymatically degrades the airway mucus layer

choices.label: C
choices.text: Destruction of ciliated epithelial cells impairs mucociliary clearance

choices.label: D
choices.text: Loss of submucosal glands eliminates production of airway mucus

choices.label: E
choices.text: Reflex vasoconstriction of nasal vessels thickens the airway secretions

explanation.summary: SARS-CoV-2 destroys ciliated epithelium of the nasopharynx and upper airway, impairing mucociliary clearance.
explanation.whyCorrect: In the upper respiratory system the virus infects and destroys ciliated epithelial cells of the nasopharynx and upper airway. The result is inflammation and impaired mucociliary clearance, which produces the familiar rhinorrhea, congestion, sinus and ear pain, sore throat, and hoarseness of early infection.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Antibody-mediated lysis of the nasal epithelium is not the mechanism of early upper airway injury in this infection.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Bacterial superinfection is not required for the upper respiratory symptoms of acute SARS-CoV-2 infection.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Mucus production is not lost; the problem is failure to move mucus, not failure to make it.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Vasoconstriction of nasal vessels does not account for the impaired clearance of secretions described.

questions.stem: A 71-year-old man hospitalized with COVID-19 pneumonia has arterial hypoxemia far more severe than predicted by the extent of consolidation on chest imaging. In addition to alveolar epithelium, SARS-CoV-2 infects and destroys a second cell type within the alveolar wall. Which of the following best describes that target and its consequence?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Airway smooth muscle cells, causing fixed narrowing of the small airways

choices.label: B
choices.text: Alveolar macrophages, causing failure to clear inhaled particulate matter

choices.label: C
choices.text: Capillary endothelial cells, causing reduced blood perfusion of the alveoli

choices.label: D
choices.text: Fibroblasts, causing immediate deposition of dense interstitial collagen

choices.label: E
choices.text: Pleural mesothelial cells, causing accumulation of exudative pleural fluid

explanation.summary: SARS-CoV-2 also infects and destroys capillary endothelial cells, reducing alveolar perfusion.
explanation.whyCorrect: Besides infecting type II pneumocytes through ACE2, the virus can infect and destroy capillary endothelial cells, leading to reduced blood perfusion of the alveoli. Loss of the perfusing capillary bed impairs gas exchange out of proportion to the visible airspace disease and also contributes to the microvascular injury and thrombotic complications of severe COVID-19.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Fixed small airway narrowing produces obstructive physiology rather than the perfusion defect described.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Impaired particulate clearance by macrophages does not explain hypoxemia disproportionate to radiographic consolidation.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Immediate dense collagen deposition is not the described endothelial mechanism of early perfusion failure.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Exudative pleural fluid accumulation is not the alveolar-wall target described in this infection.

questions.stem: Investigators find that epithelial cells infected with SARS-CoV-2 release markedly less of a key antiviral cytokine than cells infected with control viruses, and that nasopharyngeal viral titers in infected patients are correspondingly high. Which of the following viral strategies best explains these observations?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Viral proteins block assembly of the complement membrane attack complex

choices.label: B
choices.text: Viral proteins cleave secreted immunoglobulin A at its hinge region

choices.label: C
choices.text: Viral proteins degrade major histocompatibility complex class I molecules

choices.label: D
choices.text: Viral proteins inhibit the production of interferon-beta by immune cells

choices.label: E
choices.text: Viral proteins prevent maturation of the phagolysosome in macrophages

explanation.summary: SARS-CoV-2 translates proteins that blunt the innate response, notably by inhibiting interferon-beta production.
explanation.whyCorrect: SARS-CoV-2 translates many proteins that protect it from the initial innate immune response; one example is inhibition of interferon-beta production by immune cells. Slowing the innate response allows a high amount of virus to be produced, which in turn increases transmission risk.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Blocking the membrane attack complex is a complement evasion strategy and does not explain reduced cytokine release.
whyWrongByChoice.B: IgA protease activity is a bacterial mucosal evasion mechanism, not the described innate cytokine defect.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Degradation of MHC class I would impair CD8 T-cell recognition rather than reduce release of an antiviral cytokine.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Blocking phagolysosome maturation is an intracellular bacterial survival strategy unrelated to interferon production.

questions.stem: A 26-year-old woman with confirmed SARS-CoV-2 infection has rhinorrhea, ear and sinus pain, sore throat, cough, and hoarseness. Macrophage activation and recruitment drive the airway inflammation responsible for these symptoms. Which of the following sets of mediators is chiefly responsible?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Histamine, bradykinin, and leukotriene C4

choices.label: B
choices.text: Interleukin-1, interleukin-6, and tumor necrosis factor-alpha

choices.label: C
choices.text: Interleukin-2, interleukin-12, and interferon-gamma

choices.label: D
choices.text: Interleukin-4, interleukin-5, and interleukin-13

choices.label: E
choices.text: Transforming growth factor-beta, interleukin-10, and interleukin-35

explanation.summary: Acute airway inflammation in COVID-19 is driven by macrophage-derived IL-1, IL-6, and TNF-alpha.
explanation.whyCorrect: SARS-CoV-2 becomes symptomatic by inducing airway inflammation that produces the familiar upper respiratory symptoms. That inflammatory response is driven by cytokines: macrophage activation and recruitment cause increased interleukin-1, interleukin-6, and tumor necrosis factor-alpha. IL-6 is also the target of immunomodulatory therapy in severe disease.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Histamine, bradykinin, and leukotrienes are vasoactive mediators of immediate hypersensitivity, not the macrophage cytokines described.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Interleukin-2, interleukin-12, and interferon-gamma drive type 1 cell-mediated responses rather than this airway cytokine surge.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Interleukins 4, 5, and 13 are type 2 cytokines associated with allergic inflammation and eosinophil recruitment.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Transforming growth factor-beta, interleukin-10, and interleukin-35 are anti-inflammatory and would suppress, not drive, inflammation.

questions.stem: Over 3 years of genomic surveillance, a respiratory virus with an RNA genome accumulates far more sequence changes than a co-circulating virus with a DNA genome. Which of the following best explains the difference?

choices.label: A
choices.text: RNA genomes are replicated many more times within each infected cell

choices.label: B
choices.text: RNA genomes are segmented and reassort whenever two strains coinfect a cell

choices.label: C
choices.text: RNA genomes recombine with host chromosomal DNA during each replication cycle

choices.label: D
choices.text: RNA polymerases have reduced proofreading capacity compared with DNA polymerases

choices.label: E
choices.text: RNA viruses integrate a provirus that is copied by error-prone reverse transcriptase

explanation.summary: RNA viruses mutate faster because their polymerases proofread poorly.
explanation.whyCorrect: RNA viruses have a higher rate of mutation than DNA viruses because of the reduced proofreading capacity of their polymerases. This is why SARS-CoV-2 has evolved continuously, producing multiple variants that differ in transmissibility, immune escape, and treatment response.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A higher number of replication cycles is not the stated explanation for the elevated mutation rate of RNA viruses.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Reassortment requires a segmented genome, which coronaviruses do not have.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Coronaviruses do not recombine with host chromosomal DNA during replication.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Coronaviruses do not integrate a provirus or use reverse transcriptase.

questions.stem: A public health agency reports that a newly dominant SARS-CoV-2 variant displaced the previously circulating variant within weeks because it spread more efficiently between people. Sequencing shows a large number of mutations concentrated in a single viral gene. Which of the following best accounts for the increased transmissibility?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Mutations in the envelope gene that increase the stability of released virions

choices.label: B
choices.text: Mutations in the membrane gene that widen the range of tissues infected

choices.label: C
choices.text: Mutations in the nucleocapsid gene that increase genome packaging efficiency

choices.label: D
choices.text: Mutations in the polymerase gene that accelerate replication of the genome

choices.label: E
choices.text: Mutations in the spike gene that increase the infective capability of the virus

explanation.summary: Spike protein mutations explain why Omicron outcompeted Delta in transmissibility.
explanation.whyCorrect: The Omicron variant had a higher rate of transmissibility than the Delta variant, probably because of a high number of mutations to its spike protein that increased its infective capability. Because spike mediates receptor binding and entry, changes there directly affect how efficiently the virus infects a new host, and mutations in the spike glycoprotein are also a common cause of repeated infections.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Increased virion stability from envelope changes is not the explanation given for variant displacement.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A broadened tissue range would alter the disease pattern rather than explain more efficient person-to-person spread.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Nucleocapsid changes affecting genome packaging are not the described driver of increased spread between people.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Faster genome replication by the polymerase is not the mechanism identified for the variant's transmissibility advantage.

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes the origin of SARS-CoV-2 as currently understood?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It arose by reassortment between two human seasonal coronaviruses

choices.label: B
choices.text: It emerged from chronic persistent infection in immunocompromised people

choices.label: C
choices.text: It has circulated undetected in human populations since the early 1990s

choices.label: D
choices.text: It is zoonotic, probably from bats, and crossed to humans in late 2019

choices.label: E
choices.text: It was transmitted to humans from domestic poultry in Southeast Asia

explanation.summary: SARS-CoV-2 is thought to be zoonotic, probably of bat origin, with human crossover in late 2019.
explanation.whyCorrect: As with many epidemic or pandemic viral strains, SARS-CoV-2 is thought to be zoonotic, probably originating from bats or an accidental laboratory release. The crossover to humans is believed to have occurred in late 2019 in a livestock market in Wuhan, China, although exactly how the initial human infection occurred is unclear.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Reassortment requires a segmented genome and is not how this coronavirus arose.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Chronic infection in immunocompromised hosts is not the proposed origin of the pandemic strain.
whyWrongByChoice.C: SARS-CoV-2 was newly recognized in late 2019, not circulating silently for decades.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Domestic poultry are the reservoir associated with avian influenza, not with SARS-CoV-2.

questions.stem: During the 2002-2003 outbreak of one novel coronavirus, roughly 8,096 cases resulted in 774 deaths. Since the first case of a second novel coronavirus, 2,494 cases have resulted in 858 deaths. Which of the following best characterizes the second outbreak relative to the first?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A higher case-fatality rate and a larger total number of cases

choices.label: B
choices.text: A higher case-fatality rate and a smaller total number of cases

choices.label: C
choices.text: A lower case-fatality rate and a larger total number of cases

choices.label: D
choices.text: A lower case-fatality rate and a similar total number of cases

choices.label: E
choices.text: An identical case-fatality rate and a smaller total number of cases

explanation.summary: MERS-CoV has caused far fewer cases than SARS-CoV but with a much higher case-fatality rate.
explanation.whyCorrect: During the 2002-2003 SARS-CoV outbreak roughly 8,096 cases were reported with 774 deaths, a case-fatality rate of 9.6%. Since the first case of MERS, 2,494 cases have resulted in 858 deaths, a case-fatality rate of 34.4%. So the second outbreak involved fewer cases but a substantially higher proportion of deaths.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The case-fatality rate was indeed higher, but the total number of cases was smaller, not larger.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The second outbreak had both a higher case-fatality rate and fewer cases, not a lower rate with more cases.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The case-fatality rate was higher, not lower, and the case counts differ by more than threefold.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The case-fatality rates are not identical: 34.4% versus 9.6%.

questions.stem: SARS-CoV-2 has caused more than 775 million reported infections worldwide, whereas SARS-CoV and MERS-CoV together caused fewer than 11,000 cases. SARS-CoV-2 nevertheless has a far lower case-fatality rate than either of the other two. Which of the following best explains the enormous difference in case counts?

choices.label: A
choices.text: SARS-CoV-2 establishes lifelong latency in sensory ganglia after acute illness

choices.label: B
choices.text: SARS-CoV-2 is transmitted mainly by contaminated environmental surfaces

choices.label: C
choices.text: SARS-CoV-2 is transmitted primarily by the fecal-oral route in crowded settings

choices.label: D
choices.text: SARS-CoV-2 requires an ongoing animal reservoir for each human infection

choices.label: E
choices.text: SARS-CoV-2 spreads aggressively by respiratory droplets between casual contacts

explanation.summary: What SARS-CoV-2 lacks in mortality it makes up for in ease of transmission.
explanation.whyCorrect: SARS-CoV-2 has nowhere near the mortality rate of SARS-CoV or MERS-CoV, but it makes up for that in ease of transmission. Spread of SARS-CoV and MERS-CoV was largely limited to health care workers, close family, and other close contacts, whereas SARS-CoV-2 spreads aggressively via respiratory droplets, allowing it to reach hundreds of millions of people.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Coronaviruses do not establish lifelong latency in sensory ganglia.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Transmission via contaminated surfaces is possible but considered rare and does not explain the scale of spread.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Although gastrointestinal symptoms occur, the dominant route of spread is airborne particles and respiratory droplets.
whyWrongByChoice.D: After the initial crossover, spread has been human to human and does not depend on repeated animal exposure.

questions.stem: A hospital infection-control team is preparing a briefing for employees about how SARS-CoV-2 is most often acquired. Which of the following is the main risk factor for infection?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Close contact with an infected person indoors or in poorly ventilated spaces

choices.label: B
choices.text: Contact with livestock and wild animals at markets that sell live animals

choices.label: C
choices.text: Eating food prepared by an infected but asymptomatic food handler

choices.label: D
choices.text: Exposure to blood or body fluids during an unprotected needlestick injury

choices.label: E
choices.text: Touching contaminated doorknobs and other high-touch environmental surfaces

explanation.summary: Close contact with an infected person, especially indoors or in poorly ventilated spaces, is the main risk factor.
explanation.whyCorrect: The main risk factor for acquiring SARS-CoV-2 is close contact with an infected person, particularly indoors or in poorly ventilated spaces, because the virus spreads mostly by airborne particles and respiratory droplets released with sneezing, laughing, and coughing. Transmission via contaminated surfaces is possible but considered rare.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Animal contact relates to the original zoonotic crossover, not to ongoing human infection risk.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Foodborne spread is not a recognized route of transmission for this virus.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Bloodborne transmission through needlestick injury is not a described route for SARS-CoV-2.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Fomite transmission can occur when people touch their eyes, mouth, or nose after surface contact, but it is considered rare rather than the main risk factor.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old man was exposed to a household member with confirmed COVID-19 and asks how long he needs to watch for symptoms. Which of the following best describes the incubation period of SARS-CoV-2?

choices.label: A
choices.text: 1 to 3 days, with a mean of about 2 days

choices.label: B
choices.text: 2 to 14 days, with a mean of about 5 days

choices.label: C
choices.text: 3 to 8 weeks, with a mean of about 5 weeks

choices.label: D
choices.text: 6 to 24 hours, with a mean of about 12 hours

choices.label: E
choices.text: 10 to 21 days, with a mean of about 14 days

explanation.summary: The time from inoculation to symptoms is 2 to 14 days, averaging about 5 days.
explanation.whyCorrect: The time from viral inoculation to the development of symptoms ranges from 2 to 14 days, with a mean of 5 days. Acute COVID-19 effects then last up to 4 weeks after infection, while symptoms persisting beyond 3 months are classified as chronic, or long COVID.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A 1-to-3-day window is too brief and would miss most infections in exposed contacts.
whyWrongByChoice.C: An incubation of weeks to months does not apply to SARS-CoV-2.
whyWrongByChoice.D: An incubation measured in hours is far shorter than that of SARS-CoV-2.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A 10-to-21-day window overstates both the range and the mean for this virus.

questions.stem: A 41-year-old woman with a positive SARS-CoV-2 test has fever and malaise and also reports 3 days of diarrhea, nausea, and crampy abdominal pain. Which of the following best characterizes these gastrointestinal symptoms?

choices.label: A
choices.text: They are a common manifestation of acute SARS-CoV-2 infection

choices.label: B
choices.text: They are pathognomonic for the hyperinflammatory phase of the illness

choices.label: C
choices.text: They essentially exclude SARS-CoV-2 as the cause of her illness

choices.label: D
choices.text: They indicate a concurrent bacterial enteritis rather than COVID-19

choices.label: E
choices.text: They occur only in patients who are significantly immunocompromised

explanation.summary: Gastrointestinal symptoms are a common part of acute COVID-19.
explanation.whyCorrect: Initial infection symptoms range from asymptomatic to typical flu-like symptoms of fever, aches, and malaise, and gastrointestinal symptoms such as diarrhea, nausea and vomiting, and abdominal pain are also common. ACE2 is expressed in the gastrointestinal tract as well as the respiratory tract, which is why patients may develop symptoms beyond the respiratory system.

whyWrongByChoice.B: The hyperinflammatory phase is characterized by severe respiratory and systemic inflammation, not specifically by diarrhea.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Their presence does not argue against SARS-CoV-2; it is consistent with it.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A separate bacterial enteritis need not be invoked, since these symptoms are part of the ordinary presentation.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Gastrointestinal symptoms occur commonly in immunocompetent patients as well.

questions.stem: A 19-year-old college student tests positive for SARS-CoV-2 during routine screening but feels entirely well. He asks whether he can attend a crowded indoor party this evening. Which of the following is the most accurate counseling point?

choices.label: A
choices.text: He is contagious only if a repeat rapid antigen test is also positive

choices.label: B
choices.text: He is not contagious, because transmission requires coughing or sneezing

choices.label: C
choices.text: He may attend if he has remained afebrile for the preceding 24 hours

choices.label: D
choices.text: He may attend, because viral shedding begins only after fever develops

choices.label: E
choices.text: Symptoms do not correlate with infectivity, so he may still transmit the virus

explanation.summary: Symptoms do not correlate with infectivity, so asymptomatic patients can still spread SARS-CoV-2.
explanation.whyCorrect: Symptoms do not correlate with infectivity, so asymptomatic patients may spread the virus to others. Because the main risk factor for transmission is close contact indoors or in poorly ventilated spaces, an asymptomatic but infected student attending a crowded indoor gathering poses real risk to others.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Antigen testing is poorly sensitive, so a negative or single test result does not establish that he is not contagious.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Virus is released in respiratory secretions with ordinary talking and laughing, not only with coughing or sneezing.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Remaining afebrile does not indicate that he is no longer shedding infectious virus.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Shedding is not tied to the onset of fever; infectious virus can be present without any symptoms.

questions.stem: A 44-year-old woman reports fatigue, dyspnea, and cough that have persisted for 5 months after a documented SARS-CoV-2 infection. She had mild acute illness and was never hospitalized. Which of the following best describes this condition?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It affects roughly 25% of infected patients, equally in men and women

choices.label: B
choices.text: It affects roughly 30% of infected patients and is more common in men

choices.label: C
choices.text: It affects roughly 5% to 6% of patients and is more common in women

choices.label: D
choices.text: It is defined by symptoms beyond 12 months and is very rare in women

choices.label: E
choices.text: It is defined by symptoms beyond 4 weeks and affects half of all patients

explanation.summary: Long COVID means symptoms persisting more than 3 months, affects about 5% to 6% of patients, and is more common in women.
explanation.whyCorrect: Chronic symptoms may continue for more than 3 months after symptom onset. Long COVID may affect 5% to 6% of patients, and females are more affected than males (10% versus 5%). The most common symptoms are fatigue, fever, dyspnea, and cough, matching this patient's presentation.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The frequency is much lower than 25%, and the condition is not distributed equally between the sexes.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The reported frequency is far lower than 30%, and women rather than men are more affected.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The threshold is more than 3 months rather than 12 months, and women are affected about twice as often as men.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Acute effects last up to 4 weeks; chronic disease is defined by symptoms beyond 3 months, and it affects a small minority.

questions.stem: A 52-year-old woman is evaluated for chronic inflammatory disease following COVID-19 infection 6 months earlier. Which of the following findings would be LEAST expected in this setting?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Deep venous thrombosis of the lower extremity

choices.label: B
choices.text: Hepatomegaly with elevated aminotransferases

choices.label: C
choices.text: Low-grade fever persisting for several months

choices.label: D
choices.text: Pleuritic chest pain caused by pericarditis

choices.label: E
choices.text: Thrombocytosis on a complete blood count

explanation.summary: Chronic inflammatory disease after COVID-19 causes cytopenias rather than thrombocytosis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Chronic inflammatory disease secondary to COVID-19 has multiple consequences, including cytopenias, not thrombocytosis. Leg swelling from deep venous thrombi, hepatic involvement, persistent fever, and chest pain from pericarditis are all described features of the prolonged immune response that follows infection.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Leg swelling from deep venous thrombi is an expected consequence of the post-COVID procoagulant state.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Liver involvement is expected, and liver enzymes including AST and ALT are part of the long COVID laboratory evaluation.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Fever is listed among the most common long COVID symptoms along with fatigue, dyspnea, and cough.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Chest pain from pericarditis is specifically described among the symptoms attributed to prolonged immune response.

questions.stem: Five patients test positive for SARS-CoV-2 on the same day at an outpatient clinic. Which of the following patients is at greatest risk of dying from this infection?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A 28-year-old man with obesity who completed the primary vaccine series

choices.label: B
choices.text: A 35-year-old woman with mild asthma who is up to date on vaccination

choices.label: C
choices.text: A 45-year-old woman with controlled hypertension who is up to date on vaccination

choices.label: D
choices.text: A 52-year-old man with coronary artery disease who is up to date on vaccination

choices.label: E
choices.text: An 88-year-old man with diabetes and chronic kidney disease who is unvaccinated

explanation.summary: Advancing age dominates COVID-19 mortality risk and compounds with comorbidity and lack of vaccination.
explanation.whyCorrect: Using adults 18 to 39 years of age as the reference (death-risk ratio 1.0), risk rises steeply with age: 2.2 at 40 to 49 years, 4.3 at 50 to 64, 6.7 at 65 to 74, 8.5 at 75 to 84, and 10.6 at 85 years and older. Comorbidities add smaller increments individually (obesity 1.3, diabetes with complications 1.3, chronic kidney disease 1.2, coronary disease 1.1) but become significant when bundled, and being unvaccinated or not up to date also increases risk.

whyWrongByChoice.A: At 28 years of age his baseline death-risk ratio is near the reference value, and obesity adds only about 1.3-fold.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Her age group carries a ratio near 1.0, and being up to date on vaccination further lowers her risk.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A death-risk ratio of about 2.2 for her age group with controlled hypertension and current vaccination is far below that of the oldest patient.
whyWrongByChoice.D: His age group carries a ratio of about 4.3 and coronary disease adds roughly 1.1-fold, well below the risk at 85 years and older.

questions.stem: A 66-year-old man with severe COVID-19 develops multiorgan failure with a rising D-dimer and falling fibrinogen. Histologic study of his lungs shows neutrophils releasing webs of extracellular DNA and associated proteins. Which of the following best describes the role of these structures in his illness?

choices.label: A
choices.text: They deliver preformed antibody to the alveolar surface to block viral entry

choices.label: B
choices.text: They neutralize circulating cytokines and limit systemic inflammatory injury

choices.label: C
choices.text: They present viral antigen to CD8 T cells and speed clearance of the virus

choices.label: D
choices.text: They promote a pro-inflammatory and procoagulant state that consumes clotting factors

choices.label: E
choices.text: They seal damaged alveolar capillaries and restore normal alveolar gas exchange

explanation.summary: Neutrophil extracellular traps become a double-edged sword in COVID-19, driving inflammation and coagulation.
explanation.whyCorrect: Neutrophil extracellular traps (NETs) are webs of extracellular DNA and associated proteins that normally trap microbes and enhance their destruction. In COVID-19 these NETs become a double-edged sword, promoting a pro-inflammatory and procoagulant state that leads to multiorgan failure, in part through activation of the coagulation cascade and consumption of clotting factors, which explains the rising D-dimer and falling fibrinogen.

whyWrongByChoice.A: NETs consist of DNA and granule proteins, not preformed antibody delivered to the alveolar surface.
whyWrongByChoice.B: NETs amplify inflammation in this setting rather than neutralizing cytokines or limiting injury.
whyWrongByChoice.C: NETs are an innate extracellular trapping mechanism, not a pathway for antigen presentation to CD8 T cells.
whyWrongByChoice.E: NETs contribute to microvascular injury and thrombosis rather than repairing capillaries or restoring gas exchange.

questions.stem: A 74-year-old woman dies after 3 weeks of respiratory failure caused by COVID-19 pneumonia. Which of the following findings is most likely on histologic examination of her lungs?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A dense neutrophilic exudate filling alveolar spaces throughout an entire lobe

choices.label: B
choices.text: Broad septate hyphae invading and occluding pulmonary blood vessels

choices.label: C
choices.text: Caseating granulomas surrounded by cuffs of lymphocytes and epithelioid cells

choices.label: D
choices.text: Interstitial lymphocytic infiltrates with diffuse alveolar damage in the lung

choices.label: E
choices.text: Non-caseating granulomas containing multinucleated giant cells in the interstitium

explanation.summary: Advanced COVID-19 pneumonia shows diffuse inflammation with interstitial lymphocytic infiltrates and diffuse alveolar damage.
explanation.whyCorrect: In advanced COVID-19 the lungs show diffuse inflammation with interstitial lymphocytic infiltrates and diffuse alveolar damage. This viral pattern impairs gas exchange and causes dyspnea, hypoxemia, and, in severe cases, respiratory failure, and it is accompanied by surfactant dysfunction, widespread inflammation, and microvascular injury.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A dense neutrophilic exudate filling an entire lobe describes bacterial lobar pneumonia, not the interstitial viral pattern.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Angioinvasive septate hyphae indicate invasive mold infection rather than SARS-CoV-2 pneumonia.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Caseating granulomas are characteristic of mycobacterial infection rather than viral pneumonia.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Non-caseating granulomas with giant cells suggest sarcoidosis or hypersensitivity processes, not COVID-19.

questions.stem: A 63-year-old man with COVID-19 pneumonia has progressive hypoxemia, and chest imaging shows patchy loss of lung volume with collapsed alveolar units. Which of the following mechanisms best explains this alveolar collapse?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Diaphragmatic paralysis reduces the inspiratory pressure generated

choices.label: B
choices.text: Fibrotic contraction of the pleural surfaces compresses lung units

choices.label: C
choices.text: Loss of elastic recoil permits progressive alveolar overdistention

choices.label: D
choices.text: Obstruction of segmental bronchi by thick mucus plugs traps distal air

choices.label: E
choices.text: Surfactant dysfunction raises alveolar surface tension

explanation.summary: Surfactant dysfunction in COVID-19 pneumonia contributes to atelectasis.
explanation.whyCorrect: In advanced COVID-19 pneumonia, surfactant dysfunction may occur and contributes to alveolar collapse, or atelectasis, along with widespread inflammation and microvascular injury. This is mechanistically consistent with viral infection of type II pneumocytes, the surfactant-producing cells reached through the ACE2 receptor.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Diaphragmatic paralysis is a neuromuscular problem unrelated to the alveolar pathology described.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Pleural fibrosis and contraction are not features of acute COVID-19 pneumonia.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Loss of elastic recoil with overdistention describes emphysema, the opposite of alveolar collapse.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Mucus plugging with air trapping is not the described mechanism of alveolar collapse in this infection.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man with COVID-19 pneumonia deteriorates on hospital day 6 and is intubated for acute respiratory distress syndrome. Which of the following best explains his impaired gas exchange?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A rapidly accumulating transudative pleural effusion compresses the lung

choices.label: B
choices.text: Acute thrombosis of the main pulmonary artery obstructs right ventricular outflow

choices.label: C
choices.text: Bronchospasm from mast cell degranulation narrows the conducting airways

choices.label: D
choices.text: Immune complex deposits thicken the alveolar basement membrane diffusely

choices.label: E
choices.text: Pulmonary capillaries leak fluid into the alveoli, flooding the airspaces

explanation.summary: In COVID-19-associated ARDS, capillaries leak fluid into the alveoli and block gas exchange.
explanation.whyCorrect: Acute respiratory distress syndrome occurs in patients with COVID-19 pneumonia when the pulmonary capillaries leak fluid into the alveoli, reducing airflow and gas exchange. This flooding of the airspaces often requires intubation and mechanical ventilation.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A transudative pleural effusion compresses lung from outside and does not describe ARDS.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Although thrombosis is a recognized complication, ARDS in this setting is defined by capillary leak into alveoli.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Bronchospasm produces wheezing and obstructive physiology rather than the alveolar flooding of ARDS.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Immune complex deposition in the alveolar basement membrane is not the described mechanism of ARDS in this infection.

questions.stem: A 61-year-old woman hospitalized with COVID-19 develops a lower-extremity deep venous thrombosis on day 5 and an ischemic stroke on day 9 despite no prior thrombotic history. Which of the following best explains her increased thrombotic risk?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Acquired protein C deficiency resulting from hepatic synthetic failure

choices.label: B
choices.text: Antiphospholipid antibodies generated against the viral spike protein

choices.label: C
choices.text: Endothelial injury, neutrophil extracellular traps, and elevated fibrinogen

choices.label: D
choices.text: Marked reactive thrombocytosis driven by interleukin-6 release

choices.label: E
choices.text: Splenic sequestration of platelets with compensatory marrow release

explanation.summary: COVID-19 hypercoagulability arises from endothelial injury, NETs, and elevated fibrinogen with increased viscosity.
explanation.whyCorrect: COVID-19 causes an increased incidence of abnormal clotting that can lead to deep vein thrombosis, pulmonary emboli, and strokes. The hypercoagulability is likely due to a combination of endothelial injury, neutrophil extracellular traps, and elevated fibrinogen causing increased viscosity. Direct viral infection and destruction of capillary endothelial cells contributes to that endothelial injury.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Acquired protein C deficiency from liver failure is not the described mechanism of COVID-19 thrombosis.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Antiphospholipid antibodies directed at spike protein are not the stated cause of hypercoagulability here.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Chronic inflammatory disease after COVID-19 causes cytopenias, not marked reactive thrombocytosis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Splenic sequestration of platelets would reduce circulating platelet counts and does not drive thrombosis.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old woman asks her physician about the COVID-19 vaccines available in the United States. Which of the following statements is most accurate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Every available vaccine uses a replication-competent adenoviral vector

choices.label: B
choices.text: The mRNA vaccines insert viral DNA permanently into the host genome

choices.label: C
choices.text: The mRNA vaccines need no reformulation because spike rarely mutates

choices.label: D
choices.text: The protein subunit vaccine contains recombinant spike and adjuvant

choices.label: E
choices.text: Vaccination is recommended only for adults 65 years of age or older

explanation.summary: US COVID-19 vaccines are mRNA or protein based, and the protein subunit product contains recombinant spike plus adjuvant.
explanation.whyCorrect: COVID-19 vaccines available in the United States are made of mRNA or protein and are generally recommended for everyone aged 6 years and older. The protein subunit vaccine contains recombinant spike protein and adjuvant, while mRNA vaccines deliver viral mRNAs to host cells, prompting the host cells to produce the antigen and elicit an immune response without harming the cells.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The available products are mRNA or protein based, not replication-competent viral vectors.
whyWrongByChoice.B: mRNA vaccines deliver messenger RNA to the cytoplasm and do not insert DNA into the host genome.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Mutations in the spike glycoprotein are extremely common, and updated formulations are recommended to maintain protection.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Vaccination is generally recommended for everyone aged 6 years and older, not only for older adults.

questions.stem: A 31-year-old man performs a home antigen test for SARS-CoV-2 on the first day of mild symptoms, and the result is negative. He asks how much reassurance the result provides. Which of the following best describes this test?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It amplifies viral nucleic acid and remains sensitive at very low viral loads

choices.label: B
choices.text: It detects IgG antibody and turns positive several weeks after infection

choices.label: C
choices.text: It is both highly sensitive and highly specific and needs no confirmation

choices.label: D
choices.text: It is specific but poorly sensitive, so a low viral load may be missed

choices.label: E
choices.text: It requires a serum sample and must be processed in a reference laboratory

explanation.summary: Rapid antigen testing is specific but insensitive because it does not amplify viral material.
explanation.whyCorrect: Antigen testing is an immunoassay that detects antigens on the surface of SARS-CoV-2 from a nasal swab, with results in 15 minutes. While the test is specific, the lack of amplification of viral material makes it poorly sensitive, so low viral loads may not trigger a positive result. Its primary value is identifying high-viral-load patients likely to be contagious, which can guide behavior such as self-quarantine and avoiding travel.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Amplification of nucleic acid describes PCR-based NAAT, which is the more sensitive alternative.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Antibody assays detect circulating IgG weeks later and are a different test entirely.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Antigen testing is specific but not highly sensitive, so a negative result in early illness does not exclude infection.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Antigen testing uses a nasal swab and is widely available commercially for home use.

questions.stem: A 67-year-old man presents with 5 days of fever, dry cough, and progressive dyspnea. Temperature is 38.4 C (101.1 F), respiratory rate is 26/min, and oxygen saturation is 88% on room air. Auscultation reveals bilateral fine inspiratory crackles at the lung bases, and chest imaging shows bilateral peripheral ground-glass opacities. Which of the following is the best test to confirm the diagnosis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Blood sample for serum IgG antibody testing

choices.label: B
choices.text: Chest radiograph compared with prior imaging studies

choices.label: C
choices.text: Nasopharyngeal swab for antibody immunoassay testing

choices.label: D
choices.text: Nasopharyngeal swab for nucleic acid amplification testing

choices.label: E
choices.text: Sputum Gram stain with routine bacterial culture

explanation.summary: The diagnostic test of choice for COVID-19 is a nucleic acid amplification test, typically RT-PCR on a nasopharyngeal swab.
explanation.whyCorrect: The diagnostic test of choice for COVID-19 is nucleic acid amplification testing by reverse transcription polymerase chain reaction. Using PCR means even a small amount of viral RNA can be amplified to detectable levels, which makes it far more sensitive than antigen testing and the test most used in clinical settings.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Serum antibody testing is not considered diagnostic in acute illness because antibodies take weeks to develop.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Chest imaging can be normal early and its findings are not distinct enough to distinguish among pathogens.
whyWrongByChoice.C: An antibody test is performed on serum, not on a nasopharyngeal swab.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Gram stain and bacterial culture evaluate for bacterial infection and cannot identify a virus.

questions.stem: A 29-year-old woman who was never tested during a respiratory illness last winter wants to know whether that episode was COVID-19. She is currently asymptomatic and feels entirely well. Which of the following tests is most appropriate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Chest computed tomography to look for residual ground-glass opacity

choices.label: B
choices.text: Rapid antigen immunoassay performed on a nasal swab specimen

choices.label: C
choices.text: Reverse transcription polymerase chain reaction on a nasal swab

choices.label: D
choices.text: Serum assay for IgG against nonvaccine SARS-CoV-2 antigens

choices.label: E
choices.text: Serum D-dimer with C-reactive protein and ferritin levels

explanation.summary: Serologic IgG testing, directed at antigens not present in the vaccine, is used to detect prior infection.
explanation.whyCorrect: Assays that detect circulating IgG against SARS-CoV-2, typically to antigens not present in the vaccine, are less commonly used but are useful to detect prior infection. Because the antibodies often take weeks to develop, these assays are not helpful in acute illness but are exactly the test for the question this patient is asking.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Chest imaging cannot distinguish among pathogens and would not establish that the earlier illness was COVID-19.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Antigen testing detects current virus on a swab and would be negative long after the illness resolved.
whyWrongByChoice.C: RT-PCR detects viral RNA during active infection and would not document an infection from last winter.
whyWrongByChoice.E: These inflammatory and thrombotic markers are used to evaluate chronic post-COVID illness, not to confirm prior infection.

questions.stem: A 47-year-old woman has fatigue and dyspnea 4 months after a documented SARS-CoV-2 infection. Which of the following laboratory patterns would best support ongoing inflammation from chronic COVID illness?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Elevated aminotransferases with normal C-reactive protein and ferritin

choices.label: B
choices.text: Elevated C-reactive protein with high ferritin and low fibrinogen

choices.label: C
choices.text: Elevated C-reactive protein with low ferritin and high fibrinogen

choices.label: D
choices.text: Low C-reactive protein with high ferritin and elevated fibrinogen

choices.label: E
choices.text: Normal C-reactive protein with high creatinine and normal ferritin

explanation.summary: The inflammation markers used in long COVID are C-reactive protein, high ferritin, and low fibrinogen.
explanation.whyCorrect: For patients being evaluated for chronic COVID illness, the inflammation markers checked are C-reactive protein, high ferritin, and low fibrinogen. Prolonged inflammation is suggested by persistent elevations in inflammatory markers such as C-reactive protein and ferritin, and the laboratory panel also includes liver enzymes, serum creatinine, and D-dimer for thrombosis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Liver enzyme elevation assesses hepatic involvement but by itself does not demonstrate ongoing inflammation.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Ferritin is elevated rather than low, and fibrinogen is low rather than high, in this pattern.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A low C-reactive protein would not support ongoing inflammation, and fibrinogen is characteristically low.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A normal C-reactive protein and ferritin argue against ongoing inflammation; creatinine assesses renal involvement instead.

questions.stem: A 62-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes is prescribed nirmatrelvir-ritonavir 2 days after the onset of COVID-19 symptoms. She is not hypoxemic and is treated as an outpatient. Which of the following is the mechanism of action of nirmatrelvir?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It antagonizes the interleukin-6 receptor and dampens cytokine signaling

choices.label: B
choices.text: It blocks binding of the viral spike protein to the ACE2 receptor

choices.label: C
choices.text: It inhibits the viral 3CL protease and blocks cleavage of polyproteins

choices.label: D
choices.text: It prevents fusion of the viral envelope with the endosomal membrane

choices.label: E
choices.text: It terminates viral RNA synthesis as an incorporated nucleotide analog

explanation.summary: Nirmatrelvir inhibits the SARS-CoV-2 3CL protease, preventing polyprotein cleavage needed for replication.
explanation.whyCorrect: Nirmatrelvir inhibits the SARS-CoV-2 3CL protease, preventing cleavage of viral polyproteins required for replication. Given with ritonavir, it is commonly used as first-line therapy for non-hospitalized patients at high risk of progression and significantly reduces hospitalization and mortality when started within the first 5 days of symptoms.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Interleukin-6 receptor antagonism describes tocilizumab, an immunomodulator used in severe disease.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Nirmatrelvir acts on an intracellular viral enzyme rather than blocking spike-ACE2 binding.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Blocking envelope-endosome fusion is not the mechanism of this protease inhibitor.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Chain termination by an incorporated nucleotide analog is the mechanism of remdesivir.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man who takes several chronic medications is started on nirmatrelvir-ritonavir for early COVID-19, and the pharmacist screens his regimen carefully for drug interactions. Which of the following best explains why ritonavir is included in this combination?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It accelerates renal clearance of circulating inflammatory mediators

choices.label: B
choices.text: It adds direct antiviral activity against the viral RNA polymerase

choices.label: C
choices.text: It inhibits CYP3A4 metabolism, raising nirmatrelvir concentrations

choices.label: D
choices.text: It prevents resistance by inhibiting a second essential viral enzyme

choices.label: E
choices.text: It reduces the gastrointestinal adverse effects of nirmatrelvir

explanation.summary: Ritonavir is a pharmacokinetic enhancer that inhibits CYP3A4 to boost nirmatrelvir levels.
explanation.whyCorrect: Ritonavir is included as a pharmacokinetic enhancer that inhibits CYP3A4 metabolism, increasing nirmatrelvir concentrations. Because of this CYP inhibition, drug-drug interactions must be carefully evaluated in any patient taking chronic medications, which is why the pharmacy screen matters here.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Ritonavir does not enhance renal clearance of inflammatory mediators.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Ritonavir in this regimen serves a pharmacokinetic role rather than contributing antipolymerase activity.
whyWrongByChoice.D: It does not inhibit a second viral enzyme; its target in this regimen is a host metabolic enzyme.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Ritonavir is not added to mitigate gastrointestinal adverse effects of nirmatrelvir.

questions.stem: A 69-year-old woman with chronic kidney disease telephones on day 7 after the onset of COVID-19 symptoms and requests an oral antiviral. She is afebrile, and her oxygen saturation at home is 96% on room air. Which of the following best explains why oral antiviral therapy is unlikely to benefit her now?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Antivirals are contraindicated in patients with chronic kidney disease

choices.label: B
choices.text: Antivirals are effective only after the hyperinflammatory phase has begun

choices.label: C
choices.text: Antivirals are effective only in patients who require supplemental oxygen

choices.label: D
choices.text: Antivirals must be combined with corticosteroids to provide any benefit

choices.label: E
choices.text: Antivirals reduce hospitalization only when started within the first 5 days

explanation.summary: Antiviral therapy works early, while viral replication is the dominant driver of disease.
explanation.whyCorrect: Most antiviral agents are most effective when administered early in the course of illness, when viral replication is highest, and nirmatrelvir-ritonavir significantly reduces hospitalization and mortality when initiated within the first 5 days of symptoms.
