By day 7, disease in patients who progress is driven increasingly by host inflammatory injury rather than viral replication.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Chronic kidney disease is a risk factor that argues for early treatment rather than an absolute contraindication to antivirals.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The relationship is the reverse: antivirals work before, not after, the hyperinflammatory phase.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Oral antivirals are specifically used in non-hospitalized high-risk patients who do not require oxygen.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Corticosteroids are reserved for patients needing oxygen and are not required for antiviral efficacy.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old man hospitalized with COVID-19 pneumonia requires supplemental oxygen and is started on intravenous remdesivir. Which of the following is its mechanism of action?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It blocks the interleukin-6 receptor on activated inflammatory cells

choices.label: B
choices.text: It inhibits CYP3A4 and boosts levels of a companion oral antiviral

choices.label: C
choices.text: It inhibits the 3CL protease required to cleave the viral polyproteins

choices.label: D
choices.text: It is a nucleotide analog that prematurely terminates viral RNA synthesis

choices.label: E
choices.text: It suppresses cytokine production by binding glucocorticoid receptors

explanation.summary: Remdesivir is an intravenous nucleotide analog that inhibits the viral RNA-dependent RNA polymerase.
explanation.whyCorrect: Remdesivir is an intravenous nucleotide analog that inhibits RNA-dependent RNA polymerase, leading to premature termination of viral RNA synthesis. It is commonly used for hospitalized patients requiring supplemental oxygen, or as an alternative outpatient therapy when oral antivirals cannot be used.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Interleukin-6 receptor blockade describes tocilizumab, an immunomodulatory agent.
whyWrongByChoice.B: CYP3A4 inhibition to boost a companion antiviral describes ritonavir.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Inhibition of the 3CL protease is the mechanism of nirmatrelvir, not remdesivir.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Binding glucocorticoid receptors to suppress cytokine production describes dexamethasone.

questions.stem: A 44-year-old man has fever and cough 3 days after testing positive for SARS-CoV-2. His oxygen saturation is 97% on room air and he is managed at home. He requests dexamethasone because a hospitalized relative received it. Which of the following is the best reason to withhold corticosteroids?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Corticosteroids are effective only when given together with tocilizumab

choices.label: B
choices.text: Corticosteroids have no effect on the cytokines produced during this infection

choices.label: C
choices.text: Corticosteroids interact with oral antivirals and cause dangerous toxicity

choices.label: D
choices.text: Corticosteroids substantially increase the risk of venous thromboembolism

choices.label: E
choices.text: Early disease is driven by viral replication, and steroids delay viral clearance

explanation.summary: Corticosteroids are withheld in mild COVID-19 without an oxygen requirement because early disease is driven by viral replication.
explanation.whyCorrect: The timing of corticosteroid therapy is critical because the dominant mechanism of disease changes over time. During the early phase, viral replication is the primary driver and the innate immune response is essential for controlling viral spread; giving corticosteroids then can suppress that response, potentially delaying viral clearance and allowing continued replication. For this reason corticosteroids are not recommended in patients with mild disease who do not require supplemental oxygen, although they improve survival in patients who do require oxygen support.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Corticosteroids benefit patients requiring oxygen on their own; tocilizumab is an add-on for severe systemic inflammation.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Dexamethasone does reduce production of pro-inflammatory cytokines; the issue is when in the illness it is given.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A dangerous interaction with oral antivirals is not the reason corticosteroids are avoided here.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Increased thromboembolic risk from corticosteroids is not the stated reason for withholding them in mild disease.

questions.stem: A 59-year-old woman with severe COVID-19 requiring high-flow oxygen has markedly elevated inflammatory markers and worsening infiltrates despite dexamethasone. Tocilizumab is added to her regimen. Which of the following is its mechanism of action?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It antagonizes the interleukin-6 receptor and reduces inflammatory signaling

choices.label: B
choices.text: It blocks the ACE2 receptor and prevents further entry of virus into cells

choices.label: C
choices.text: It depletes circulating B cells and lowers production of autoantibodies

choices.label: D
choices.text: It inhibits the viral RNA-dependent RNA polymerase in infected cells

choices.label: E
choices.text: It neutralizes tumor necrosis factor-alpha released by activated macrophages

explanation.summary: Tocilizumab is an IL-6 receptor antagonist used with corticosteroids in severe COVID-19 with systemic inflammation.
explanation.whyCorrect: In patients with severe disease, additional immunomodulatory therapy may be considered. Tocilizumab is an interleukin-6 receptor antagonist that reduces the inflammatory signaling associated with cytokine-mediated lung injury. These agents are typically used in combination with corticosteroids in patients demonstrating systemic inflammation, consistent with IL-6 being one of the macrophage-derived cytokines driving inflammation in this infection.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Blocking the ACE2 receptor is not the mechanism of this immunomodulatory antibody.
whyWrongByChoice.C: B-cell depletion is the mechanism of a different class of monoclonal antibody and is not used here.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Inhibition of the RNA-dependent RNA polymerase describes remdesivir, an antiviral.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Tocilizumab targets the interleukin-6 receptor rather than neutralizing tumor necrosis factor-alpha.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old man develops abrupt fever, myalgias, and cough in January. Sequencing of the virus recovered from a nasal washing shows an enveloped particle whose linear, negative-sense, single-stranded RNA genome is divided into eight separate pieces. Which of the following viruses was most likely recovered?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Influenza virus

choices.label: B
choices.text: Measles virus

choices.label: C
choices.text: Metapneumovirus

choices.label: D
choices.text: Parainfluenza virus

choices.label: E
choices.text: Respiratory syncytial virus

explanation.summary: Among these respiratory viruses, only influenza virus carries a multisegmented genome.
explanation.whyCorrect: Influenza virus is the medically relevant member of Orthomyxoviridae, and its linear, single-stranded, negative-sense RNA genome is broken into 7 or 8 segments. Orthomyxoviridae, Pneumoviridae, and Paramyxoviridae are all enveloped with ss(-)RNA genomes, so segmentation is the feature that separates influenza from the rest. That segmented genome is also what permits reassortment and antigenic shift.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Measles virus is a paramyxovirus and likewise carries a continuous ss(-)RNA genome.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Metapneumovirus is also Pneumoviridae and carries a single continuous ss(-)RNA genome.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Parainfluenza virus is a paramyxovirus with a continuous, unsegmented ss(-)RNA genome.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Respiratory syncytial virus is a member of Pneumoviridae and its ss(-)RNA genome is continuous, not segmented.

questions.stem: In a research laboratory, separate cultures are infected with influenza virus and with respiratory syncytial virus, and newly synthesized viral RNA is labeled. The label accumulates in the nucleus of influenza-infected cells but remains in the cytoplasm of RSV-infected cells. Which of the following best explains this difference?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Influenza virus is a DNA virus that must integrate into host chromosomes

choices.label: B
choices.text: Influenza virus is an RNA virus that is an exception to cytoplasmic replication

choices.label: C
choices.text: Respiratory syncytial virus copies its genome using a host DNA polymerase

choices.label: D
choices.text: Respiratory syncytial virus is a DNA virus while influenza virus is an RNA virus

choices.label: E
choices.text: Respiratory syncytial virus lacks an envelope and therefore cannot reach the nucleus

explanation.summary: Influenza virus replicates in the nucleus, breaking the rule that RNA viruses replicate in the cytoplasm.
explanation.whyCorrect: As a general rule RNA viruses replicate in the cytoplasm and DNA viruses replicate in the nucleus. Orthomyxoviridae are one of the exceptions: influenza virus uses its own RNA-dependent RNA polymerase to copy its genome in the nucleus despite being an RNA virus. Paramyxoviridae and Pneumoviridae, including RSV, replicate in the cytoplasm like most other RNA viruses.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Influenza virus has an RNA genome and does not make or integrate a DNA copy.
whyWrongByChoice.C: RSV carries its own RNA-dependent RNA polymerase and does not use a host DNA polymerase.
whyWrongByChoice.D: RSV is an RNA virus, not a DNA virus; both viruses in this experiment have RNA genomes.
whyWrongByChoice.E: RSV is enveloped, and envelope status does not determine the compartment in which a genome is copied.

questions.stem: A 9-month-old infant is admitted with wheezing and hypoxemia. A multiplex PCR panel identifies respiratory syncytial virus, a member of the family Pneumoviridae. Which of the following viruses belongs to that same family?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Influenza virus

choices.label: B
choices.text: Measles virus

choices.label: C
choices.text: Metapneumovirus

choices.label: D
choices.text: Mumps virus

choices.label: E
choices.text: Parainfluenza virus

explanation.summary: Pneumoviridae contains respiratory syncytial virus and metapneumovirus.
explanation.whyCorrect: Pneumoviridae contains two medically relevant viruses: respiratory syncytial virus and metapneumovirus. Both are common causes of pneumonia in children, both carry continuous linear ss(-)RNA genomes, and both replicate in the cytoplasm. Their transmission, clinical presentation, risk factors, and seasonality are closely matched.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Influenza virus is the medically relevant member of Orthomyxoviridae.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Measles virus belongs to Paramyxoviridae.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Mumps virus belongs to Paramyxoviridae.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Parainfluenza virus belongs to Paramyxoviridae.

questions.stem: A 16-month-old boy has two days of runny nose followed by a barking cough and inspiratory stridor that is worse at night. He is diagnosed with croup. Which of the following viruses is the most common cause of this illness?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Influenza virus

choices.label: B
choices.text: Metapneumovirus

choices.label: C
choices.text: Mumps virus

choices.label: D
choices.text: Parainfluenza virus

choices.label: E
choices.text: Respiratory syncytial virus

explanation.summary: Parainfluenza virus is the most common cause of croup.
explanation.whyCorrect: Parainfluenza virus is a member of Paramyxoviridae and is the most common cause of croup, though it also causes other infections of the upper and lower respiratory tract. Like the other viruses in these three families it is enveloped with a linear ss(-)RNA genome, and it replicates in the cytoplasm.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Influenza virus characteristically causes abrupt fever, aches, and cough rather than croup.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Metapneumovirus closely resembles RSV and typically causes bronchiolitis and pneumonia.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Mumps virus causes an acute viral illness with a risk of encephalitis and is prevented by MMR vaccine.
whyWrongByChoice.E: RSV is the leading cause of bronchiolitis and pneumonia in children under 1 year of age, not of croup.

questions.stem: A microbiology course groups influenza virus, respiratory syncytial virus, and measles virus together because their families share several structural features. Which of the following features is common to Orthomyxoviridae, Pneumoviridae, and Paramyxoviridae?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A double-stranded DNA genome that is copied in the host nucleus

choices.label: B
choices.text: A non-enveloped capsid that resists drying on contaminated surfaces

choices.label: C
choices.text: A positive-sense RNA genome translated directly by host ribosomes

choices.label: D
choices.text: A segmented genome that permits genetic reassortment between strains

choices.label: E
choices.text: An envelope surrounding a linear, negative-sense RNA genome

explanation.summary: All three families are enveloped viruses with linear, single-stranded, negative-sense RNA genomes.
explanation.whyCorrect: Orthomyxoviridae, Pneumoviridae, and Paramyxoviridae share both structure and clinical manifestations: all are enveloped viruses with linear, single-stranded, negative-sense RNA genomes. The distinctions between them lie elsewhere, in genome continuity and replication site.

whyWrongByChoice.A: None of these families has a DNA genome; all three carry RNA.
whyWrongByChoice.B: All three families are enveloped rather than naked.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Their genomes are negative-sense, so they cannot be translated directly and must first be copied.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Only Orthomyxoviridae has a multisegmented genome; Pneumoviridae and Paramyxoviridae genomes are continuous.

questions.stem: Surveillance of respiratory disease in dairy herds identifies an influenza virus that is not one of the types responsible for seasonal epidemics in people. Which of the following types is it most likely to be?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Influenza A

choices.label: B
choices.text: Influenza B

choices.label: C
choices.text: Influenza C

choices.label: D
choices.text: Influenza D

choices.label: E
choices.text: Parainfluenza virus

explanation.summary: There are three human influenza types, A, B, and C; influenza D infects cattle.
explanation.whyCorrect: Influenza A and B are the two types that cause seasonal epidemics in humans, and influenza C is a human type that is simply less prevalent than A or B. Influenza D is the additional type that infects cattle rather than people.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Influenza A is a human type and the main driver of seasonal epidemics and of pandemics.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Influenza B is one of the two human types that drive seasonal epidemics.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Influenza C is a human influenza type; it is less prevalent than A or B but still infects people.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Parainfluenza virus is a paramyxovirus and is not an influenza virus at all.

questions.stem: A health system is deciding when to add staff to its urgent care clinics for influenza. In the United States, the number of influenza cases peaks most reliably during which of the following intervals?

choices.label: A
choices.text: August through September

choices.label: B
choices.text: Cases are spread evenly across the year

choices.label: C
choices.text: December through February

choices.label: D
choices.text: June through August

choices.label: E
choices.text: March through May

explanation.summary: Influenza season begins in the colder months and peaks between December and February.
explanation.whyCorrect: Flu season usually starts in the colder months and peaks between December and February. Each year in the United States between 9 and 41 million people get influenza, with 12,000 to 52,000 deaths, and the totals vary substantially from year to year with the virulence of the circulating strain and the efficacy of the annual vaccine.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Late summer and early fall precede the seasonal rise rather than the peak.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Influenza activity is strongly seasonal rather than evenly distributed.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Summer is the low point of influenza activity, and it is when vaccine strains are chosen for the coming season.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Late spring falls after the peak, as case counts are declining.

questions.stem: A hospital infection control team is writing guidance to limit the spread of influenza on an inpatient ward. Which of the following best describes how influenza virus is transmitted?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Bloodborne spread through shared needles and transfusion

choices.label: B
choices.text: Direct inoculation through breaks in the skin barrier

choices.label: C
choices.text: Fecal-oral spread from water contaminated with sewage

choices.label: D
choices.text: Respiratory droplets and contaminated inanimate surfaces

choices.label: E
choices.text: Vector-borne spread by the bite of an infected mosquito

explanation.summary: Influenza spreads by respiratory droplets and by fomites.
explanation.whyCorrect: Influenza virus spreads through respiratory droplets and through fomites, the inanimate object surfaces that can transmit infectious agents. Respiratory syncytial virus spreads the same way, which is why droplet precautions and surface disinfection are central to controlling both on a ward.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Influenza is not a bloodborne pathogen.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Influenza infects the epithelium lining the respiratory tract, not inoculated skin wounds.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Influenza is a respiratory pathogen and is not acquired from contaminated water.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Influenza has no arthropod vector.

questions.stem: An investigational drug is designed to block the influenza surface glycoprotein that attaches the virion to its target cell. Binding to which of the following host molecules would this drug prevent?

choices.label: A
choices.text: CD4 molecules on the surface of helper T lymphocytes

choices.label: B
choices.text: Heparan sulfate within the endothelial basement membrane

choices.label: C
choices.text: Integrin receptors on the surface of alveolar macrophages

choices.label: D
choices.text: Mannose receptors on the surface of dendritic cells

choices.label: E
choices.text: Sialic acid residues on respiratory epithelial cells

explanation.summary: Hemagglutinin attaches influenza to sialic acid residues on respiratory epithelium.
explanation.whyCorrect: Influenza virus has two major surface glycoproteins, hemagglutinin (HA) and neuraminidase (NA). HA is the attachment protein and binds sialic acid residues found on the epithelial cells lining the respiratory tract. Antibodies directed at HA block viral attachment for exactly this reason.

whyWrongByChoice.A: CD4 is not the receptor for influenza hemagglutinin.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Heparan sulfate in basement membrane is not the target of hemagglutinin.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Integrins are not the receptor influenza uses for attachment.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Mannose receptors on dendritic cells are not the attachment target of influenza.

questions.stem: In a cell culture experiment, newly assembled influenza virions remain tethered to the surface of the epithelial cell in which they were made, and the infection fails to spread to neighboring cells. Loss of which of the following viral proteins best explains this finding?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Hemagglutinin

choices.label: B
choices.text: Matrix protein 2

choices.label: C
choices.text: Neuraminidase

choices.label: D
choices.text: Ribonucleoprotein

choices.label: E
choices.text: RNA-dependent RNA polymerase

explanation.summary: Neuraminidase cleaves sialic acid so assembled virions can leave the cell and infect neighbors.
explanation.whyCorrect: Neuraminidase cleaves sialic acid residues, allowing the virus to leave host cells once it has been assembled so that it can go on to infect flanking epithelial cells. Without functioning NA, progeny virions stay bound by hemagglutinin to the sialic acid on the cell that produced them and the infection cannot spread.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Hemagglutinin binds sialic acid to mediate entry; losing it would block attachment, not release.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Matrix protein 2 is a proton channel needed for fusion and uncoating during entry.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Ribonucleoprotein is the complex of viral RNA with its associated proteins, not the release enzyme.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The RNA-dependent RNA polymerase copies the genome in the nucleus; its loss would stop genome replication.

questions.stem: A compound is engineered to plug the influenza integral membrane protein that conducts protons across the viral envelope. Which of the following steps of the influenza life cycle is most directly impaired?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Acidification needed for fusion and uncoating

choices.label: B
choices.text: Attachment of hemagglutinin to respiratory epithelium

choices.label: C
choices.text: Cleavage of sialic acid from newly formed virions

choices.label: D
choices.text: Insertion of glycoprotein spikes into the envelope

choices.label: E
choices.text: Transcription of viral RNA within the host nucleus

explanation.summary: The M2 proton channel maintains the pH influenza needs to fuse with the host membrane and uncoat.
explanation.whyCorrect: Matrix protein 2 is an integral membrane protein that functions as a proton channel. It maintains the correct pH needed for the virus to fuse with the host cell envelope and to uncoat once inside the host cell. Blocking M2 leaves the genome trapped inside an intact particle, so replication never begins.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Attachment is mediated by hemagglutinin binding sialic acid residues.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Cleaving sialic acid to release progeny is the job of neuraminidase.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Envelope glycoprotein insertion is not the function of the proton channel.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Genome copying in the nucleus is carried out by the viral RNA-dependent RNA polymerase.

questions.stem: A public health laboratory reports that a circulating influenza A strain is H3N2. Which of the following does this designation indicate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The strain carries three hemagglutinin copies per two neuraminidase

choices.label: B
choices.text: The strain carries type 3 hemagglutinin and type 2 neuraminidase

choices.label: C
choices.text: The strain has 3 genome segments and 2 surface proteins

choices.label: D
choices.text: The strain replicates in the nucleus and matures in the cytoplasm

choices.label: E
choices.text: The strain was the third isolate typed in the second wave

explanation.summary: Influenza A subtypes name which HA type and which NA type the strain carries.
explanation.whyCorrect: Influenza A viruses are described by differences in HA and NA. There are currently 18 known types of HA and 11 known types of NA, and strains are classified by which combination they possess. H1N1 means the virus carries type 1 HA and type 1 NA, so H3N2 carries type 3 HA and type 2 NA.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The numbers are not a ratio of spike proteins on the virion.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The influenza genome is divided into 7 or 8 segments regardless of subtype designation.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Replication site is a family-level feature and is not encoded in the subtype name.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The numbers refer to glycoprotein types, not to the order in which isolates were identified.

questions.stem: Purification of influenza virions recovers viral RNA tightly bound to proteins, a complex collectively called ribonucleoprotein, which includes an enzyme packaged inside the particle. Which of the following best describes what that enzyme does?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Caps host messenger RNA for translation in the cytoplasm

choices.label: B
choices.text: Cleaves sialic acid to release assembled progeny virions

choices.label: C
choices.text: Copies the viral RNA genome inside the host cell nucleus

choices.label: D
choices.text: Integrates a DNA copy of the genome into host chromosomes

choices.label: E
choices.text: Transports protons across the viral envelope during entry

explanation.summary: Influenza carries its own RNA-dependent RNA polymerase, which copies the genome in the nucleus.
explanation.whyCorrect: Internally, influenza virus contains its own RNA-dependent RNA polymerase, closely associated with the viral RNA. Influenza RNA plus its associated proteins, including the polymerases, are collectively called ribonucleoproteins, and the virus uses this polymerase to make copies of its genome in the nucleus. That same polymerase lacks proofreading ability, which is why errors accumulate over time.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The packaged enzyme copies the viral genome rather than servicing host messenger RNA.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Cleaving sialic acid to release virions is the function of neuraminidase, a surface glycoprotein.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Influenza does not make a DNA copy of its genome and does not integrate into host chromosomes.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Proton transport across the envelope is the function of matrix protein 2.

questions.stem: A 40-year-old woman who received last season's influenza vaccine develops influenza this season. Sequencing shows that the circulating strain differs from last year's by a handful of point mutations in the hemagglutinin gene, and her existing antibodies bind it poorly. Which of the following processes is responsible?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Antigenic drift

choices.label: B
choices.text: Antigenic shift

choices.label: C
choices.text: Complementation between co-infecting strains

choices.label: D
choices.text: Genetic reassortment

choices.label: E
choices.text: Integration of viral genes into host DNA

explanation.summary: Antigenic drift is the gradual accumulation of point mutations that slowly alters HA and NA.
explanation.whyCorrect: Antigenic drift refers to the gradual accumulation of point mutations in the genome, leading to small changes in antigens. Because the influenza RNA polymerase lacks proofreading ability, errors occur frequently; most are harmful to the virus, but occasional changes in the HA or NA genes provide an advantage by altering these surface glycoproteins. Antibodies from prior infection or vaccination then bind poorly, allowing reinfection, which is why drift drives seasonal epidemics and annual vaccine updates.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Antigenic shift is an abrupt, major change in the viral genome, not an accumulation of a few point mutations.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Complementation between co-infecting strains does not change the hemagglutinin gene sequence antibodies recognize.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Reassortment requires two influenza viruses to infect the same cell and swap whole RNA segments.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Influenza copies its RNA genome in the nucleus and does not integrate genes into host DNA.

questions.stem: A pig is simultaneously infected with a human influenza A strain and an avian influenza A strain. Progeny virions are recovered that carry the hemagglutinin gene of the avian strain together with the remaining segments of the human strain. Which of the following processes produced these progeny?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Phenotypic mixing of envelope proteins without genetic change

choices.label: B
choices.text: Point mutation within the hemagglutinin gene segment

choices.label: C
choices.text: Reassortment of the segmented RNA genomes

choices.label: D
choices.text: Recombination between two continuous RNA genomes

choices.label: E
choices.text: Transduction of viral genes by a bacteriophage

explanation.summary: Co-infection of one cell by two segmented viruses lets their RNA segments repackage into new variants.
explanation.whyCorrect: When two influenza viruses infect the exact same cell, their RNA segments mix as new virions are assembled, a phenomenon called genetic reassortment. Reassortment can occur in any virus with a segmented genome and is what drives antigenic shift, the abrupt, major change in a viral genome. When shift produces antigens humans have never encountered, the result is a virus with pandemic potential.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Phenotypic mixing would not place an avian hemagglutinin gene into the progeny genome.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Point mutation produces small, gradual antigenic changes, which is antigenic drift rather than segment exchange.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The influenza genome is segmented rather than continuous, and whole segments are swapped here.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Bacteriophages transfer genes between bacteria and have no role in influenza genetics.

questions.stem: Pandemic influenza arises from abrupt, major changes in the viral genome, and these pandemic-generating changes occur in only one of the influenza types. Which of the following features of that type best explains why?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It infects humans and a broad range of other animals

choices.label: B
choices.text: It is the only type included in the annual vaccine

choices.label: C
choices.text: It is the only type that replicates in the host nucleus

choices.label: D
choices.text: It is the only type whose polymerase lacks proofreading

choices.label: E
choices.text: It is the only type with a segmented RNA genome

explanation.summary: Antigenic shift occurs only in influenza A because of its broad host range.
explanation.whyCorrect: Antigenic shift is the major cause of pandemic influenza and occurs only in influenza type A. Influenza A can infect humans and a broad range of other animals such as pigs and birds, so HA or NA from a predominantly animal strain can reassort with a human influenza A strain. That combination is far more likely to generate a novel influenza virus to which the human population has no immunity.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Annual vaccines routinely include both influenza A and influenza B strains.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Replication in the nucleus is shared by all Orthomyxoviridae and does not confer pandemic potential.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Lack of proofreading is a general property of the influenza polymerase and underlies drift, not shift.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Influenza B is also segmented, and reassortment between two human B strains can technically happen.

questions.stem: Two human influenza B strains co-infect the same cell and exchange RNA segments. Despite this exchange, no strain with pandemic potential emerges. Which of the following best explains this outcome?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Influenza B circulates only in humans, so its strains differ too little

choices.label: B
choices.text: Influenza B lacks a segmented genome, so human strains cannot exchange segments

choices.label: C
choices.text: Influenza B lacks hemagglutinin and neuraminidase on its surface

choices.label: D
choices.text: Influenza B produces lifelong immunity after a single infection

choices.label: E
choices.text: Influenza B replicates in the cytoplasm and therefore cannot reassort

explanation.summary: Influenza B is confined to humans, so its strains are too similar for reassortment to create a novel antigen.
explanation.whyCorrect: Antigenic shift does not occur in influenza B or C because of their limited diversity. Influenza B circulates only in humans, so the genetic differences between B strains are relatively small compared with the differences between avian and human influenza A strains. Reassortment between two human B strains can technically happen, but the resulting changes will not amount to antigenic shift.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Influenza B does have a segmented genome, which is why reassortment between B strains is possible at all.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Influenza B carries surface glycoproteins and is a target of the annual vaccine.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Influenza infection does not produce lifelong immunity; drift alone permits repeated reinfection.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Orthomyxoviridae replicate in the nucleus, and replication site is not what limits shift in type B.

questions.stem: Avian influenza has repeatedly infected people who handle poultry, without any intervening reassortment in an animal host. Nevertheless, these events have not produced pandemics. Which of the following best explains why?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Existing seasonal vaccines fully neutralize avian strains

choices.label: B
choices.text: The virus cannot bind sialic acid on human epithelium

choices.label: C
choices.text: The virus lacks a segmented genome and cannot drift

choices.label: D
choices.text: The virus replicates only at temperatures near 25 degrees C

choices.label: E
choices.text: The virus spreads poorly from person to person

explanation.summary: Avian influenza can infect humans directly but spreads poorly between them, so it has not caused pandemics.
explanation.whyCorrect: Avian influenza, the bird flu, has jumped directly to humans without the need for genetic reassortment. It has not caused pandemics because of its limited ability to spread between people. A pandemic requires not only a novel antigen that the population has never encountered but also efficient human-to-human transmission.

whyWrongByChoice.A: No influenza vaccine provides complete protection, and seasonal vaccines are chosen against circulating human strains.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The stem states that people have been infected, so the virus is clearly able to enter human respiratory cells.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Avian influenza is an influenza A virus and therefore carries a segmented genome.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Efficient growth near 25 degrees C with poor growth at core body temperature describes the live attenuated vaccine strain.

questions.stem: Lung tissue from patients who died during the 1918 H1N1 pandemic was examined for bacterial infiltrates in the respiratory tract, and most specimens showed evidence of bacterial infection. Which of the following was the most common cause of death during that pandemic?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Fulminant viral myocarditis

choices.label: B
choices.text: Kidney failure from rhabdomyolysis

choices.label: C
choices.text: Post-influenza viral encephalitis

choices.label: D
choices.text: Reye syndrome from salicylate use

choices.label: E
choices.text: Secondary bacterial pneumonia

explanation.summary: Most 1918 deaths were caused by secondary bacterial pneumonia complicating H1N1 infection.
explanation.whyCorrect: When lung biopsies from victims of the 1918 flu were tested for bacterial infiltrates, most patients showed evidence of secondary bacterial infection. Spanish influenza did kill patients directly, but the most common cause of mortality was secondary bacterial pneumonia as a complication of the H1N1 infection. Because this preceded antibiotics, little could be done beyond supportive care; the pandemic infected up to 500 million people and killed 50 to 100 million.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Myocarditis is a recognized complication of influenza but was not the leading cause of death in 1918.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Rhabdomyolysis and multi-organ failure occur but are far less common than secondary pneumonia.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Encephalitis is an uncommon complication of influenza rather than the usual cause of death.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Reye syndrome is a rare complication limited to children and teens and did not drive pandemic mortality.

questions.stem: Two patients are seen the same afternoon. The first describes symptoms that began gradually with sneezing, a stuffy nose, and a sore throat, and she has had no fever. The second says that fever, body aches, chills, and headache all began suddenly a few hours earlier. Which of the following features most strongly favors influenza in the second patient?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Abrupt onset with fever and body aches

choices.label: B
choices.text: Sneezing as the leading complaint

choices.label: C
choices.text: The complete absence of cough

choices.label: D
choices.text: The presence of a sore throat

choices.label: E
choices.text: The presence of nasal congestion

explanation.summary: Influenza starts abruptly with fever and aches, whereas a cold starts gradually with upper airway symptoms.
explanation.whyCorrect: Influenza and the common cold overlap heavily, but symptom onset is abrupt with flu and gradual with a cold. Fever, aches, and fatigue are usual with flu and rare or slight with a cold, while sneezing, stuffy nose, and sore throat are common with a cold and only sometimes present with flu. Chest discomfort, cough, and headache are also more prominent with influenza.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Sneezing is common with a cold and is only sometimes seen with influenza.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Chest discomfort and cough are common with influenza, so their absence would argue against it.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Sore throat is a common cold symptom and only sometimes accompanies influenza.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Nasal congestion is common with a cold and only sometimes present with influenza.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old man improves after 4 days of influenza, then abruptly worsens on day 6 with high fever, productive cough, and a new focal infiltrate on chest radiograph. Which of the following organisms is an uncommon cause of pneumonia in general but is one of the most common causes of this particular complication?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Haemophilus influenzae

choices.label: B
choices.text: Mycobacterium tuberculosis

choices.label: C
choices.text: Pseudomonas aeruginosa

choices.label: D
choices.text: Staphylococcus aureus

choices.label: E
choices.text: Streptococcus pneumoniae

explanation.summary: S. aureus is an uncommon cause of pneumonia overall yet a leading cause of post-influenza pneumonia.
explanation.whyCorrect: Secondary bacterial pneumonia is a frequent complication of influenza, driven by a weakened immune system together with migration of normal flora of the nasopharynx. The most common causes are Streptococcus pneumoniae, Staphylococcus aureus, and Haemophilus influenzae. Among these, S. aureus is distinctive because it is an uncommon cause of pneumonia in general but one of the most common causes of secondary infection during or after influenza.

whyWrongByChoice.A: H. influenzae is one of the three listed post-influenza pathogens but is not the one singled out this way.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Tuberculosis causes a chronic pneumonia and is not a described complication of influenza.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Gram-negative organisms cause secondary pneumonia mainly in the hospital setting rather than this pattern.
whyWrongByChoice.E: S. pneumoniae is a common post-influenza pathogen but is also a leading cause of pneumonia generally.

questions.stem: A 9-year-old girl with 3 days of fever, cough, and myalgias is given an over-the-counter salicylate-containing product by her parents. Two days later she becomes lethargic and confused, with vomiting and an enlarged, tender liver. Which of the following complications has most likely developed?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Influenza myocarditis with cardiogenic shock

choices.label: B
choices.text: Reye syndrome

choices.label: C
choices.text: Rhabdomyolysis with acute kidney injury

choices.label: D
choices.text: Secondary bacterial meningitis

choices.label: E
choices.text: Viral encephalitis from direct influenza invasion

explanation.summary: Aspirin given to a child with a flu-like illness can precipitate Reye syndrome, swelling of the brain and liver.
explanation.whyCorrect: Reye syndrome is a rare complication of influenza in children and teens that causes life-threatening swelling of the brain and liver. Its cause is poorly understood, but it follows viral infections such as influenza or chickenpox and is strongly associated with aspirin use in children and teens. For this reason aspirin should never be taken when a child or teen has flu-like symptoms or chickenpox.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Myocarditis produces heart failure and hemodynamic collapse rather than confusion with hepatomegaly.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Rhabdomyolysis presents with muscle injury and kidney failure rather than encephalopathy with liver swelling.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Bacterial meningitis is not the complication linked to aspirin use during a flu-like illness.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Encephalitis from influenza would not explain the hepatomegaly, and the salicylate exposure is the key clue.

questions.stem: A clinic is identifying which patients should be prioritized for early evaluation because they are at increased risk of severe influenza. Which of the following patients meets a recognized risk factor for severe influenza infection?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A 4-year-old boy with no chronic medical problems

choices.label: B
choices.text: A 22-year-old woman with seasonal allergic rhinitis

choices.label: C
choices.text: A 30-year-old man with a body mass index of 28 kg/m2

choices.label: D
choices.text: A 35-year-old man with a history of episodic migraine

choices.label: E
choices.text: A 41-year-old man with a body mass index of 44 kg/m2

explanation.summary: A body mass index of 40 kg/m2 or higher is a listed risk factor for severe influenza.
explanation.whyCorrect: A body mass index of 40 kg/m2 or higher is among the major risk factors for severe influenza infection. The full list also includes adults 65 years and older, children younger than 2, pregnant people, asthma, organ disorders and diseases of the kidney, heart, or lung, metabolic disorders, people younger than 19 on long-term aspirin-containing medications, people with weakened immune systems, and people who have had a stroke.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Children younger than 2 years are at increased risk, and this child is past that age cutoff.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Allergic rhinitis is not on the list; asthma is the listed airway condition.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A body mass index of 28 kg/m2 falls below the 40 kg/m2 threshold that defines increased risk.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Migraine is not a listed risk condition; a prior stroke is the listed neurological risk factor.

questions.stem: A 62-year-old woman presents in January with one day of abrupt fever, myalgias, and cough. A rapid influenza diagnostic test performed in clinic returns negative in 12 minutes. Which of the following is the most appropriate interpretation of this result?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A viral culture on monkey kidney cells is required before any treatment

choices.label: B
choices.text: Influenza is excluded and no further influenza testing is warranted

choices.label: C
choices.text: Influenza is still possible and RT-PCR can confirm it if needed

choices.label: D
choices.text: The negative result confirms a bacterial rather than a viral illness

choices.label: E
choices.text: The test is highly sensitive, so repeating the rapid test is the next step

explanation.summary: A negative rapid influenza test does not rule out influenza; RT-PCR is the definitive test.
explanation.whyCorrect: Rapid influenza diagnostic tests give results in less than 15 minutes by identifying influenza A and B antigens, and combined with the clinical presentation they are usually enough for diagnosis. Their major weakness is the number of false negatives and positives they produce, so a negative result does not rule out influenza. RT-PCR is the most rapid and reliable method for a definitive diagnosis, and appropriate samples include nasal washings, throat swabs, and gargles.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Culture on monkey kidney cells or in eggs is rarely needed and is far slower than PCR.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Because of frequent false negatives, a negative rapid test cannot exclude influenza.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A negative antigen test says nothing about a bacterial cause and does not confirm one.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Poor sensitivity is precisely the problem with these tests, so repeating the same assay adds little.

questions.stem: A live attenuated influenza vaccine strain has been engineered so that it replicates efficiently at about 25 degrees C but poorly at about 37 degrees C. Which of the following best describes the consequence of this property for how the vaccine is used?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It is chemically inactivated and purified before it is administered

choices.label: B
choices.text: It is given intranasally and establishes a mild, self-limiting infection

choices.label: C
choices.text: It must be injected intramuscularly to reach core body temperature

choices.label: D
choices.text: It produces complete lifelong protection after a single dose

choices.label: E
choices.text: It replicates in the lower airway to generate systemic immunity

explanation.summary: Cold adaptation confines the live attenuated vaccine strain to the nasopharynx, so it is given intranasally.
explanation.whyCorrect: The live attenuated influenza vaccine is cold-adapted and temperature sensitive, replicating efficiently at roughly 25 degrees C, the temperature of the nasopharynx, but poorly at core body temperature near 37 degrees C. It is administered through the nose and establishes a mild, self-limiting infection confined to the upper airway.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Chemical inactivation after growth in eggs or cell culture describes the inactivated vaccine.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Intramuscular injection describes the inactivated vaccine, not the cold-adapted live strain.
whyWrongByChoice.D: No influenza vaccine provides complete protection, and vaccination must be repeated annually.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The temperature restriction is exactly what keeps the strain out of the warmer lower airway.

questions.stem: In October, a 29-year-old woman who is 20 weeks pregnant and a 30-year-old man with a documented egg allergy both present for influenza vaccination. Which of the following is the most appropriate plan?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Inactivated vaccine for the pregnant patient; any influenza vaccine for the egg-allergic patient

choices.label: B
choices.text: Inactivated vaccine for the pregnant patient; no influenza vaccine for the egg-allergic patient

choices.label: C
choices.text: Live attenuated intranasal vaccine for both patients at today's visit

choices.label: D
choices.text: Live attenuated vaccine for the pregnant patient; any influenza vaccine for the egg-allergic patient

choices.label: E
choices.text: No influenza vaccine for either patient until the season has ended

explanation.summary: The live vaccine is contraindicated in pregnancy, while egg allergy no longer restricts any influenza vaccine.
explanation.whyCorrect: The live attenuated vaccine should not be given to severely immunocompromised individuals, pregnant people, or those with certain chronic conditions such as children with asthma, so an inactivated intramuscular vaccine is the appropriate choice in pregnancy. Egg allergy is no longer considered a contraindication, and people with egg allergies can receive any influenza vaccine with standard precautions.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Withholding vaccine for egg allergy is outdated; these patients may receive any influenza vaccine.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The live vaccine is contraindicated in pregnancy, so it cannot be given to both patients.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The live attenuated vaccine is specifically contraindicated during pregnancy.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Both patients can be safely vaccinated now, and deferring past the season forfeits protection.

questions.stem: A patient asks why she still caught influenza despite being vaccinated in the fall. Which of the following best describes influenza vaccine performance in a season when the vaccine strains match the circulating strains well?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It is roughly 50 to 70 percent effective at preventing infection

choices.label: B
choices.text: It prevents all severe disease but no mild infections at all

choices.label: C
choices.text: It prevents infection only in adults over 65 years of age

choices.label: D
choices.text: It prevents roughly 95 percent of infections when strains are matched

choices.label: E
choices.text: It works only when it is given after the season has begun

explanation.summary: Even in well-matched seasons influenza vaccine is only about 50 to 70 percent effective at preventing infection.
explanation.whyCorrect: No influenza vaccine provides complete protection. Efficacy depends on individual factors and on how well the strains, which are chosen in the summer, match the strains that actually circulate. In well-matched seasons influenza vaccination is 50 to 70 percent effective at preventing infection. Strains are selected annually by WHO from global surveillance data, and national regulatory agencies such as the FDA adopt those recommendations for production.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Vaccination reduces infection as well as severe disease, but it prevents neither completely.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Vaccination benefits all age groups, not only adults over 65.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Influenza vaccine efficacy never approaches this level, even when strains are well matched.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Vaccine is given before and early in the season so immunity is present when transmission rises.

questions.stem: An 82-year-old woman dies after a viral pneumonia. Autopsy lung tissue shows large multinucleated cells formed by fusion of adjacent respiratory epithelial cells. Which of the following viral proteins is directly responsible for this finding?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Influenza hemagglutinin

choices.label: B
choices.text: Influenza matrix protein 2

choices.label: C
choices.text: Influenza neuraminidase

choices.label: D
choices.text: RSV F protein

choices.label: E
choices.text: RSV G protein

explanation.summary: The RSV fusion protein fuses neighboring host cells into syncytia, the feature that names the virus.
explanation.whyCorrect: The RSV fusion (F) protein mediates fusion of the virus with the target cell once the virus has bound using the G protein. F protein can also cause host cells to fuse together, forming a large multinucleated cell called a syncytia. That property is why the organism is called respiratory syncytial virus.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Hemagglutinin binds sialic acid on respiratory epithelium to mediate influenza attachment.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Matrix protein 2 is an influenza proton channel needed for fusion of the virion and uncoating.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Neuraminidase cleaves sialic acid so that assembled influenza virions can leave the cell.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The G protein mediates binding of RSV to airway epithelial cells but does not fuse cells together.

questions.stem: An investigational monoclonal antibody prevents respiratory syncytial virus from attaching to epithelial cells in the airway, without affecting fusion of already-bound virus. Which of the following viral proteins does this antibody most likely target?

choices.label: A
choices.text: F protein

choices.label: B
choices.text: G protein

choices.label: C
choices.text: Hemagglutinin

choices.label: D
choices.text: Matrix protein 2

choices.label: E
choices.text: Neuraminidase

explanation.summary: The RSV G protein mediates binding to airway epithelial cells.
explanation.whyCorrect: Two RSV proteins matter for pathogenesis. The G protein, a glycoprotein, mediates binding of RSV to epithelial cells in the airway. The F protein then mediates fusion once the virus has bound to target cells using the G protein. An antibody that blocks attachment but not fusion therefore targets G.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The F protein acts after attachment, mediating fusion and syncytia formation.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Hemagglutinin is an influenza glycoprotein and is not present on RSV.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Matrix protein 2 is an influenza proton channel and is not an RSV attachment protein.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Neuraminidase is an influenza surface enzyme involved in release of progeny virions.

questions.stem: A 5-month-old infant presents in December with 3 days of cough and coryza followed by tachypnea, wheezing, and intercostal retractions. Diffuse wheezes are heard throughout both lung fields. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this infant's illness?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Influenza D virus, an orthomyxovirus

choices.label: B
choices.text: Measles virus, a morbillivirus

choices.label: C
choices.text: Mumps virus, a paramyxovirus

choices.label: D
choices.text: Respiratory syncytial virus

choices.label: E
choices.text: Streptococcus pneumoniae, a diplococcus

explanation.summary: RSV is the most common cause of bronchiolitis and pneumonia in children under 1 year of age.
explanation.whyCorrect: RSV is the most common cause of pneumonia and bronchiolitis in children under 1 year of age. Bronchiolitis is inflammation of the small airways of the lungs, and it typically follows a few days of minor cold-like symptoms. Most cases of RSV begin in late fall, which fits this December presentation.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Influenza D is the type that infects cattle rather than people.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Measles virus is likewise prevented by MMR vaccine, so few cases occur annually in the United States.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Mumps virus causes an acute viral illness with a risk of encephalitis and is prevented by MMR vaccine.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Childhood vaccination has greatly reduced S. pneumoniae pneumonia, which is why RSV now predominates.

questions.stem: A 3-year-old boy who had a documented respiratory syncytial virus infection at 8 months of age develops another RSV infection this winter. His mother asks how this is possible. Which of the following best explains the repeat infection?

choices.label: A
choices.text: RSV infection does not convey lifelong immunity

choices.label: B
choices.text: RSV integrates into host DNA and reactivates later from latency

choices.label: C
choices.text: RSV spreads only by fomites, which bypasses mucosal immunity

choices.label: D
choices.text: RSV undergoes antigenic shift yearly, creating entirely novel antigens

choices.label: E
choices.text: The first infection was too mild to reach the lower respiratory tract

explanation.summary: RSV infection does not produce lifelong immunity, so reinfection is common.
explanation.whyCorrect: By age 2, almost all children have had at least one RSV infection, but those infections do not convey lifelong immunity, so reinfection is possible and common. RSV causes 58,000 to 80,000 hospitalizations every year in children under 5 and 177,000 hospitalizations in older adults, and healthy adults typically experience only minor symptoms on reinfection.

whyWrongByChoice.B: RSV is an RNA virus that replicates in the cytoplasm and does not integrate or establish latency.
whyWrongByChoice.C: RSV spreads by respiratory droplets as well as fomites, and route of spread is not why immunity wanes.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Antigenic shift requires a segmented genome and occurs only in influenza A; the RSV genome is continuous.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Reinfection occurs regardless of how severe the first episode was.

questions.stem: A 33-year-old woman at 33 weeks of gestation is offered a recombinant respiratory syncytial virus vaccine in early October. Which of the following best describes how this vaccination protects her newborn?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It induces maternal IgG that crosses the placenta to the neonate

choices.label: B
choices.text: It primes the neonate to respond to an RSV vaccine given at birth

choices.label: C
choices.text: It provides the infant with preformed monoclonal antibody at birth

choices.label: D
choices.text: It stimulates fetal B cells to make their own anti-F antibody

choices.label: E
choices.text: It transfers attenuated virus that immunizes the fetus directly

explanation.summary: Maternal RSV vaccination generates IgG that crosses the placenta and protects the newborn.
explanation.whyCorrect: RSV vaccination with a recombinant vaccine is recommended between 32 and 36 weeks of pregnancy, preferably before or during RSV season. Vaccinating the pregnant individual induces production of IgG that crosses the placenta and provides protection to the neonate. Clinical trials show about 80 percent protection against severe RSV illness in the first 3 months of life and about 70 percent in the first 6 months.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Protection comes from transplacental antibody, not from priming for a newborn vaccine dose.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Preformed monoclonal antibody describes passive therapy with nirsevimab or palivizumab.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Protection is passive maternal antibody rather than an active fetal antibody response.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The vaccines approved in the United States are two protein-based products and one mRNA vaccine, not live virus given to the fetus.

questions.stem: A 2-month-old girl was born in September and her mother received no respiratory syncytial virus vaccine during pregnancy. It is now October, the start of RSV season. Which of the following is the most appropriate preventive measure for this infant?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A passive antibody such as nirsevimab given to the infant

choices.label: B
choices.text: A recombinant RSV vaccine given to the infant now

choices.label: C
choices.text: A recombinant RSV vaccine given to the mother now

choices.label: D
choices.text: An mRNA-based RSV vaccine given to the infant now

choices.label: E
choices.text: No preventive measure, as she is outside the eligible window

explanation.summary: Infants under 8 months whose mothers were not vaccinated receive passive antibody for their first RSV season.
explanation.whyCorrect: Passive antibody therapies, nirsevimab and palivizumab, provide passive protection against RSV for infants. They are recommended for babies younger than 8 months who are born during or entering their first RSV season if the birthing parent was not vaccinated during pregnancy, or if the infant was born within 14 days of maternal vaccination. This 2-month-old fits that description exactly.

whyWrongByChoice.B: The recombinant vaccine is given to the pregnant individual, not to the infant.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Maternal vaccination is recommended at 32 to 36 weeks of pregnancy and cannot help an infant already born.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The approved RSV vaccines are for pregnant people and older adults rather than for young infants.
whyWrongByChoice.E: She is younger than 8 months and entering her first RSV season, which is precisely the eligible group.

questions.stem: An 80-year-old woman living in a nursing home received a respiratory syncytial virus vaccine two years ago. She asks whether she needs another dose this fall. Which of the following is the most appropriate response?

choices.label: A
choices.text: One dose is sufficient, as the RSV vaccine is not given annually

choices.label: B
choices.text: She needs a repeat dose every six months during RSV season

choices.label: C
choices.text: She needs a repeat dose every year, as with influenza vaccine

choices.label: D
choices.text: She should receive nirsevimab instead at the start of each season

choices.label: E
choices.text: She was never eligible, since the vaccine is for adults under 60

explanation.summary: The adult RSV vaccine is a single dose, not an annual vaccination.
explanation.whyCorrect: For patients aged 75 and older, and for adults aged 60 to 74 who are at increased risk for severe RSV disease, the CDC recommends a single dose of RSV vaccine. This is not an annual vaccination; one shot is sufficient. Increased risk includes chronic heart or lung disease, certain other chronic medical conditions, and residence in nursing homes or other long-term care facilities.

whyWrongByChoice.B: There is no recommendation for repeat RSV dosing within a season.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Annual redosing describes influenza vaccine, which must be updated for drifting strains each year.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Nirsevimab is a passive antibody used in infants, not in older adults.
whyWrongByChoice.E: At 80 years of age and living in a nursing home she is squarely within the recommended group.

questions.stem: A 7-month-old infant is admitted with bronchiolitis in January. The clinician wants a single test that can distinguish respiratory syncytial virus from influenza and from other respiratory pathogens, because the symptoms are nonspecific and co-infection is possible. Which of the following is the most appropriate test?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Multiplex PCR respiratory panel

choices.label: B
choices.text: Rapid antigen test for influenza A and B

choices.label: C
choices.text: Serology for RSV-specific IgG

choices.label: D
choices.text: Sputum Gram stain and bacterial culture

choices.label: E
choices.text: Viral culture in monkey kidney cells

explanation.summary: Combination nucleic acid panels identify RSV, influenza, and MPV at once and detect co-infection.
explanation.whyCorrect: RSV, influenza, and metapneumovirus are all identified by RT-PCR. Combination NAAT assays are often used because symptoms are fairly nonspecific and patients can be co-infected with multiple pathogens. A panel such as BIOFIRE Respiratory 2.1 uses PCR to screen for 22 viruses and bacteria in less than 2 hours, which also reduces the workload placed on the laboratory.

whyWrongByChoice.B: A rapid antigen test detects only influenza A and B and produces frequent false negatives and positives.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Serology does not give a rapid answer about which virus is causing the current illness.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Gram stain and bacterial culture would not identify any of the viruses in question.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Culture on monkey kidney cells is rarely needed and is far too slow for this decision.

questions.stem: A 14-month-old boy has bronchiolitis in February. A respiratory panel is negative for respiratory syncytial virus but positive for a virus in the same family that was first identified in 2001 and accounts for roughly 5 to 12 percent of acute respiratory infections in children. Which of the following is the virus?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Influenza C virus

choices.label: B
choices.text: Measles virus

choices.label: C
choices.text: Metapneumovirus

choices.label: D
choices.text: Mumps virus

choices.label: E
choices.text: Parainfluenza virus

explanation.summary: Metapneumovirus is the RSV-like Pneumoviridae member first identified in 2001.
explanation.whyCorrect: Metapneumovirus is a recently discovered virus that was first identified in 2001 and shares the Pneumoviridae family with RSV. Its transmission, clinical presentation, risk factors, and seasonality mirror RSV: it mainly affects young children, older adults, and immunocompromised individuals, and it causes upper and lower respiratory tract infections including bronchiolitis and pneumonia. Although it circulates less widely than RSV, it accounts for approximately 5 to 12 percent of acute respiratory infections in children and is identified by RT-PCR.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Influenza C is an orthomyxovirus with a segmented genome and is less prevalent than influenza A or B.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Measles virus is a paramyxovirus prevented by MMR vaccine, so few cases occur annually.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Mumps virus is a paramyxovirus prevented by MMR vaccine and carries a risk of encephalitis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Parainfluenza virus belongs to Paramyxoviridae and is best known as the most common cause of croup.

questions.stem: A 2-year-old boy is brought to the clinic in October with 2 days of runny nose, sore throat, and low-grade fever. Last night he developed a harsh, seal-like cough and a high-pitched noise when he breathes in, both of which were worse after he went to bed. He is alert and drooling is absent. Which of the following is the most likely causal organism?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Measles virus

choices.label: B
choices.text: Mumps virus

choices.label: C
choices.text: Parainfluenza virus type 1

choices.label: D
choices.text: Parainfluenza virus type 3

choices.label: E
choices.text: Parainfluenza virus type 4

explanation.summary: PIV-1 is the most common cause of croup (laryngotracheobronchitis), with fall outbreaks and a barking cough plus stridor that worsen at night.
explanation.whyCorrect: Croup begins with mild upper respiratory symptoms and progresses to a harsh, seal-like barking cough with hoarseness and stridor that worsens at night. PIV-1 is the most common cause of croup/LTB in infants and children, and its outbreaks occur most often in the fall, matching this October presentation.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Measles produces the 3Cs and a descending maculopapular rash, neither of which is present here.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Mumps causes parotid gland swelling with fever and myalgia, not a barking cough with stridor.
whyWrongByChoice.D: PIV-3 causes severe lower respiratory disease such as bronchiolitis and pneumonia, not classic croup.
whyWrongByChoice.E: PIV-4 is the rarest PIV type and usually produces only moderate upper respiratory symptoms.

questions.stem: A 7-month-old infant is admitted in May with 3 days of cough and increasing work of breathing. She is tachypneic with diffuse wheezes and crackles, and she has no barking cough or stridor. A respiratory viral panel is positive for a parainfluenza virus. Which type is most likely responsible?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Mumps virus

choices.label: B
choices.text: Parainfluenza virus type 1

choices.label: C
choices.text: Parainfluenza virus type 2

choices.label: D
choices.text: Parainfluenza virus type 3

choices.label: E
choices.text: Parainfluenza virus type 4

explanation.summary: PIV-3 is a major cause of severe lower respiratory tract infection in infants, including bronchiolitis and pneumonia, and peaks March through June.
explanation.whyCorrect: In children younger than 1 year, PIV-3 is a common cause of bronchitis, bronchiolitis, and pneumonia. PIV-3 infections occur in any season, but March through June is the peak, which fits a May admission with lower respiratory findings rather than croup.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Mumps virus targets the parotid glands and other glandular tissue rather than the lower airways.
whyWrongByChoice.B: PIV-1 chiefly produces croup and other upper respiratory illness, and its outbreaks cluster in the fall.
whyWrongByChoice.C: PIV-2 causes disease similar to PIV-1 but much less often, and it also peaks in the fall.
whyWrongByChoice.E: PIV-4 is the rarest type and typically causes moderate upper respiratory infection only.

questions.stem: An 18-month-old girl has a barking cough, hoarseness, and inspiratory stridor. An anteroposterior radiograph of the neck is obtained. Which of the following findings is most likely to be seen?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A large layering pleural effusion on the left

choices.label: B
choices.text: A thumbprint sign at the epiglottis

choices.label: C
choices.text: Dense lobar consolidation of the right lower lobe

choices.label: D
choices.text: Hyperinflation with flattened hemidiaphragms

choices.label: E
choices.text: Tapered subglottic narrowing of the tracheal air column

explanation.summary: Croup causes inflammatory narrowing of the upper trachea, seen radiographically as the steeple sign.
explanation.whyCorrect: Croup inflames the larynx, windpipe, and bronchi. The resulting narrowing of the subglottic tracheal air column tapers to a point on an AP neck film, an appearance called the steeple sign, and this same narrowing produces the barking cough and stridor.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A pleural effusion is not part of the airway inflammation that causes croup.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A thumbprint appearance reflects a swollen epiglottis, which is not the lesion described in croup.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Lobar consolidation indicates pneumonia rather than the upper airway inflammation of croup.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Hyperinflation reflects distal small airway obstruction, not narrowing at the subglottis.

questions.stem: A medical student is asked to summarize the four parainfluenza virus types. Which type is the rarest cause of disease overall and most commonly produces only moderate upper respiratory tract infection?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Human metapneumovirus

choices.label: B
choices.text: Parainfluenza virus type 1

choices.label: C
choices.text: Parainfluenza virus type 2

choices.label: D
choices.text: Parainfluenza virus type 3

choices.label: E
choices.text: Parainfluenza virus type 4

explanation.summary: PIV-4 is the rarest of the four parainfluenza types and usually causes moderate upper respiratory illness.
explanation.whyCorrect: Of the four PIV types, PIV-4 causes disease least often. When it does cause illness, moderate upper respiratory tract infection is the most common clinical manifestation rather than croup or lower respiratory disease.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Human metapneumovirus is a separate virus and, with RSV and PIV-3, is a leading cause of childhood lower respiratory infection.
whyWrongByChoice.B: PIV-1 is the leading cause of croup and is one of the more frequently encountered types.
whyWrongByChoice.C: PIV-2 causes disease less often than PIV-1 but is not the rarest type.
whyWrongByChoice.D: PIV-3 is very common and is a major cause of severe lower respiratory infection in infants.

questions.stem: A 3-year-old boy had documented croup caused by parainfluenza virus type 1 at 14 months of age. He now presents with croup again, and testing identifies parainfluenza virus type 2. Which of the following best explains why the earlier infection did not protect him?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Antibody made in infancy is exclusively IgA and is no longer produced after the first year of life

choices.label: B
choices.text: Maternal antibody blocks the infant from mounting any antibody response to all four PIV types

choices.label: C
choices.text: The segmented genome reassorts between types, generating a new subtype with every infection

choices.label: D
choices.text: The surface antigens of the PIV types are distinct, so immunity to one does not extend to the others

choices.label: E
choices.text: The virus integrates into host DNA and reactivates whenever cell-mediated immunity declines with age

explanation.summary: Infection with one PIV type does not protect against the others because their surface antigens are distinct.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that infection by one type of PIV does not provide protection against other types, since the surface antigens are distinct. Reinfection is therefore common, and children may have repeated PIV illnesses caused by different types.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Children do generate lasting antibody, and by age 3 virtually all possess antibodies against PIV-3.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Maternal antibody does not abolish the infant's own response; most children are infected and seroconvert early.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Reassortment of a segmented genome is a feature of influenza viruses, not the parainfluenza viruses.
whyWrongByChoice.E: PIV does not establish a latent, integrated state that reactivates; each episode is a new infection.

questions.stem: Several toddlers in the same daycare room develop croup within a week of one another. Which of the following best describes how parainfluenza virus is transmitted between these children?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Bites from an arthropod vector that feeds on infected hosts

choices.label: B
choices.text: Consumption of unpasteurized milk from an infected animal

choices.label: C
choices.text: Ingestion of contaminated food and water by the fecal-oral route

choices.label: D
choices.text: Percutaneous exposure to infected blood or body fluids

choices.label: E
choices.text: Respiratory droplets and contact with contaminated fomites

explanation.summary: PIV spreads by respiratory droplets and fomites, which is why it moves rapidly through daycares, schools, and families.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that PIV is spread by respiratory droplets and fomites and that these viruses are particularly good at spreading rapidly among closely knit populations such as families, schools, and daycares. A daycare cluster of croup fits this transmission pattern exactly.

whyWrongByChoice.A: No arthropod vector is involved in parainfluenza transmission.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Unpasteurized milk transmits foodborne bacterial pathogens, not parainfluenza virus.
whyWrongByChoice.C: PIV is a respiratory pathogen and is not acquired by the fecal-oral route.
whyWrongByChoice.D: PIV is not a bloodborne pathogen and does not require percutaneous exposure.

questions.stem: A pediatrician is counseling a parent about how common parainfluenza virus type 3 infection is in early childhood. Which of the following pairs of figures is most accurate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: About 25% infected in the first year of life; antibodies present in nearly all children by age 8

choices.label: B
choices.text: About 40% infected in the first year of life; antibodies present in nearly all children by age 6

choices.label: C
choices.text: Fewer than 10% infected in the first year of life; antibodies present in nearly all children by age 10

choices.label: D
choices.text: Nearly all infected in the first month of life; antibodies present in nearly all children by age 1

choices.label: E
choices.text: Over 60% infected in the first year of life; antibodies present in nearly all children by age 3

explanation.summary: Over 60% of infants are infected with PIV-3 in their first year, and by age 3 virtually all children have antibodies to it.
explanation.whyCorrect: PIV-3 is an extremely common infection in infancy: more than 60% of infants are infected in the first year of life, and by age three virtually all children possess antibodies against PIV-3. Most children are infected in the first or second year of life, and reinfection is common.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A quarter of infants is far below the observed rate of more than 60%.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Forty percent still understates infant infection, and seroprevalence is near universal well before age 6.
whyWrongByChoice.C: This underestimates infant infection badly; PIV-3 infects the majority of infants in year one.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Infection is not essentially universal within the first month of life; it accrues over the first years.

questions.stem: A 52-year-old woman who received a lung transplant 4 months ago has 3 days of cough, congestion, and dyspnea. Because she is at high risk for severe disease, the team wants to identify the responsible respiratory virus quickly and exclude other agents. Which of the following is the most appropriate test?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Culture of a nasal swab on Thayer-Martin agar

choices.label: B
choices.text: Gram stain and routine bacterial culture of sputum

choices.label: C
choices.text: Nucleic acid amplification testing of a nasopharyngeal specimen

choices.label: D
choices.text: Paired serum IgG titers drawn 4 weeks apart

choices.label: E
choices.text: Serum cold agglutinin titer obtained at presentation

explanation.summary: Nucleic acid amplification testing such as PCR rapidly identifies PIV along with the other respiratory viruses that mimic it.
explanation.whyCorrect: Identification of PIV is rarely needed because supportive therapy suffices in healthy hosts, but in patients at high risk for severe disease testing is valuable to rule out other infectious agents. Nucleic acid amplification testing, like PCR, can rapidly identify PIV and the other common respiratory viruses that cause similar presentations.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Thayer-Martin agar is a selective bacterial medium and will not recover a respiratory virus.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Bacterial stain and culture do not detect viruses and would miss PIV entirely.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Paired titers require weeks and are retrospective, so they cannot guide care in a deteriorating patient.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Cold agglutinins are a nonspecific test and do not identify parainfluenza virus.

questions.stem: An unvaccinated 4-year-old with fever, cough, coryza, conjunctivitis, and white spots on the buccal mucosa arrives in a busy clinic. Which of the following is the most appropriate immediate management?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Airborne precautions with an N95, with a throat swab sent for RT-PCR

choices.label: B
choices.text: Contact precautions in an open bay, with a stool specimen sent for virus

choices.label: C
choices.text: Droplet precautions with a surgical mask, with blood cultures drawn

choices.label: D
choices.text: No precautions until the rash becomes confluent, then routine testing

choices.label: E
choices.text: Standard precautions alone, with a serum IgG titer sent from the clinic

explanation.summary: Suspected measles requires an N95 and prompt isolation, plus a throat or nasopharyngeal swab for RT-PCR and serum for IgM.
explanation.whyCorrect: Measles is extremely contagious and spreads predominantly through airborne droplets, so an N95 mask and isolating the patient are critical to prevent spread. A throat or nasopharyngeal swab should be collected for RT-PCR along with serum for measles IgM, and infection control and local or state public health offices should be contacted.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Contact precautions in an open bay leave other patients exposed, and stool is not the diagnostic specimen.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A surgical mask is inadequate for an airborne pathogen, and blood cultures address bacterial disease.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Waiting delays isolation during the period when the patient is already highly contagious.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Standard precautions do not stop airborne spread, and an IgG titer does not confirm acute measles.

questions.stem: A student asks why measles cases continue to be reported in the United States. Which of the following statements is most accurate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Measles disappears each winter and returns each summer from an animal reservoir

choices.label: B
choices.text: Measles has never been eliminated in the United States and remains endemic nationwide

choices.label: C
choices.text: Measles was eliminated in 2000, and cases still occur in travelers and low-vaccination areas

choices.label: D
choices.text: Measles was eliminated when the vaccine was licensed in 1963, and outbreaks then stopped

choices.label: E
choices.text: Measles was eradicated worldwide in 1980, and all current cases are vaccine-derived

explanation.summary: Measles was officially eliminated from the U.S. in 2000 through vaccination, but importation and low vaccination coverage keep producing outbreaks.
explanation.whyCorrect: Elimination was declared in 2000, yet cases still occur in travelers and in areas with low vaccination rates. Coverage has slipped: in the 2022-2023 school year only 93.1% of kindergartners had received MMR, leaving roughly 250,000 kindergartners unprotected, and outbreaks have been increasing over the last decade.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Measles has no animal reservoir; resurgence comes from importation into susceptible populations.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Endemic transmission was interrupted; elimination was formally declared in 2000.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Vaccine licensure in 1963 sharply reduced cases, but elimination was not achieved until 2000.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Smallpox, not measles, was eradicated globally, and U.S. measles cases are wild-type infections.

questions.stem: A clinic is deciding which adult patients to prioritize for early evaluation during a community outbreak of respiratory viral illness. Which of the following groups is most likely to experience exacerbations and further complications from these infections?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Patients with COPD, chronic asthma, or cystic fibrosis
