choices.label: B
choices.text: Patients with stable primary hypothyroidism

choices.label: C
choices.text: Patients with symptomatic knee osteoarthritis

choices.label: D
choices.text: Patients with treated iron deficiency anemia

choices.label: E
choices.text: Patients with well-controlled essential hypertension

explanation.summary: Chronic lung disease is the comorbidity that most consistently worsens outcomes from these respiratory viruses.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that, as with all the viruses discussed, people with lung diseases such as COPD, chronic asthma, and cystic fibrosis are high-risk groups who commonly have exacerbations of symptoms along with further complications. Comorbidities that affect the lungs can rapidly worsen during any of these respiratory tract infections.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Stable hypothyroidism is not among the comorbidities that worsen these infections.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Osteoarthritis is a joint disease and does not affect pulmonary reserve.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Treated iron deficiency anemia does not impair airway or pulmonary reserve in this way.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Controlled hypertension is not identified as a risk factor for severe respiratory viral disease here.

questions.stem: A 9-month-old infant is hospitalized in July with parainfluenza pneumonia. Which of the following best identifies the likely type and explains the timing?

choices.label: A
choices.text: PIV-1, because it is the most common cause of bronchiolitis in infants

choices.label: B
choices.text: PIV-1, because its outbreaks are concentrated in the summer months

choices.label: C
choices.text: PIV-2, because it circulates only during the fall and winter months

choices.label: D
choices.text: PIV-3, because it circulates in any season and peaks March through June

choices.label: E
choices.text: PIV-4, because it is the leading cause of pneumonia in young infants

explanation.summary: PIV-3 causes severe lower respiratory disease in infants and, unlike PIV-1 and PIV-2, occurs in any season with a spring peak.
explanation.whyCorrect: PIV-1 and PIV-2 outbreaks tend to occur in the fall, whereas PIV-3 infections can occur in any season, with March through June the peak. A July pneumonia in an infant therefore points to PIV-3, which is a major cause of bronchitis, bronchiolitis, and pneumonia in children younger than 1 year.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Bronchiolitis in infants is attributed to PIV-3, not PIV-1.
whyWrongByChoice.B: PIV-1 outbreaks cluster in the fall, and PIV-1 causes croup rather than infant pneumonia.
whyWrongByChoice.C: PIV-2 also peaks in the fall and causes PIV-1-like illness at much lower frequency.
whyWrongByChoice.E: PIV-4 is the rarest type and typically causes only moderate upper respiratory infection.

questions.stem: A 19-year-old college student has 3 days of mild fever, headache, muscle aches, and fatigue. On examination there is tender swelling over both cheeks just in front of and below the ears, obscuring the angle of the mandible. Which of the following is the most likely causal organism?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Human herpesvirus 6

choices.label: B
choices.text: Measles virus

choices.label: C
choices.text: Mumps virus

choices.label: D
choices.text: Parainfluenza virus type 1

choices.label: E
choices.text: Parainfluenza virus type 3

explanation.summary: Swelling of one or both parotid glands with fever, headache, myalgia, and fatigue is the hallmark of mumps.
explanation.whyCorrect: Mumps presents with mild fever, headache, muscle aches, tiredness, and loss of appetite together with swelling of one or both parotid glands. Most of these symptoms are shared with many viral illnesses, so the parotid swelling is the finding that distinguishes mumps from similar infections.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Human herpesvirus 6 causes roseola, with high fever followed by a truncal rash.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Measles produces cough, coryza, conjunctivitis, Koplik spots, and a descending rash, not parotitis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: PIV-1 causes croup with a barking cough and stridor rather than glandular swelling.
whyWrongByChoice.E: PIV-3 causes lower respiratory infection in young children, not parotitis in a young adult.

questions.stem: A 21-year-old man develops parotid swelling and is diagnosed with mumps. He wants to know approximately when he was exposed. Which of the following best represents the incubation period of mumps virus?

choices.label: A
choices.text: 1 to 2 days

choices.label: B
choices.text: 3 to 5 days

choices.label: C
choices.text: 7 to 10 days

choices.label: D
choices.text: 16 to 18 days

choices.label: E
choices.text: 21 to 28 days

explanation.summary: The incubation period of mumps is roughly 16 to 18 days from exposure to symptom onset.
explanation.whyCorrect: After entering the respiratory tract, mumps virus replicates and spreads to the parotid glands, central nervous system, pancreas, and testes. Incubation of the virus is roughly 16 to 18 days, so an exposure about two and a half weeks before symptom onset is the relevant one.

whyWrongByChoice.A: This is far too short for mumps and would suggest a rapid-onset respiratory illness.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Three to five days is shorter than the mumps incubation period.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Seven to ten days is closer to the measles range of 7 to 14 days, not mumps.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Three to four weeks overestimates the mumps incubation period.

questions.stem: A 20-year-old woman is diagnosed with mumps on the day her parotid swelling began. Student health asks how long she should be kept away from classmates and when she was already contagious. Which of the following best describes the infectious period for mumps?

choices.label: A
choices.text: From 2 days before symptom onset until 5 days afterward

choices.label: B
choices.text: From 4 days before swelling until 4 days afterward

choices.label: C
choices.text: From 7 days before onset until 14 days afterward

choices.label: D
choices.text: Only after the parotid swelling has fully resolved

choices.label: E
choices.text: Only during the days on which fever is present

explanation.summary: Patients with mumps are infectious from 2 days before symptoms begin until 5 days after onset.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that patients are infectious 2 days prior to symptoms beginning and 5 days afterward. This pre-symptomatic window is important because some patients have only minor cold-like symptoms yet can still spread the virus to others.

whyWrongByChoice.B: The 4-days-before to 4-days-after window describes measles around rash onset, not mumps.
whyWrongByChoice.C: This overstates the period in both directions relative to the described infectious window.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Infectivity precedes and accompanies the swelling rather than following its resolution.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Transmission is not confined to febrile days; spread begins before any symptoms appear.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old man with mumps develops unilateral testicular pain and swelling. Approximately what proportion of postpubertal males with mumps develop orchitis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Less than 0.1%

choices.label: B
choices.text: About 1%

choices.label: C
choices.text: About 15% to 30%

choices.label: D
choices.text: About 50% to 60%

choices.label: E
choices.text: About 75%

explanation.summary: Orchitis complicates roughly 15% to 30% of mumps cases in postpubertal males and may be unilateral or bilateral.
explanation.whyCorrect: Mumps complications are more frequent in adults than in children, and orchitis occurs in about 15% to 30% of postpubertal males, involving one or both testes. Although uncommon, infertility and sterility can follow as a consequence of orchitis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Orchitis is a common complication, not a vanishingly rare one.
whyWrongByChoice.B: One percent greatly understates how often orchitis complicates postpubertal mumps.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A rate above half is higher than what is observed.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Three quarters of postpubertal males is well above the reported frequency.

questions.stem: A hospital reviews the rare deaths that have occurred among its mumps cases over several decades. Which of the following complications is the most common cause of mortality associated with mumps virus?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Aseptic meningitis and encephalitis

choices.label: B
choices.text: Oophoritis with ovarian infarction

choices.label: C
choices.text: Orchitis progressing to sterility

choices.label: D
choices.text: Pancreatitis with hemorrhagic necrosis

choices.label: E
choices.text: Permanent sensorineural hearing loss

explanation.summary: Central nervous system involvement, specifically aseptic meningitis and encephalitis, accounts for most mumps deaths.
explanation.whyCorrect: Mumps is generally a self-limiting illness with low mortality, but the virus spreads to the central nervous system as well as the parotid glands, pancreas, and testes. Aseptic meningitis and encephalitis are the most common causes of mortality associated with mumps virus.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Oophoritis is a rare complication and is not a common cause of mortality.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Orchitis is common and can rarely cause infertility, but it is not a usual cause of death.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The pancreas is a site of spread, but pancreatitis is not the leading fatal complication.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Hearing loss, whether temporary or permanent, is disabling rather than fatal.

questions.stem: A 22-year-old woman presents 2 days after the onset of parotid swelling during a campus mumps outbreak. Which of the following is the preferred specimen for confirming the diagnosis by RT-PCR?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Buccal swab taken after massaging over Stensen duct for 30 seconds

choices.label: B
choices.text: Cerebrospinal fluid obtained by lumbar puncture at the bedside

choices.label: C
choices.text: Nasopharyngeal aspirate collected during the febrile prodrome

choices.label: D
choices.text: Stool specimen collected on the day the patient presents to clinic

choices.label: E
choices.text: Urine specimen collected within the first 24 hours of symptoms

explanation.summary: A buccal swab taken after massaging the parotid gland for 30 seconds is the preferred RT-PCR specimen for mumps.
explanation.whyCorrect: Diagnosis of mumps is commonly made clinically, but the two most common laboratory methods are RT-PCR and measurement of IgM titers. Massaging the parotid gland for 30 seconds before swabbing the buccal mucosa expresses virus-containing saliva from Stensen duct, which is why this is the preferred sample for RT-PCR.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Lumbar puncture is invasive and reserved for suspected central nervous system disease.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A nasopharyngeal aspirate is not the preferred sample, and the prodrome precedes the optimal window.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Stool is not a diagnostic specimen for mumps virus.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Urine is not identified as the preferred specimen for mumps RT-PCR.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old man presents 8 days after the onset of parotiditis and asks whether a confirmatory swab is still worth collecting. Which of the following best describes the recommended timing of the buccal swab for mumps RT-PCR?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Ideally 10 days after parotiditis, and no earlier than 7 days afterward

choices.label: B
choices.text: Ideally 14 days after parotiditis, and no later than 21 days afterward

choices.label: C
choices.text: Ideally 3 days after parotiditis, and no later than 5 days afterward

choices.label: D
choices.text: Ideally 3 days after parotiditis, and up to 10 days afterward

choices.label: E
choices.text: Ideally on the day of exposure, and no later than 2 days afterward

explanation.summary: The buccal swab for mumps RT-PCR is ideally collected 3 days after parotiditis but can still be done up to 10 days afterward.
explanation.whyCorrect: Ideally the sample would be collected 3 days after parotiditis, but it can be done up to 10 days afterward. A patient presenting on day 8 is therefore still within the usable collection window, so the swab should be obtained rather than deferred.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Day 10 is the outer limit of the window, not the ideal collection day.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Two to three weeks after parotiditis is beyond the usable window for RT-PCR.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The ideal day is correct, but the window extends to 10 days rather than closing at 5.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Virus is not detectable in buccal secretions at the moment of exposure, weeks before parotiditis.

questions.stem: A 26-year-old woman has clinical parotitis and a buccal swab has been sent for RT-PCR. Which of the following additional laboratory tests is most commonly paired with RT-PCR to support a diagnosis of mumps?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Heterophile antibody (monospot) test

choices.label: B
choices.text: Mumps IgG avidity testing on cord blood

choices.label: C
choices.text: Mumps-specific IgM antibody titer

choices.label: D
choices.text: Serum cold agglutinin titer

choices.label: E
choices.text: Tzanck smear of the buccal mucosa

explanation.summary: IgM antibody testing is the serologic complement to RT-PCR for confirming acute mumps.
explanation.whyCorrect: The two most common ways to diagnose mumps are RT-PCR and measuring IgM titers. IgM antibodies against mumps virus can be tested to support a diagnosis, and this is typically paired with RT-PCR for laboratory confirmation.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The heterophile antibody test screens for infectious mononucleosis, not mumps.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Cord blood avidity testing addresses congenital infection, which is not the scenario here.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Cold agglutinins are nonspecific and are not used to confirm mumps.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A Tzanck smear looks for multinucleated giant cells in herpesvirus lesions.

questions.stem: A 21-year-old man who received two documented doses of MMR in childhood develops parotitis during a mumps outbreak at his university, and RT-PCR confirms mumps. Which of the following best explains this finding?

choices.label: A
choices.text: He must have received MMRV, which omits the mumps component entirely

choices.label: B
choices.text: Mumps vaccine effectiveness is about 88% and immunity can wane over time

choices.label: C
choices.text: Mumps vaccine is not part of the routine U.S. childhood immunization schedule

choices.label: D
choices.text: Natural mumps infection and vaccination both fail to induce any antibody

choices.label: E
choices.text: The mumps component is a killed vaccine and never induces protective immunity

explanation.summary: MMR is about 88% effective against mumps after two doses, and waning immunity permits breakthrough cases in vaccinated young adults.
explanation.whyCorrect: After two doses the MMR vaccine is 88% effective for mumps, a lower figure than its 97% effectiveness for measles and rubella. Vaccine efficacy is roughly 90% after the two recommended doses but the immune response can diminish over time, which is why outbreaks since 2006 have occurred predominantly in young adults and in vaccinated people.

whyWrongByChoice.A: MMRV contains the mumps component and adds live attenuated varicella-zoster virus.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Mumps vaccination has been routine since the 1960s and reduced cases by about 99%.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Both vaccination and infection induce antibody; the issue is incomplete and waning protection.
whyWrongByChoice.E: All U.S.-licensed mumps vaccines contain live attenuated virus and do induce immunity.

questions.stem: During a mumps outbreak in a university dormitory, a healthy 20-year-old resident with two documented doses of MMR is identified as being at increased risk because of her close-contact living situation. Which of the following is the most appropriate recommendation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Administer a third dose of MMR vaccine

choices.label: B
choices.text: Administer a third dose of varicella vaccine

choices.label: C
choices.text: No intervention, since two doses confer lifelong mumps immunity

choices.label: D
choices.text: Repeat the entire two-dose MMR series over 6 months

choices.label: E
choices.text: Withhold vaccine and administer immune globulin instead

explanation.summary: During a mumps outbreak, a third dose of MMR may be recommended for individuals at increased risk, such as those in close-contact settings.
explanation.whyCorrect: Because mumps protection is incomplete and wanes over time, breakthrough cases occur even in previously vaccinated adults. During a mumps outbreak, a third dose of MMR may be recommended for individuals at increased risk, such as those in close-contact settings like dormitories.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Varicella vaccine targets varicella-zoster virus and provides no mumps protection.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Two doses do not guarantee lifelong mumps immunity; the response diminishes over time.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A single additional dose is what is recommended, not a repeat of the whole series.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Immune globulin is used for measles post-exposure prophylaxis, not for mumps outbreak control.

questions.stem: Mumps virus enters the host through the respiratory tract and then replicates and disseminates. Which of the following groups of sites does it characteristically spread to?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Bone marrow, thymus, and the peripheral lymph node chains

choices.label: B
choices.text: Colon, gallbladder, adrenal glands, and the renal pelvis

choices.label: C
choices.text: Liver, spleen, kidneys, and the hepatic portal circulation

choices.label: D
choices.text: Parotid glands, central nervous system, pancreas, and testes

choices.label: E
choices.text: Skin, synovial joints, heart valves, and the aortic root

explanation.summary: After respiratory entry, mumps virus replicates and spreads to the parotid glands, CNS, pancreas, and testes.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that after entering the respiratory tract the virus replicates and spreads to the parotid glands, central nervous system, pancreas, and testes. This tissue tropism explains the classic parotitis as well as the complications of aseptic meningitis, encephalitis, and orchitis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Mumps is not described as a primary marrow or thymic pathogen.
whyWrongByChoice.B: These abdominal organs other than the pancreas are not typical mumps targets.
whyWrongByChoice.C: These organs are not the characteristic targets of mumps dissemination.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Skin, joints, and valves are not the sites mumps virus seeds after respiratory entry.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old woman with RT-PCR-confirmed mumps develops bilateral lower abdominal pain, and pelvic imaging shows inflammation of both ovaries. Which of the following complications of mumps has she developed?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Endometritis

choices.label: B
choices.text: Mastitis

choices.label: C
choices.text: Oophoritis

choices.label: D
choices.text: Orchitis

choices.label: E
choices.text: Salpingitis

explanation.summary: Oophoritis, inflammation of the ovaries, is a rare complication of mumps in females.
explanation.whyCorrect: Alongside the much more common orchitis in postpubertal males, mumps can rarely cause oophoritis, which is inflammation of the ovaries, and mastitis, which is swelling of the breast tissue. Inflammation of both ovaries during confirmed mumps is therefore oophoritis.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Endometritis involves the uterine lining and is not a described mumps complication.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Mastitis is swelling of breast tissue, not ovarian inflammation.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Orchitis is inflammation of the testis and does not apply to this patient.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Salpingitis involves the fallopian tubes and is not the complication described.

questions.stem: An unvaccinated 5-year-old girl has a temperature of 40.0°C (104.0°F) and has been ill for 2 days. Her clinician expects the earliest signs of measles. Which of the following triads is characteristic of this prodrome?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Chills, constipation, and confusion

choices.label: B
choices.text: Conjunctivitis, chorioretinitis, and cataracts

choices.label: C
choices.text: Coryza, costochondritis, and colitis

choices.label: D
choices.text: Cough, coryza, and conjunctivitis

choices.label: E
choices.text: Cough, cyanosis, and digital clubbing

explanation.summary: The earliest signs of measles are the 3Cs: cough, coryza, and conjunctivitis, usually with high fever.
explanation.whyCorrect: The earliest signs of measles are the 3Cs, meaning cough, coryza (runny nose), and conjunctivitis (irritated, watery eyes). Fever, which may be high at more than 104°F/40°C, is often present, and this prodrome precedes Koplik spots and the rash.

whyWrongByChoice.A: These nonspecific findings are not the measles prodrome and omit respiratory signs entirely.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Chorioretinitis and cataracts suggest congenital infection rather than acute measles.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Costochondritis and colitis are not features of the measles prodrome.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Cyanosis and clubbing indicate chronic hypoxemia rather than an acute measles prodrome.

questions.stem: A 6-year-old unvaccinated boy has had fever, cough, coryza, and conjunctivitis for 3 days. Examination of his oral cavity reveals a finding fairly specific for measles early in infection. Which of the following best describes it?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A gray pseudomembrane firmly adherent to the tonsils and posterior pharynx

choices.label: B
choices.text: A strawberry tongue with circumoral pallor and perioral desquamation

choices.label: C
choices.text: Grouped painless vesicles on an erythematous base at the vermilion border

choices.label: D
choices.text: Punched-out shallow ulcers on the soft palate appearing with the rash

choices.label: E
choices.text: Tiny white spots inside the mouth resembling grains of salt, often painful

explanation.summary: Koplik spots are tiny white, salt-grain-like spots in the mouth appearing 2 to 3 days after the initial measles symptoms.
explanation.whyCorrect: Koplik spots usually occur 2 to 3 days after the initial symptoms and are tiny white spots that appear in the mouth. They look like a grain of salt and can be painful, and they are fairly specific for measles early in the infection, before the rash appears.

whyWrongByChoice.A: An adherent pseudomembrane is a feature of bacterial pharyngeal disease, not measles.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Strawberry tongue with circumoral pallor is not part of the measles enanthem.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Vesicles at the vermilion border suggest a herpesvirus lesion rather than measles.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Koplik spots are raised white spots preceding the rash, not palatal ulcers appearing with it.

questions.stem: A 7-year-old unvaccinated child has 3 days of high fever, cough, coryza, and conjunctivitis. Careful examination of the buccal mucosa shows no white spots. Which of the following is the best interpretation of this finding?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Koplik spots appear only after the rash, so the examination was too early

choices.label: B
choices.text: Koplik spots appear only in vaccinated patients, so absence is expected here

choices.label: C
choices.text: Koplik spots are a feature of roseola, so their absence argues for measles

choices.label: D
choices.text: Koplik spots occur in about 80% of cases, so absence does not exclude measles

choices.label: E
choices.text: Measles is excluded, since Koplik spots are present in every case

explanation.summary: Koplik spots are present in roughly 80% of measles patients, so their absence does not rule out the diagnosis.
explanation.whyCorrect: Koplik spots are fairly specific for measles when present, but they are found in only about 80% of patients. A lack of Koplik spots therefore does not rule out measles, and in an unvaccinated child with the 3Cs and high fever the diagnosis must still be pursued with isolation and RT-PCR.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Koplik spots precede the rash, appearing 2 to 3 days after the initial symptoms.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Koplik spots are a feature of measles infection itself and are unrelated to vaccination status.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Koplik spots are associated with measles, not roseola.
whyWrongByChoice.E: They are not universal; roughly one in five measles patients never shows them.

questions.stem: An unvaccinated 4-year-old has had fever, cough, coryza, and conjunctivitis for 4 days. His parents are told that a rash is likely to appear shortly. Which of the following best describes the expected rash?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A maculopapular rash beginning on the face at the hairline and spreading downward

choices.label: B
choices.text: A sandpaper-like rash beginning in the axillae and the inguinal creases

choices.label: C
choices.text: Pink macules that begin on the trunk once the high fever has abruptly broken

choices.label: D
choices.text: Target lesions on the palms and soles that then spread toward the trunk

choices.label: E
choices.text: Vesicles appearing in crops at different stages of healing, beginning on the trunk

explanation.summary: The measles rash is maculopapular, begins on the face at the hairline about 3 to 5 days after symptom onset, and spreads downward.
explanation.whyCorrect: About 3 to 5 days after initial symptom onset a rash appears consisting of flat and raised red spots that first appear on the face at the hairline. It quickly spreads downward to the neck, trunk, arms, legs, and feet, and small lesions may join to form a larger confluent rash.

whyWrongByChoice.B: A sandpaper rash in the flexures is not the measles exanthem.
whyWrongByChoice.C: A truncal rash appearing after defervescence describes roseola.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Target lesions on palms and soles are not characteristic of measles.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Crops of vesicles at differing stages describe varicella, not measles.

questions.stem: A child with confirmed measles developed his rash yesterday. The health department is identifying the window during which he could transmit the virus to others. Which of the following best describes the period of contagiousness in measles?

choices.label: A
choices.text: From 2 days before symptoms begin until 5 days afterward

choices.label: B
choices.text: From 24 hours before fever begins until the rash fully fades

choices.label: C
choices.text: From about 4 days before the rash appears until 4 days afterward

choices.label: D
choices.text: Only during the days on which the rash is visible

choices.label: E
choices.text: Only during the first 24 hours of the initial fever

explanation.summary: Measles patients are contagious from about 4 days before rash onset until 4 days after the rash appears.
explanation.whyCorrect: Patients spread measles before they have the hallmark symptoms: they are contagious from about 4 days before rash onset until 4 days after it appears. This is concerning because the early symptoms are nonspecific and easily mistaken for other viral illnesses, so the virus spreads rapidly before the rash is recognized.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The 2-days-before to 5-days-after window describes mumps rather than measles.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Contagiousness starts days before the rash and ends about 4 days after it appears, not when it fades.
whyWrongByChoice.D: A large share of transmission occurs during the prodrome, before any rash is visible.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Infectivity spans roughly a week, not a single day of fever.

questions.stem: A measles case is confirmed in a waiting room shared by many unvaccinated children. Which of the following best characterizes how measles spreads and how efficiently it infects susceptible contacts?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Airborne spread, with about 90% of susceptible contacts becoming infected

choices.label: B
choices.text: Bloodborne spread, with about 30% of susceptible contacts becoming infected

choices.label: C
choices.text: Fecal-oral spread, with about 10% of household contacts becoming infected

choices.label: D
choices.text: Sexual transmission, with about 50% of susceptible partners becoming infected

choices.label: E
choices.text: Vector-borne spread, with about 5% of susceptible persons becoming infected

explanation.summary: Measles spreads predominantly by airborne droplets and has an attack rate of roughly 90% among susceptible contacts.
explanation.whyCorrect: Measles virus is extremely contagious and spreads predominantly through airborne droplets generated by coughing and sneezing; the virus can remain suspended in the air after the infected person has left the area, and contaminated surfaces can transmit it as well. With an attack rate of around 90% among susceptible contacts, it spreads rapidly before the hallmark rash is recognized.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Measles is a respiratory pathogen, not a bloodborne one.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Fecal-oral spread is not the route of measles transmission.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Measles is not a sexually transmitted infection.
whyWrongByChoice.E: No arthropod vector is involved in measles transmission.

questions.stem: A public health officer is preparing talking points for parents during a measles outbreak and wants to name the complication responsible for most measles deaths in children. Which of the following should be named?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Diarrhea with dehydration

choices.label: B
choices.text: Encephalitis

choices.label: C
choices.text: Otitis media

choices.label: D
choices.text: Pneumonia

choices.label: E
choices.text: Subacute sclerosing panencephalitis

explanation.summary: Pneumonia occurs in about 1 in 20 children with measles and is the most common cause of measles death.
explanation.whyCorrect: Among the complications of measles, pneumonia affects roughly 1 in 20 children and is the most common cause of death due to measles. Ear infections occur in about 1 in 10 children and diarrhea in fewer than 1 in 10, but neither drives mortality the way pneumonia does.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Diarrhea is reported in fewer than 1 in 10 patients and is not the leading fatal complication.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Encephalitis occurs in about 1 in 1000 children and can be fatal, but it is far less common than pneumonia.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Ear infections are the most frequent complication but are not a common cause of death.
whyWrongByChoice.E: SSPE is fatal but rare, developing years after infection rather than during the acute illness.

questions.stem: A clinician counsels the parents of an unvaccinated child about the risks of measles. Which of the following statements about the frequency of measles complications in children is correct?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Diarrhea occurs in about 1 in 100 children

choices.label: B
choices.text: Ear infection occurs in about 1 in 100 children

choices.label: C
choices.text: Encephalitis occurs in about 1 in 1000 children

choices.label: D
choices.text: Encephalitis occurs in about 1 in 20 children

choices.label: E
choices.text: Pneumonia occurs in about 1 in 1000 children

explanation.summary: Measles encephalitis occurs in roughly 1 in 1000 children and can cause death, hearing loss, or intellectual disability.
explanation.whyCorrect: The complication rates taught in this brick are ear infections in about 1 in 10 children, diarrhea in fewer than 1 in 10, pneumonia in 1 in 20, and encephalitis in 1 in 1000. Encephalitis at 1 in 1000 is the figure stated, and it can lead to death, hearing loss, or intellectual disabilities.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Diarrhea is reported in fewer than 1 in 10 children, not 1 in 100.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Ear infections are far more common, occurring in about 1 in 10 children.
whyWrongByChoice.D: One in 20 is the pneumonia rate; encephalitis is roughly fifty times less common.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Pneumonia is much more frequent than this, affecting about 1 in 20 children.

questions.stem: A 12-year-old boy is evaluated for 6 months of personality change and worsening memory, now accompanied by myoclonic jerks, ataxia, and seizures. He was never vaccinated and had a febrile illness with a descending rash at 11 months of age, from which he fully recovered. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Acute disseminated encephalomyelitis two weeks after a rash

choices.label: B
choices.text: Acute measles encephalitis occurring within days of the rash

choices.label: C
choices.text: Congenital rubella syndrome presenting in late childhood

choices.label: D
choices.text: Reye syndrome triggered by aspirin during a viral illness

choices.label: E
choices.text: Subacute sclerosing panencephalitis from persistent measles virus

explanation.summary: SSPE is a rare, fatal late complication of measles marked by apparent recovery followed by progressive neurodegeneration years later.
explanation.whyCorrect: SSPE is characterized by initial recovery from measles followed by progressive neurodegeneration typically 6 to 10 years later, and risk is higher in children infected before age 2. The pathology is due to persistence of virus along with chronic inflammation, and early behavioral changes and memory loss are followed by seizures, myoclonus, ataxia, and eventually dementia and death.

whyWrongByChoice.A: ADEM is a monophasic demyelinating illness within weeks of infection, not a progressive years-later decline.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Acute measles encephalitis occurs during or just after the acute illness, not a decade later.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Congenital rubella syndrome is present from birth and follows in-utero infection.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Reye syndrome is an acute encephalopathy with hepatic dysfunction, not a slow neurodegeneration.

questions.stem: An 11-month-old girl had 4 days of sudden high fever to 40.0°C (104.0°F) with irritability. The fever resolved today and she developed a pink maculopapular rash on the trunk that is spreading to her neck and extremities. She has had no cough, runny nose, or red eyes. Which of the following is the most likely causal organism?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Human herpesvirus 6

choices.label: B
choices.text: Measles virus

choices.label: C
choices.text: Mumps virus

choices.label: D
choices.text: Parainfluenza virus type 1

choices.label: E
choices.text: Varicella-zoster virus

explanation.summary: Roseola, caused by HHV-6 or HHV-7, produces high fever that resolves before a truncal rash appears, distinguishing it from measles.
explanation.whyCorrect: Roseola is characterized by a sudden high fever of 39 to 40°C lasting 3 to 5 days, often with irritability; once the fever resolves the child develops a pink maculopapular rash that starts on the trunk and spreads to the neck and extremities. Measles instead begins with a prodrome of fever, cough, coryza, and conjunctivitis followed by Koplik spots and a rash that starts on the face and moves downward while fever persists.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Measles requires the 3Cs prodrome and produces a face-first descending rash while the child is still febrile.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Mumps causes parotid swelling rather than a generalized maculopapular rash.
whyWrongByChoice.D: PIV-1 causes croup with a barking cough and stridor, not a febrile exanthem.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Varicella produces pruritic vesicles in crops rather than a pink maculopapular rash after defervescence.

questions.stem: The parents of a healthy 12-month-old ask what is actually in the MMR vaccine their pediatrician has recommended. Which of the following best describes its contents?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A chemically inactivated measles virus toxoid

choices.label: B
choices.text: Inactivated whole measles and mumps virions

choices.label: C
choices.text: Live attenuated measles, mumps, and rubella viruses

choices.label: D
choices.text: Measles messenger RNA in lipid nanoparticles

choices.label: E
choices.text: Purified measles surface glycoprotein subunits

explanation.summary: All U.S.-licensed measles and mumps vaccines contain live attenuated measles, mumps, and rubella viruses, hence the name MMR.
explanation.whyCorrect: Every measles and mumps vaccine licensed for use in the U.S. contains live, attenuated measles, mumps, and rubella viruses and is therefore termed MMR. Some preparations add further targets, such as MMRV, which also contains live attenuated varicella-zoster virus.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Toxoid vaccines target bacterial exotoxins; measles virus produces no such toxin.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The licensed product uses live attenuated virus, not inactivated whole virions.
whyWrongByChoice.D: MMR is not an mRNA vaccine.
whyWrongByChoice.E: MMR is not a purified subunit vaccine.

questions.stem: An unvaccinated 30-year-old man shared a household with a person who was diagnosed with measles 2 days ago. He is asymptomatic. Which of the following is the most appropriate management for this exposure?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A routine third dose of MMR vaccine given after 28 days

choices.label: B
choices.text: MMR vaccine or immune globulin as post-exposure prophylaxis

choices.label: C
choices.text: Observation only, since post-exposure prophylaxis is ineffective in measles

choices.label: D
choices.text: Oral acyclovir for 10 days beginning immediately

choices.label: E
choices.text: Varicella-zoster immune globulin given within 96 hours

explanation.summary: After a measles exposure, post-exposure prophylaxis with MMR or immune globulin is used rather than a routine third dose.
explanation.whyCorrect: For most patients the vaccine provides lifelong immunity to measles and rubella, so a routine third dose is not part of measles management. In the event of measles exposure, post-exposure prophylaxis with MMR or immune globulin is used instead, which is what an unvaccinated household contact should receive.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A third dose applies to mumps outbreak settings, not to measles post-exposure management.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Post-exposure prophylaxis is specifically recommended after measles exposure and is not futile.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Acyclovir treats herpesvirus infections and has no activity against measles virus.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Varicella-zoster immune globulin targets varicella exposure, not measles.

questions.stem: A virology laboratory characterizes the rotavirus particle recovered from the stool of an infant with vomiting and watery diarrhea. Which of the following best describes the structure and genome of this virus and the other members of its family?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Double-stranded DNA genome, nonenveloped, icosahedral capsid

choices.label: B
choices.text: Double-stranded RNA genome, enveloped, helical capsid

choices.label: C
choices.text: Double-stranded RNA genome, nonenveloped, icosahedral capsid

choices.label: D
choices.text: Single-stranded RNA genome, enveloped, icosahedral capsid

choices.label: E
choices.text: Single-stranded RNA genome, nonenveloped, helical capsid

explanation.summary: Reoviridae, the family containing rotavirus, are nonenveloped icosahedral viruses with a double-stranded RNA genome.
explanation.whyCorrect: Reoviridae store their genetic information as complementary strands of double-stranded RNA rather than as a single strand. Like Caliciviridae and Matonaviridae, they are nonenveloped and have an icosahedral capsule. The defining difference from those two families is the double-stranded, segmented nature of the reovirus genome.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Reoviruses store their genetic information as RNA, not as DNA.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The genome is correct, but reoviruses are nonenveloped and the capsid is icosahedral, not helical.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Reoviruses are not single-stranded RNA viruses and they carry no lipid envelope.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Reoviruses are not single-stranded RNA viruses, and their capsid is icosahedral rather than helical.

questions.stem: Norovirus and rubella virus are assigned to different viral families, yet the two are discussed together because they share several basic features. Which of the following features is shared by members of Caliciviridae and Matonaviridae?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A double-stranded RNA genome inside an icosahedral capsid

choices.label: B
choices.text: A helical nucleocapsid surrounded by a host-derived lipid bilayer

choices.label: C
choices.text: A negative-sense single-stranded RNA genome with an envelope

choices.label: D
choices.text: A positive-sense single-stranded RNA genome with no envelope

choices.label: E
choices.text: A segmented genome that permits genetic reassortment

explanation.summary: Caliciviridae and Matonaviridae are both nonenveloped, icosahedral, positive-sense single-stranded RNA viruses.
explanation.whyCorrect: These two families are presented together precisely because their characteristics overlap so closely. Both store their genetic information as (+)ssRNA, both are nonenveloped, and both have an icosahedral capsule. Reoviridae shares the nonenveloped icosahedral shape but differs in having a double-stranded, segmented genome.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A double-stranded RNA genome is the hallmark of Reoviridae; these two families carry single-stranded RNA.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Both families have an icosahedral capsule and lack a lipid envelope entirely.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Neither family is enveloped, and neither carries a negative-sense genome.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A segmented genome and reassortment are features of Reoviridae, not of Caliciviridae or Matonaviridae.

questions.stem: Surveillance identifies a rotavirus strain whose genome carries pieces derived from two different parent strains that were circulating in the same community. Which feature of this virus best explains how the new strain arose?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Its capsid proteins are acquired from the host cell membrane as the particle buds out

choices.label: B
choices.text: Its envelope glycoproteins accumulate point mutations gradually over successive seasons

choices.label: C
choices.text: Its genome is divided into separate dsRNA segments that can be exchanged during coinfection

choices.label: D
choices.text: Its polymerase copies the genome through a DNA intermediate that integrates into the host

choices.label: E
choices.text: Its positive-sense RNA is translated directly into one large polyprotein that is then cleaved

explanation.summary: Rotavirus has a segmented dsRNA genome, so coinfecting strains can swap segments and produce novel variants through reassortment.
explanation.whyCorrect: The reovirus genome is broken into 10 to 12 different dsRNA pieces. When two strains infect the same cell, the virus can mix up pieces of its genome and produce novel variants, a process called genetic reassortment. This is why rotavirus shows high genetic diversity and why new strains continue to emerge.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Rotavirus is nonenveloped and does not acquire host membrane during release.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Rotavirus has no envelope, and gradual point mutation does not explain a genome built from two parents.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Rotavirus is an RNA virus that does not use a DNA intermediate or integrate into host DNA.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A single translated polyprotein does not create hybrid genomes drawn from two parent strains.

questions.stem: A student reviewing viral taxonomy notes that rubella virus was originally grouped with the togaviruses but was recently reclassified. Rubella virus is now the only medically significant member of which of the following families?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Adenoviridae

choices.label: B
choices.text: Caliciviridae

choices.label: C
choices.text: Matonaviridae

choices.label: D
choices.text: Reoviridae

choices.label: E
choices.text: Togaviridae

explanation.summary: Rubella virus is the only medically significant member of Matonaviridae, having been recently moved out of Togaviridae.
explanation.whyCorrect: Matonaviridae contains a single virus of clinical importance, rubella virus, the cause of rubella. Rubella was originally part of the Togaviridae family but was recently reclassified into Matonaviridae. Its structure, (+)ssRNA and nonenveloped with an icosahedral capsule, is why it is taught alongside Caliciviridae.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Adenoviridae includes enteric adenovirus, a separate cause of watery diarrhea.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Caliciviridae contains norovirus and sapovirus, both causes of gastroenteritis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Reoviridae contains rotavirus and is defined by a segmented dsRNA genome.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Togaviridae is the family rubella was moved out of, not its current assignment.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old woman develops abrupt nausea, vomiting, and watery nonbloody diarrhea on the fourth day of a cruise. Twenty-two other passengers and several crew members have reported the same illness within the past 36 hours, and most recover within 2 days. Which of the following is the most likely causative agent?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Enterotoxigenic Escherichia coli

choices.label: B
choices.text: Norovirus

choices.label: C
choices.text: Rotavirus

choices.label: D
choices.text: Rubella virus

choices.label: E
choices.text: Sapovirus

explanation.summary: Norovirus is the most common cause of diarrhea on cruise ships and the leading cause of acute viral gastroenteritis overall.
explanation.whyCorrect: Explosive, rapidly spreading vomiting and watery diarrhea in a closed setting such as a cruise ship is the classic norovirus pattern. Norovirus is the most common cause of acute gastroenteritis and the most common cause of diarrhea on cruise ships, and illness is short-lived and self-limiting.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Enterotoxigenic E. coli causes travelers' diarrhea through heat-labile and heat-stable toxins, not this outbreak pattern.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Rotavirus is primarily a disease of young children and is far less likely in an adult shipboard outbreak.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Rubella causes a rash illness spread by respiratory droplets and does not cause watery diarrhea.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Sapovirus causes an identical syndrome but the large majority of clinical cases occur in children under 5.

questions.stem: A public health officer is asked how much of the annual United States norovirus burden is actually attributable to cruise ships, since shipboard outbreaks dominate news coverage. Although norovirus is the most common cause of diarrhea on cruise ships, cruise ship outbreaks account for approximately what proportion of reported norovirus infections each year?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Less than 0.01%

choices.label: B
choices.text: About 1%

choices.label: C
choices.text: About 15%

choices.label: D
choices.text: About 35%

choices.label: E
choices.text: About 58%

explanation.summary: Cruise ship outbreaks are highly visible but represent only about 1% of reported norovirus infections annually.
explanation.whyCorrect: Most of the time a norovirus outbreak is reported in the media, it is on a cruise ship, which distorts perception of where transmission occurs. Norovirus is indeed the most common cause of diarrhea on cruise ships, but shipboard outbreaks account for only 1% of the total reported cases of norovirus infection annually.

whyWrongByChoice.A: This understates the shipboard contribution, which is on the order of 1%.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Cruise ships account for a far smaller share than this; the great majority of cases are community acquired.
whyWrongByChoice.D: No more than a small fraction of annual norovirus cases are linked to cruise ships.
whyWrongByChoice.E: 58% is the share of United States foodborne illness caused by norovirus, not the cruise ship share.

questions.stem: An epidemiologist reviewing United States foodborne illness data notes that a single viral agent accounts for the majority of cases. Norovirus alone is responsible for approximately what percentage of foodborne illness in the United States?

explanation.summary: Norovirus causes roughly 58% of foodborne illness in the United States.
explanation.whyCorrect: Most cases of acute gastroenteritis are caused by viruses, and norovirus is the single most common cause. Noroviruses alone are responsible for 58% of foodborne illnesses in the United States, which is why food handling and hand hygiene are central to control.

whyWrongByChoice.A: 1% is the share of annual norovirus cases traced to cruise ship outbreaks.
whyWrongByChoice.B: This substantially understates the norovirus share of foodborne illness.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Norovirus accounts for well over a third of foodborne illness in the United States.
whyWrongByChoice.E: No single agent accounts for nine-tenths of foodborne illness.

questions.stem: A county health department is deciding when to increase staffing for viral gastroenteritis surveillance. Reported norovirus outbreaks in the United States, which number roughly 2,500 each year, reach their peak during which of the following months?

choices.label: A
choices.text: April

choices.label: B
choices.text: August

choices.label: C
choices.text: January

choices.label: D
choices.text: June

choices.label: E
choices.text: October

explanation.summary: Norovirus outbreaks in the United States number about 2,500 per year and peak around January.
explanation.whyCorrect: Surveillance data on average reported norovirus outbreaks by month show a pronounced winter peak, with cases peaking around January and falling to a trough in the summer months. Nonfoodborne transmission accounts for most of that winter surge.

whyWrongByChoice.A: April falls on the declining limb of the outbreak curve, well below the winter peak.
whyWrongByChoice.B: August is near the annual minimum for reported outbreaks.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Summer months represent the annual low point for reported norovirus outbreaks.
whyWrongByChoice.E: October is on the rising limb but well below the January peak.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old man had laboratory-confirmed norovirus gastroenteritis 14 months ago and now presents with an identical illness after attending a catered event. Which of the following best explains why he was susceptible again?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Many strains circulate, and immunity to one does not protect against another

choices.label: B
choices.text: Prior mucosal immunity is erased by each subsequent gastrointestinal illness

choices.label: C
choices.text: The current illness is a relapse of the original inadequately treated infection

choices.label: D
choices.text: The viral genome integrates into host DNA and is re-expressed months later

choices.label: E
choices.text: The virus establishes lifelong latency and reactivates during periods of stress

explanation.summary: There are many norovirus strains, and infection with one does not confer immunity to another, so repeat infections occur throughout life.
explanation.whyCorrect: Norovirus exists as many different strains. Infection with one does not convey immunity to another, so repeated norovirus infections throughout a person's life are possible and expected. This is also why prevention depends on hand washing, avoiding raw or undercooked shellfish, and washing produce rather than on acquired immunity.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Unrelated gastrointestinal illness does not erase immunity to a previously encountered strain.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Norovirus infection is self-limiting and has no specific treatment, so relapse of an untreated case is not the mechanism.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Norovirus is an RNA virus and does not integrate into host DNA.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Norovirus does not establish latency; each episode is a new infection.

questions.stem: During a norovirus outbreak in a long-term care facility, staff have been using an alcohol-based hand rub between residents, and transmission has continued unabated. Which property of norovirus best explains why this measure is inadequate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The virus forms environmentally resistant endospores on the skin surface

choices.label: B
choices.text: The virus has no lipid envelope, so the sanitizer has no membrane to disrupt

choices.label: C
choices.text: The virus is shed only in vomitus, to which hand rubs are not routinely applied

choices.label: D
choices.text: The virus replicates within host phagocytes, which shields it from topical antiseptics

choices.label: E
choices.text: The virus requires a contact time longer than 5 minutes with any agent

explanation.summary: Alcohol sanitizers work by disrupting a lipid envelope, which norovirus lacks, making it notoriously resistant to them.
explanation.whyCorrect: Enveloped viruses have a lipid membrane that alcohol-based sanitizers disrupt, inactivating the virus. Norovirus is nonenveloped, so there is no membrane to dissolve and the particle is far more resistant. This is why the CDC recommends hand washing with soap and water, which physically removes virus, rather than alcohol hand rubs.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Viruses do not form endospores; that is a bacterial survival structure.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Norovirus is shed in stool as well as vomitus and spreads by the fecal-oral route.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Norovirus infects the gastrointestinal tract rather than hiding inside phagocytes.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The 5-minute contact time applies to bleach left on surfaces, not to a universal requirement of all agents.

questions.stem: After a norovirus outbreak in a school cafeteria, the environmental services team asks how to decontaminate the hard surfaces in the kitchen. Which of the following is the recommended approach?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Apply a quaternary ammonium cleaner and rinse it off immediately afterward

choices.label: B
choices.text: Apply bleach and leave it on the surface for at least 5 minutes

choices.label: C
choices.text: Heat all surfaces and utensils to 145 degrees Fahrenheit for one minute

choices.label: D
choices.text: Use a low-concentration bleach solution and wipe it away at once

choices.label: E
choices.text: Wipe surfaces with 70% isopropyl alcohol and allow them to air dry

explanation.summary: Surface decontamination for norovirus requires bleach left in contact with the surface for at least 5 minutes.
explanation.whyCorrect: Norovirus is highly resistant to many common disinfectants, to heat up to 145 degrees Fahrenheit, and even to low-concentration bleach solutions. The CDC recommendation is therefore to leave bleach on surfaces for at least 5 minutes, along with hand washing using soap and water, cooking shellfish thoroughly, and washing clothes in hot water.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Norovirus resists many common disinfectants, and immediate rinsing eliminates any contact time.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Norovirus is resistant to heat up to 145 degrees Fahrenheit, so this temperature is not reliable.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Norovirus resists low-concentration bleach, and wiping it away at once removes the needed contact time.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Alcohol works on enveloped viruses; nonenveloped norovirus resists it.

questions.stem: Five members of a family become ill after a shared church potluck. Vomiting and watery diarrhea began in all five within a narrow window after the meal, and norovirus is later confirmed. Which of the following best represents the usual incubation period of this virus?

choices.label: A
choices.text: 1 to 3 hours

choices.label: B
choices.text: 4 to 7 days

choices.label: C
choices.text: 4 to 8 hours

choices.label: D
choices.text: 12 to 23 days

choices.label: E
choices.text: 12 to 48 hours

explanation.summary: Norovirus has a relatively short incubation period averaging 12 to 48 hours.
explanation.whyCorrect: Once infected with norovirus, the incubation period is relatively short, on average 12 to 48 hours. The virus then infects the gastrointestinal tract and produces acute vomiting and watery diarrhea. This short interval is part of why point-source outbreaks appear so explosive.

whyWrongByChoice.A: This is far shorter than the norovirus incubation period.
whyWrongByChoice.B: This is longer than the usual norovirus incubation period; sapovirus runs 1 to 4 days.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Norovirus symptoms typically begin later than this, on average 12 to 48 hours after exposure.
whyWrongByChoice.D: 12 to 23 days is the incubation period of rubella, not norovirus.

questions.stem: A previously healthy 27-year-old woman has 2 days of vomiting and large-volume watery nonbloody stools, and norovirus RNA is detected in her stool. Which of the following best describes the mechanism producing her symptoms?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A preformed heat-stable enterotoxin acting directly on gastric afferent nerves

choices.label: B
choices.text: Destruction of intestinal lymphoid tissue with loss of the mucosal barrier

choices.label: C
choices.text: Infection of the gastrointestinal tract causing malabsorption and altered motility

choices.label: D
choices.text: Invasion of the colonic mucosa with ulceration and inflammatory exudate formation

choices.label: E
choices.text: Secretory chloride loss driven by irreversible adenylate cyclase activation

explanation.summary: Norovirus infects the gastrointestinal tract and produces malabsorption and altered gut motility, which drives acute vomiting and diarrhea.
explanation.whyCorrect: After a short incubation, the virus infects the gastrointestinal tract and leads to malabsorption and altered gut motility. This combination triggers the acute vomiting and watery, nonbloody diarrhea that characterize the illness, along with abdominal cramps, nausea, low-grade fever, and malaise.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Norovirus causes disease by infecting gut epithelium, not through a preformed toxin.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Norovirus does not act by destroying gut lymphoid tissue.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Mucosal invasion with inflammatory exudate produces bloody or inflammatory diarrhea, not the watery nonbloody stool of norovirus.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Irreversible adenylate cyclase activation describes a bacterial toxin mechanism, not viral gastroenteritis.

questions.stem: A 71-year-old man with confirmed norovirus gastroenteritis has had 12 hours of vomiting and diarrhea. He is orthostatic with dry mucous membranes and cannot keep liquids down. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Empiric azithromycin with loperamide

choices.label: B
choices.text: Intravenous vancomycin and metronidazole

choices.label: C
choices.text: Oral ribavirin for a 5-day course

choices.label: D
choices.text: Pooled immunoglobulin given intravenously

choices.label: E
choices.text: Supportive care with intravenous rehydration

explanation.summary: Norovirus is self-limiting and treated supportively; dehydration is the principal risk and may require intravenous rehydration.
explanation.whyCorrect: Cases of norovirus are self-limiting and require only supportive therapy, and complications are rare. The biggest risk to patients is dehydration, and severe disease is usually seen in the elderly, children, and immunocompromised populations. In those patients, monitoring and intravenous rehydration may be required.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Antibiotics do not treat a viral infection, and the priority in this dehydrated patient is fluid replacement.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Antibacterial therapy has no role in viral gastroenteritis.
whyWrongByChoice.C: There is no specific antiviral treatment for norovirus.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Immunoglobulin is not a treatment for norovirus infection.

questions.stem: An outbreak investigator sends patient stool samples and environmental swabs from a banquet hall to the state laboratory to confirm norovirus as the source. Which of the following is the preferred test, and how sensitive is it?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Gram stain of stool, which detects heavy viral shedding

choices.label: B
choices.text: Latex agglutination, which requires 10,000 or more copies

choices.label: C
choices.text: RT-PCR, which can detect as few as 10 to 100 viral copies

choices.label: D
choices.text: Serum IgG titer, which rises within 24 hours of onset

choices.label: E
choices.text: Stool culture on selective media, read at 48 hours

explanation.summary: RT-PCR detecting viral RNA is the preferred norovirus test and is sensitive down to 10 to 100 copies.
explanation.whyCorrect: The preferred method to detect norovirus is detection of viral RNA by RT-PCR. The test is very sensitive and can detect as few as 10 to 100 copies of the virus. Samples from a patient such as vomit or stool, or from a potentially contaminated area such as water, food, or the environment, can all be screened effectively.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Gram stain visualizes bacteria; viral particles cannot be seen this way.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The preferred assay is RT-PCR, and its detection limit is far lower than this.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Serology does not identify the source of an acute point-source outbreak.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Viruses are not recovered on bacterial stool culture media.

questions.stem: A 40-year-old man develops abrupt vomiting and watery diarrhea 30 hours after a restaurant meal, and three dining companions who shared the same dishes are also ill. Which of the following food exposures is the most likely source of his norovirus infection?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Fried rice that had been reheated once

choices.label: B
choices.text: Home-canned green beans in the appetizer

choices.label: C
choices.text: Raw oysters served on the half shell

choices.label: D
choices.text: Soft cheese made from unpasteurized milk

choices.label: E
choices.text: Unpasteurized apple cider served at the table

explanation.summary: Consuming raw or undercooked shellfish is a classic route of norovirus transmission.
explanation.whyCorrect: Common methods of norovirus transmission include direct contact with an infected person, eating contaminated food or drink, touching contaminated surfaces and then the mouth, and consuming raw or undercooked shellfish. Cooking shellfish thoroughly is one of the specific CDC recommendations for preventing norovirus illness.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Reheated rice is not one of the norovirus exposures described for this virus.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Home-canned vegetables are not a recognized norovirus vehicle.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Raw-milk cheese is not among the exposures emphasized for norovirus transmission.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Unpasteurized cider is not among the shellfish and contaminated food exposures highlighted for norovirus.

questions.stem: An outbreak of acute vomiting and watery diarrhea affects 14 children at a daycare center, nearly all of them younger than 5 years. Stool RT-PCR is negative for rotavirus and norovirus but positive for another member of Caliciviridae. Which of the following agents is responsible?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Cytomegalovirus

choices.label: B
choices.text: Measles virus

choices.label: C
choices.text: Rubella virus

choices.label: D
choices.text: Sapovirus

choices.label: E
choices.text: Zika virus

explanation.summary: Sapovirus is the other clinically relevant calicivirus and causes gastroenteritis mostly in children younger than 5.
explanation.whyCorrect: Like norovirus, sapovirus is a member of Caliciviridae and causes gastroenteritis. All age groups can be affected, but the majority of clinical cases occur in children under 5 years old, and the elderly and immunocompromised are also susceptible. Daycares, nursing homes, and schools are common places for outbreaks.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Cytomegalovirus is a TORCH pathogen and is not a member of Caliciviridae.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Measles virus causes rubeola, a distinct rash illness unrelated to Caliciviridae.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Rubella is a Matonaviridae member causing a rash illness, not gastroenteritis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Zika virus is a TORCH agent associated with microcephaly, not daycare gastroenteritis.

questions.stem: A 3-year-old boy at a daycare center develops acute onset of vomiting and watery diarrhea, and sapovirus is confirmed by RT-PCR. Which of the following is the usual incubation period of this virus?

choices.label: A
choices.text: 1 to 4 days

choices.label: B
choices.text: 3 to 6 weeks

choices.label: C
choices.text: 6 to 12 hours

choices.label: D
choices.text: 7 to 10 days

choices.label: E
choices.text: 12 to 23 days

explanation.summary: Sapovirus has an incubation period of 1 to 4 days, followed by acute onset of symptoms.
explanation.whyCorrect: Mirroring norovirus, sapovirus symptoms are usually mild and self-resolving with supportive care. Once infected, the incubation period is 1 to 4 days, with acute onset of symptoms that are identical to those of norovirus: vomiting and watery nonbloody diarrhea, abdominal cramps, nausea, low-grade fever, and malaise.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Sapovirus symptoms appear within days, not weeks.
whyWrongByChoice.C: This is shorter than the sapovirus incubation period.
whyWrongByChoice.D: 7 to 10 days is the interval over which rubella symptoms resolve, not the sapovirus incubation.
whyWrongByChoice.E: 12 to 23 days is the incubation period of rubella virus.

questions.stem: Two separate outbreaks of acute vomiting and watery diarrhea occur in the same city during the same week. The symptoms, severity, and duration of illness are identical in the two groups. Which of the following is required to determine whether norovirus or sapovirus caused each outbreak?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Careful review of the symptom pattern and clinical time course

choices.label: B
choices.text: Comparing the degree of dehydration between the two groups

choices.label: C
choices.text: Determining whether children or adults predominate in each group

choices.label: D
choices.text: Laboratory testing of patient specimens for viral RNA

choices.label: E
choices.text: Measuring the ratio of vomiting to diarrhea in each patient

explanation.summary: Norovirus and sapovirus cannot be separated on clinical grounds; detection of viral RNA is what identifies the agent.
explanation.whyCorrect: Norovirus and sapovirus cannot be distinguished based on clinical presentation alone, because their symptoms are identical. Laboratory testing, specifically detection of viral RNA, is used to determine which virus is the source of an outbreak. Since there is no specific treatment for either, identification serves outbreak investigation and rules out other causes of watery diarrhea such as E. coli.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The clinical presentations of these two viruses are indistinguishable, which is precisely the problem.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Both viruses are usually mild and self-limiting, with dehydration as the shared main risk.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Age skew is suggestive at best; sapovirus favors young children but does not spare adults.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The symptom mix does not differ between norovirus and sapovirus infection.

questions.stem: The parents of a 2-month-old infant ask about the rotavirus vaccine at a well-child visit. Which of the following best describes this vaccine?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A conjugated polysaccharide vaccine given subcutaneously

choices.label: B
choices.text: A live attenuated vaccine given orally

choices.label: C
choices.text: A messenger RNA vaccine given in two intramuscular doses

choices.label: D
choices.text: A recombinant subunit vaccine given intramuscularly

choices.label: E
choices.text: An inactivated whole-virus vaccine given intramuscularly

explanation.summary: The rotavirus vaccine is an oral, live attenuated vaccine available in two formulations that differ in the strains included.
explanation.whyCorrect: Aside from rigorous hygiene, rotavirus is prevented by vaccination. The rotavirus vaccine is an oral vaccine, and there are two main formulations that differ in the strains they include; both are live attenuated. Because it is live attenuated, severely immunocompromised patients should not receive it.

whyWrongByChoice.A: There is no polysaccharide component to the rotavirus vaccine.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The rotavirus vaccine is not an mRNA product and is not given intramuscularly.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The vaccine uses attenuated live virus rather than a recombinant subunit.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The rotavirus vaccine is live attenuated and is given by mouth, not by injection.

questions.stem: A pediatrician is reviewing the rotavirus immunization schedule with a new nurse. The first dose should be given before which age, and the series should be completed by which age?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Before 6 months; completed by 12 months

choices.label: B
choices.text: Before 6 weeks; completed by 6 months

choices.label: C
choices.text: Before 8 weeks; completed by 12 months

choices.label: D
choices.text: Before 12 months; completed by 24 months

choices.label: E
choices.text: Before 15 weeks; completed by 8 months

explanation.summary: Rotavirus vaccination should start before 15 weeks of age and the series should be finished before 8 months.
explanation.whyCorrect: It is recommended to start rotavirus vaccination before 15 weeks of age and to complete the series before 8 months. Keeping to this window matters because the vaccine protects 90% of children from hospitalization and 70% from disease of any kind, and because the burden of rotavirus falls heaviest on the youngest children.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Starting as late as 6 months falls outside the recommended window for the first dose.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Vaccination need not begin this early, and the completion deadline is later than 6 months.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The first dose window extends to 15 weeks, and the series is completed before 8 months.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Both the start and completion deadlines given here are far later than recommended.

questions.stem: A 5-month-old infant develops episodic crying with drawing up of the legs and bloody stools 6 days after receiving a dose of rotavirus vaccine. Imaging shows one segment of bowel telescoped into another. Approximately what is the risk of this complication among infants who receive the vaccine?

choices.label: D
choices.text: 1 in 200 to 1 in 500

explanation.summary: Intussusception is a very rare adverse effect of rotavirus vaccine, occurring in roughly 1 in 20,000 to 1 in 100,000 vaccinated infants.
explanation.whyCorrect: Although very rare, intussusception is a recognized side effect of the rotavirus vaccine. It is a type of bowel blockage in which the bowel folds into itself like a telescope, and it occurs in 1 in 20,000 to 1 in 100,000 infants who receive the vaccine. Surgery is sometimes needed to correct it.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The true rate is considerably lower than this.
whyWrongByChoice.B: This still overstates the risk relative to the reported 1 in 20,000 to 1 in 100,000 range.
whyWrongByChoice.D: This overstates the risk by orders of magnitude; the complication is described as very rare.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Roughly 1 in 6,000 is the frequency of encephalitis complicating rubella, not vaccine-associated intussusception.

questions.stem: A parent who is hesitant about immunization asks how well the rotavirus vaccine actually works. Which of the following best describes its protection?

choices.label: A
choices.text: About 50% against hospitalization and about 30% against disease of any kind

choices.label: B
choices.text: About 70% against hospitalization and about 50% against disease of any kind

choices.label: C
choices.text: About 90% against hospitalization and about 70% against disease of any kind

choices.label: D
choices.text: About 95% against hospitalization and about 95% against disease of any kind

choices.label: E
choices.text: Nearly 100% against hospitalization and about 90% against disease of any kind

explanation.summary: Rotavirus vaccine prevents about 90% of hospitalizations and about 70% of rotavirus disease of any severity.
explanation.whyCorrect: The vaccine protects 90% of children from hospitalization and 70% from disease of any kind overall. Side effects are usually mild. Rotavirus has high genetic diversity from reassortment and new strains keep emerging, but the vaccines cover the most common disease-causing strains and remain effective.

whyWrongByChoice.A: These figures are far below the reported effectiveness of the vaccine.
whyWrongByChoice.B: This understates protection against both hospitalization and overall disease.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Protection against disease of any kind is considerably lower than protection against hospitalization.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Nearly complete protection describes two doses of MMR against rubella, not rotavirus vaccine.

questions.stem: A 2-month-old infant is found on newborn screening to have severe combined immunodeficiency. The pediatric team decides to withhold the rotavirus vaccine. Which of the following is the reason for this decision?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The infant is below the minimum age for the first dose of the series

choices.label: B
choices.text: The vaccine contains inactivated virus and would provide no benefit here

choices.label: C
choices.text: The vaccine contains live attenuated virus, unsafe in profound immunocompromise

choices.label: D
choices.text: The vaccine is given orally and would be poorly absorbed in this infant

choices.label: E
choices.text: The vaccine's strain coverage excludes the strains circulating locally

explanation.summary: Rotavirus vaccine is live attenuated, so severely immunocompromised infants should not receive it.
explanation.whyCorrect: Both main formulations of the rotavirus vaccine are live attenuated. As with any attenuated vaccine, severely immunocompromised patients should not receive it, because the attenuated organism can still cause disease in a host without competent immunity. The same principle applies to the live-attenuated MMR vaccine.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A 2-month-old is within the recommended window, which begins before 15 weeks of age.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The vaccine contains live attenuated virus, not inactivated virus.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Oral administration is the normal route for this vaccine and is not the problem.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The available vaccines do cover the most common circulating strains and remain effective.

questions.stem: Four children aged 2 to 5 years who attend the same daycare present with a 3-day history of severe watery diarrhea, vomiting, and low-grade fever. None of the four has received any routine childhood vaccination because of parental preference, while the remaining fully vaccinated children at the daycare are well. Which of the following is the most likely etiologic agent?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Enterotoxigenic Escherichia coli

choices.label: B
choices.text: Norovirus

choices.label: C
choices.text: Rotavirus

choices.label: D
choices.text: Rubella virus

choices.label: E
choices.text: Sapovirus

explanation.summary: Illness confined to the unvaccinated children points to rotavirus, the only one of these gastroenteritis agents with a vaccine.
explanation.whyCorrect: Rotavirus is a common source of watery diarrhea in children, and vaccination provides substantial protection. The fact that only the children who have not received routine childhood vaccinations are ill, while their vaccinated peers are well, strongly indicates rotavirus. Symptoms lasting 3 days with vomiting and low-grade fever fit the expected 3 to 8 day course.

whyWrongByChoice.A: There is no routine childhood vaccine against enterotoxigenic E. coli.
whyWrongByChoice.B: There is no norovirus vaccine, so vaccination status would not separate the ill from the well children.
whyWrongByChoice.D: These children are at risk for rubella because they are unvaccinated, but rubella causes a rash illness, not watery diarrhea.
whyWrongByChoice.E: There is no sapovirus vaccine, so the vaccination pattern would not be explained.

questions.stem: A 14-month-old boy is exposed to a cousin with laboratory-confirmed rotavirus gastroenteritis. Which of the following best describes the expected onset and duration of illness if he becomes infected?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Onset at 10 to 14 days; duration about 3 days

choices.label: B
choices.text: Onset at 3 weeks; duration 2 to 3 weeks

choices.label: C
choices.text: Onset at 5 to 7 days; duration 1 to 2 days

choices.label: D
choices.text: Onset within 4 hours; duration 12 to 24 hours

choices.label: E
choices.text: Onset within 48 hours; duration 3 to 8 days

explanation.summary: Rotavirus symptoms usually begin within 48 hours of exposure and persist for 3 to 8 days.
explanation.whyCorrect: Symptoms of rotavirus usually begin within 48 hours after exposure and persist for 3 to 8 days. Clinically the illness is indistinguishable from norovirus and sapovirus, producing acute vomiting and watery nonbloody diarrhea, abdominal cramps, nausea, low-grade fever, and malaise.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A 10 to 14 day incubation does not fit rotavirus; that interval suggests a rash illness such as rubella.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Rotavirus illness begins within days, not weeks, and resolves within about a week.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Onset is faster than this, and rotavirus illness typically outlasts 2 days.
whyWrongByChoice.D: This onset is too rapid and the illness lasts considerably longer than a single day.

questions.stem: An unvaccinated 22-year-old returns from international travel with low-grade fever, a rash, and tender nodes behind the ears. Rubella virus is confirmed by RT-PCR. Which of the following is the usual route of transmission of this virus?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Bite of an infected Aedes species mosquito

choices.label: B
choices.text: Direct contact with ulcerating vesicular lesions

choices.label: C
choices.text: Fecal-oral spread from contaminated food or water

choices.label: D
choices.text: Percutaneous exposure to infected blood products

choices.label: E
choices.text: Respiratory droplets from an infected person

explanation.summary: Rubella is a moderate illness spread by respiratory droplets, unlike the fecal-orally transmitted gastroenteritis viruses in this brick.
explanation.whyCorrect: Rubella virus causes rubella, sometimes called German measles or 3-day measles, and it is a moderate illness spread by respiratory droplets. Rubella is no longer endemic in the United States because of routine MMR vaccination, so the cases that do occur are seen in travelers and the unvaccinated, roughly 10 per year.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Mosquito transmission applies to arboviruses such as Zika, not to rubella.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Ulcerating vesicular lesions are characteristic of HSV, another TORCH pathogen.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Fecal-oral spread is the route for norovirus, sapovirus, and rotavirus, not rubella.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Rubella is not a bloodborne infection.

questions.stem: A 19-year-old unvaccinated woman develops a mild fever, malaise, and a rash that is later attributed to rubella virus. Which of the following best describes the rash of rubella?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A maculopapular rash starting on the face and spreading downward

choices.label: B
choices.text: An eruption beginning on the lower legs and moving upward

choices.label: C
choices.text: Confluent plaques that desquamate after about 3 weeks

choices.label: D
choices.text: Painful targetoid lesions concentrated on the palms and soles

choices.label: E
choices.text: Vesicular lesions appearing in successive crops over the trunk
